Asher told CNN in a February email: “DC crime fell substantially in 2025 but it was not anywhere near the safest city in America.” Of the 50 largest cities tracked by Asher’s Real-Time Crime Index , he said, “DC had the 9th highest murder rate and 12th highest violent crime rate in 2025 of the 50 largest cities in the Real-Time Crime Index.” Trump’s intervention happened in August ; in the period running from August through December 2025, Asher said, “DC had the 18th highest murder rate and 17th highest violent crime rate.” “Even in the post-intervention period, DC’s murder rate was more than 5 times higher than San Diego and San Jose and roughly 3 times higher than cities like San Francisco, New York, and Seattle,” he said. And he added that crime in the capital was “falling considerably” prior to Trump’s Guard deployment, and continued to fall after the deployment, “in a way that is hard to determine the impact of the deployment itself.” Trump could have accurately said the capital has had some prolonged recent stretches without a murder; the Washington Post reported that it began the year with a highly unusual three-week period with no homicides. But that stretch ended January 21. Trump repeated his claim that Somali residents of Minnesota have committed $19 billion in fraud, saying: “There’s been no more stunning example than Minnesota, where members of the Somali community have pillaged an estimated $19 billion from the American taxpayer. We have all the information, and in actuality, the number is much higher than that.” It’s possible this “$19 billion” figure will be proven true, but nothing close to that figure has been proven to date. In December, a federal prosecutor, Joseph Thompson, claimed that “half or more” of $18 billion in federal funds billed by 14 Medicaid services in Minnesota deemed at high risk for fraud – and now under a third-party audit ordered by Gov. Tim Walz – might be fraudulent. But $9 billion is not $19 billion, Thompson didn’t say all of the possible fraud was committed by Somali residents, and Walz’s administration challenged Thompson’s claim. One Walz administration official said in December that they had “evidence of tens of millions of dollars in fraud to this point,” not $9 billion; Walz himself said, “You should be equally outraged about $1 or whatever that number is, but they’re using that number without the proof behind it.” And Thompson – who resigned in January amid tension with the Trump administration over its handling of an ICE officer fatally shooting Renée Good – made clear at the time that the “half or more” comment was an early estimate rather than a firm number. The top official in charge of the federal government’s disaster response has taken to social media to double down on his claim that he’s experienced “teleportation” – an experience he insists was real and connected to his religious beliefs – while also saying his remarks have been taken out of context. “Haters gonna hate,” Gregg Phillips, a senior official at the Federal Emergency Management Agency, wrote in one comment defending himself earlier this month. “I know what I’ve experienced,” he wrote in another post , in what appeared to be a poem where he refers to people ridiculing what they don’t understand and to Jesus Christ rising from the dead. CNN previously reported that Phillips, who serves as associate administrator for the Office of Response and Recovery at FEMA, described in a podcast last year multiple episodes in which he said he was suddenly teleported miles away — including once to a Waffle House roughly 50 miles from where he had been. CNN also reported Phillips had a history of violent rhetoric towards public officials. He said in a podcast last year that he’d like to punch “that b*tch” in the mouth, referring to former President Joe Biden who had just left office, before adding, “He deserves to die.” In another podcast, Phillips said that migrants were coming to kill Americans while warning people to be armed. The appointment of Phillips had previously drawn skepticism from some career FEMA officials over his lack of experience and past comments spreading election fraud conspiracy theories, though several told CNN earlier this year that his work during major storms had tempered some of those concerns. Phillips’ recent comments come as he was taken off the schedule to testify last week at a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on the impacts of the partial shutdown of DHS, which oversees FEMA. Neither FEMA nor Phillips responded to a comment request from CNN asking why he did not attend. On Truth Social, the social media platform founded by President Donald Trump, Phillips described the teleportation incidents as tied to a “spiritual journey” during a period he said he was undergoing cancer treatments and pointed to biblical examples of supernatural events. “I have no regrets for my words nor my faith in my Savior, Jesus Christ,” Phillips wrote after CNN’s report, while arguing his comments were taken out of context. “The Bible has many examples of the power of God.” At the hearing, Rep. Bennie Thompson, the ranking House Democrat on the committee, said Phillips’ appointment raised “serious concerns.” “Mr. Phillips reportedly claims to have been involuntarily teleported multiple times, including once to a Waffle House in Georgia,” Thompson said. Pointing to Phillips’ comments about Biden, Thompson added: “That kind of violent rhetoric and wild conspiracy theories are troubling for someone who holds a leadership position at DHS.” Democratic Rep. Tim Kennedy described Phillips as “wildly unfit for his role as head of FEMA response and recovery,” citing “his violent statements about former President Biden” and “deeply troubling bigoted comments about immigrants.” Kennedy added: “All of which, to me, makes him wholly disqualified to hold his position on its own — but only to be outdone by his claims of being teleported to a Waffle House.” On Truth Social, in other posts responding to criticism, Phillips also shared a passage from the New Testament Book of Acts in which the Holy Spirit “snatched” away the apostle Phillip after a baptism on a road between Jerusalem and Gaza, with the text then describing him as appearing in the city of Azotus miles away. In another exchange on the platform, Phillips was asked whether he had personally experienced such a phenomenon. “Yes,” he replied , adding that “the Bible calls it transported or translated.” Phillips added that the comments on teleporting to the Waffle House were taken out of context, though he has declined to say how. “Out of context,” he wrote.  “This was a discussion during medical treatments in what we believed to be the last 3 months of my life. Some of the episodes we couldn’t show. The other translation was to a church.” Neither FEMA nor Phillips responded to multiple requests for comment on what part of CNN’s past reporting was taken out of context. In previously reported podcast appearances, Phillips described multiple incidents in which he said he was physically teleported, calling the experiences frightening and uncontrollable. “I was with my boys one time and I was telling them I was gonna go to Waffle House and get Waffle House. And I ended up at a Waffle House – this was in Georgia and I end up at a Waffle House like 50 miles away from where I was,” Phillips said in a January 2025 podcast episode. “It was real,” Phillips said, adding at another point: “Teleporting is no fun.” In the same discussion, Phillips also described another episode in which he said his vehicle was “lifted up” while he was driving and carried dozens of miles before being set down near a church.

President Donald Trump was swiftly escorted off the stage by Secret Service after shots were fired at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner in Washington, DC, on Saturday. Trump, Vice President JD Vance and members of the president's Cabinet are all safe. At a news conference following the incident, the president said the suspect was “taken down” by members of the Secret Service. Several US Secret Service agents yelled, “shots fired” during the event, which was being held at the Washington Hilton. CNN’s Wolf Blitzer was outside the main ballroom when he saw a gunman opening fire on the ground just a few feet away. He was among the dozens of attendees who took cover as law enforcement swarmed.

The heartland Democrat is making a comeback. Democrats this year are seriously contesting more races for governor and senator across the industrial Midwest and Farm Belt than at any point since the early years of Barack Obama’s presidency. The party still faces substantial skepticism from many heartland voters, especially on cultural issues, but frustration over the high cost of living has loosened the GOP’s grip on the middle of the country. The two parties are locked in competitive governor and/or Senate races not only in traditional battlegrounds such as Michigan and Wisconsin, but also in states that moved solidly red since Obama’s era — including Ohio, Iowa, and maybe even Nebraska and Kansas. “These states are all on the playing field,” says David Kochel, a longtime GOP strategist who has worked in Iowa and elsewhere across the region. Each race presents some unique local dynamics. But the common theme is the erosion of President Donald Trump’s support in states that almost all went in his favor in 2024 — including a notable decline among the working-class White and rural voters who represent such an outsize share of the electorate in these places. “They were sold a bill of goods in 2024 that their life was going to get easier — and it’s got a hell of a lot harder,” says Eva Kemp, director of paid media and partnerships at American Bridge, a Democratic advocacy group that focuses on recapturing working-class voters. Across this broad battlefield, the key races may turn on whether Republicans can remind conservative-leaning voters of why they have grown so skeptical of Democrats since Obama’s day — or if Democrats can keep them focused on their immediate disenchantment with Trump and the economy. “In the first Trump term what you would see in rural areas is people whispering to you, like, ‘I don’t want anyone to know I’m a Democrat,’” says Heidi Heitkamp a former Democratic Senator from North Dakota and founder of the One Country Project, a group promoting the party’s revival in rural America. “Now there are more and more people willing to say, ‘This is not normal, this is not right, and you know better.’” When Barack Obama took office, the industrial heartland and the Farm Belt remained highly competitive between the two parties. Different analysts use different boundaries when describing which states fit under those headings. But one definition, running from West to East, might include North and South Dakota, Nebraska and Kansas; Minnesota, Iowa and Missouri; Wisconsin, Illinois, Michigan, Indiana, Ohio and Pennsylvania (which emphatically does not like to be classified as part of the Midwest, but usually behaves like it politically.) In 2009, Democrats controlled 18 of the 26 Senate seats from those 13 states, and eight of their 13 governorships. It might seem unimaginable today, but Democrats then held both Senate seats in North Dakota, as well as single seats in South Dakota, Nebraska, Iowa and Indiana. Obama carried eight of those 13 states in 2008. At that point, “people were less tribal and more willing to reward performance,” says Heitkamp. What followed was a decade of decline for Democrats. The big blow was the 2010 midterm backlash against Obama’s tumultuous first two years. In 2010, Democrats lost Senate seats in North Dakota, Indiana, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and even Illinois, Obama’s home state. Republicans simultaneously flipped control of governor’s mansions in Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. Obama rallied to run well across the region in his 2012 reelection. But Democrats then suffered further Senate losses there in 2012, 2014 and especially 2018 (when Heitkamp and incumbents in Missouri and Indiana were ousted). Today, after all these shifts, the partisan balance in the Senate has inverted from 2009: Republicans now hold 18 of these states’ 26 Senate seats. Republicans also control 7 of the 13 governorships, compared to five when Obama took office. Heitkamp says the growing willingness of Republicans to support federal farm subsidies, and the Democratic Party’s turn left on social issues, both accelerated the reversal. At the presidential level, Democrats have fallen just as hard. In 2024, Kamala Harris lost all these states except reliably blue Illinois and Minnesota, with Trump’s share of the vote soaring to 55% or more in the former battlegrounds of Ohio and Iowa. For dazed Democrats emerging from 2024, the heartland looked more like a wasteland. Two years later, Democrats have their best opportunity in years to regain a foothold in the Midwest. In governor’s races, Democrats are strongly favored to hold seats in Pennsylvania and Illinois (behind incumbents Josh Shapiro and J.B. Pritzker) and Minnesota (where Sen. Amy Klobuchar is heavily favored to succeed Tim Walz, who has been weakened by the state’s welfare fraud scandal .) In Michigan, Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson is favored over Republican John James in an open seat race. After David Crowley’s dramatic comeback primary victory over socialist Francesca Hong last week, Democratic strategists believe the Milwaukee County executive holds a better hand than Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany for Wisconsin’s open seat. Democrats haven’t elected a governor since 2006 in either Iowa or Ohio. But in Iowa, Democrat Rob Sand, the state auditor, is in a strong position against Republican Zach Lahn. In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton, the former state Health Department director, is locked in a tight race with former GOP presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. Democrats believe they remain competitive in the race to succeed outgoing Democratic Gov. Laura Kelley in Kansas and consider Nebraska a “sleeper” opportunity against GOP Gov. Jim Pillen. In Senate races, the Democrats’ best opportunities to flip Republican seats are in Ohio (where former Sen. Sherrod Brown may have established an edge over Republican Jon Husted) and Iowa (where Republican US Rep. Ashley Hinson is considered a slight favorite over Democratic State Rep. Josh Turek). Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist minister, and independent Dan Osborn, a populist Navy veteran and former union official, remain viable, if longer-shot, possibilities against low-key Republican incumbents in Kansas (Sen. Roger Marshall) and Nebraska (Sen. Pete Ricketts.) In contrast with the governors’ contests, heartland Democrats face two serious challenges to hold Senate seats in states where they have chosen nominees much more liberal than their typical Midwestern candidates. After a divisive primary in Michigan , Abdul El-Sayed must broaden his appeal against Republican Mike Rogers; after another ideologically divisive primary , Democrat Peggy Flanagan, the lieutenant governor, is in a better position in more reliably blue Minnesota, particularly after the backlash against the killings of two local residents by federal agents — but she will likely be hurt by her proximity to the state’s Covid-era fraud scandal . The two parties are battling as well over four highly competitive House seats in Pennsylvania; three each in Iowa, Ohio and Michigan; and one in both Nebraska and Wisconsin. In all these ways, the middle of the country is at the center of 2026’s political struggle. For all their inevitable local variation, these races present each party with several similar dynamics, starting with the nature of the campaign debate. “At the end of the day, Democrats are hoping what (matters) is people’s lived reality on the economy and that they are going to say, ‘the Republicans are in charge and I blame them,’” says Kochel, in a view echoed by many Democrats. “If Republicans are successful, it’s that ‘I don’t want to go back to what Joe Biden was doing.’” The common demographic challenge for Democrats is that White voters without a four-year college degree — Trump’s core group — cast half or more of the votes in 2024 in many of these states, including Wisconsin, Iowa and Michigan, and just under half in most of the rest, including Ohio, Pennsylvania and Minnesota, according to census data analyzed by demographer William Frey of the Brookings Metro think tank. And apart from Illinois, all these states also rank above the national average in the share of their population that lives in rural areas, according to census figures . The key to the Republican consolidation of the heartland states since the early 2000s has been the Democrats’ collapse with these overlapping constituencies of White working-class and rural voters. Amid this retreat, Democrats have held their own — and even gained ground — in population centers. Harris, for instance, won Ohio’s prosperous Franklin County, around Columbus, by an even larger margin in 2024 than Obama did in 2008, and ran only 2 points below his total in Polk County, which revolves around Des Moines. Yet, while Obama comfortably carried both states in 2008, Harris lost each by double digits. In both states, Democrats have suffered death by a thousand cuts — relentless Republican gains in mid-sized and smaller places. In 2026, Democrats can reasonably expect to recover with minority voters across the region who moved toward Trump in 2024, given the sharp decline in his national approval among nonwhite adults. And Democrats are on track to run better than in 2024 among college-educated White voters. Public polls in the past few months have shown Trump’s disapproval rating rising past 60% among White voters with at least a four-year degree in Wisconsin , Ohio , Iowa and Pennsylvania . Those attitudes mean that, in competitive races, Democrats will be well positioned if they can show almost any improvement among the GOP’s best constituencies. In these culturally conservative states, Democrats remain highly unlikely to win most blue-collar White or rural voters. But, given their likely gains elsewhere, it may be enough for the party just to lose by less in the GOP’s small-town strongholds. Pete Giangreco, a Democratic strategist with extensive experience across the region, points to that dynamic as the key to Democratic chances in Iowa and Ohio, the two biggest heartland prizes that have drifted away. What’s brought Ohio and Iowa into play is that “the dark red parts of (them) are going to be light red, and that’s a big deal,” Giangreco says. “When you are losing counties by 50 points, instead of 60 to 70, it’s a different ballgame.” The economy is, by far, the best lever for Democrats hoping to regain ground with blue-collar Whites and rural residents in the heartland states. In 2024, Trump posted huge margins among Whites without a four-year college degree in all these states where exit polls were conducted. But disappointment in his economic record has depressed his approval rating with them to around 50-50 in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin and the upper 50s in Ohio . Likewise, farmers across the heartland are being squeezed between rising costs for fuel and fertilizer and disruption of export markets in the international tussling over Trump’s tariffs. One recent Iowa study calculated one-fifth of the state’s farms were “finally vulnerable,” well over double the level in 2022. Trump’s ratings are suffering not only because voters are broadly unhappy about the economy, but because so many believe his policies have compounded their problems — with the Iran war, for instance, directly linked to rising gas prices. “This is not like people need a University of Chicago economics paper to explain why gas prices are high,” Giangreco says. Medicaid cuts in the 2025 GOP tax-and-spending bill that disproportionately stress rural hospitals add another pain point. And while many elected officials and political strategists in both parties have long considered tariffs attractive to working-class voters, Kemp says even blue-collar White men have reluctantly turned against them because of their impact on prices. “Much as they might want manufacturing to come back to the US, what they say in focus groups is that their day-to-day lives are hurting because of it,” she says. Against all these headwinds, Republicans are not defenseless. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act created a $50 billion fund specifically for rural hospitals. Trump wants to channel another $50 billion in federal subsidies to farms this year, a breathtaking sum that would provide roughly one-third of all income for farmers, according to a recent analysis by the Environmental Working Group, an environmental analysis and advocacy group. Usually, federal payments account for only about one-tenth of farm income, says Anne Schechinger, the group’s senior director of agriculture and climate research. Mark Graul, a longtime GOP strategist in Wisconsin, says the key for Republicans, especially in the gubernatorial elections, will be to try to decouple from the discontent about Washington. “You have to localize the election and do your best not to allow Democrats to make this a referendum on what’s happened in Washington DC,” Graul says. But as Graul notes, that’s not easy to do. He learned that when he ran the Wisconsin gubernatorial campaign in 2006 for GOP Rep. Mark Green, who lost amid pervasive discontent with another Republican president (George W. Bush) over another Mideast war (Iraq). “I’ve lived it,” Graul said with a sigh. “I know how hard it is.” Still, for all the doubts polls across these states register about Trump, they also make clear that Democrats have hardly repaired their own dents, especially among the key non-college and rural constituencies. “You can talk all day about how Trump has taken some hits with some of these populations, but the only thing less popular is the Democratic Party,” says Kochel. In many of the heartland states Democrats are contesting this year, they will still need a perfect storm to win. But it no longer seems impossible that high gas prices, depressed farm incomes, an unpopular war, an erratic president, and some strong candidate recruitment can produce exactly that.

While warning of the rise of socialism on the left, President Donald Trump is simultaneously conducting his own experiments in economic theory, putting his nationalist spin on American capitalism. The fear of socialism is built on the idea that government intervention stifles free private enterprise, which capitalists view as the bedrock of American greatness. Trump, however, is using his view of the national interest — which frequently appears to coincide with his own personal interest — as an excuse to get the government involved in all sorts of markets. Without asking Congress, Trump’s administration has bought stakes in dozens of private companies. These range from the massive – a nearly $9 billion lifeline to Intel in exchange for nearly 10% of the company – to much smaller stakes in mineral, quantum computing and semiconductor companies, according to a list of 30 investments . Tracking these investments, which barely register when they’re announced by the Commerce or Defense departments, is Tad DeHaven, a policy analyst at the libertarian-leaning CATO institute. The administration argues that these are minority stakes and that the government is not interfering in the free market, but DeHaven notes the United States now has a monetary interest in the companies. Even if the Trump administration says it won’t meddle in the operation of these companies, the genie is out of the bottle and the government will now have an incentive, according to DeHaven, “to privilege the companies that the government has ownership stakes in, and to disfavor competitors, and not just existing competitors, but potential competitors.” In an odd bit of political opposites attract, this is an issue that aligns the Trump administration with Sen. Bernie Sanders, the democratic socialist Independent from Vermont who previously ran for president as a Democrat. During debate over the bipartisan CHIPs Act , which allocated taxpayer money to prop up a US semiconductor industry, Sanders pushed unsuccessfully for language that would give the government “a piece” of profits from those companies. Now, for some of these unprecedented investments, the Trump administration is using money Congress earmarked in the CHIPS Act for the semiconductor industry. The law envisioned federal funding as subsidies to companies. Trump is using it as Sanders might have preferred it. Another area where Trump and Sanders agree, at least in principle, is in the need for a US sovereign wealth fund — the kind of massive investment vehicle found in oil-rich countries like Norway and Saudi Arabia, among others. Sanders would impose a one-time tax on AI companies, seizing 50% of their stock to create a US wealth fund to back social projects. “The principle is simple: When a public resource generates wealth, the public should share in that wealth,” Sanders said in a statement when he announced the proposal in June. Last February, Trump directed his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to explore the development of a sovereign wealth fund , but those plans have not progressed more than a year later. The fund, according to the order Trump signed, is meant to “ lessen the burden of taxes on American families and small businesses, establish economic security for future generations, and promote United States economic and strategic leadership internationally.” That language sounds very similar to something Sanders might say. The problem is finding funds to start it when the national debt is approaching $40 trillion. Republicans, who under Trump twice cut corporate tax rates, would never agree to Sanders’ one-time AI tax. Trump’s claims of foreign investment in the US are wildly overstated . DeHaven, who opposes a sovereign wealth fund, says the US economy has done quite well without one. “I think they need to explain how is it the U.S. made it 250 years and became the world’s economic global superpower without this,” he said. Tariffs, at their core, are protectionist and anti-competitive. But “tariff” is Trump’s favorite word , as he would often say on the campaign trail with promises to use them to pay down the debt and reignite American manufacturing. As president, Trump has bragged about using tariffs to exact concessions from foreign governments and to benefit US industries, although the evidence that the policy has worked is lacking. Trump, however, is determined to continue interfering in markets. After the US Supreme Court rejected his tariff scheme as an unconstitutional overreach, he has tried to find ways to implement tariffs in other ways. Trump has also sought to have the US government intervene in other countries’ economies, potentially distorting markets abroad the way he sometimes has at home. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has overseen support for governments the Trump administration likes with multibillion-dollar efforts to prop up — some might say bail out — currencies in both Japan and Argentina . The US government has a long history of bailouts – for banks, for airlines, for car companies. But those were generally approved by lawmakers first and drew blowback for the moral hazard and corporate socialism of using taxpayer dollars to rescue companies that made bad bets. Meanwhile, the US has stifled commerce in countries it doesn’t like. Cuba is a communist country, so it’s not right to say the US has shut down the energy market there. But the US imposed what is effectively an oil embargo on the nation, plunging Cubans into darkness in an effort to turn the country against its communist regime. In Iran, the US has also imposed an embargo on ships docking in the Strait of Hormuz. That action, a complicated response put in place when Trump’s war effort there did not go according to plan, has so far failed to ease pressure on the worldwide oil market. In fact, Trump may have launched the war thinking the US could take control of Iran’s oil supply. That’s essentially what happened in Venezuela, where the US captured the country’s then leader, Nicolás Maduro, and essentially took over its oil industry. That Venezuela model has its defenders, but it’s far from free market capitalism. Trump has groused about oil prices recently after he came to office promising to lower them, but his war on Iran has driven them up. He recently demanded that oil executives force prices down, at the same time noting his demand was far from capitalist. “Based on a shortage, they’re making too much money. I don’t like it, and I should be the last one to say because I’m a big free enterprise guy — nobody bigger,” Trump said in the Oval Office earlier this month. His own self-awareness about exceptions to support of free enterprise is something a lot of Americans can identify with. CNN’s Aaron Blake wrote last month about recent polling from Fox News that echoes Gallup data from last year. It suggests steady views of socialism, but significant drops in views of capitalism. In the Fox News poll, Americans are effectively split — 50% viewed capitalism favorably versus 46% who viewed it unfavorably. He keys in on one particular data point: Only 41% of Republican registered voters have a strongly favorable view of capitalism in the most recent Fox News poll. Another 20% of Republicans registered voters expressed a somewhat favorable view of capitalism. BLAKE: Just to underscore, fewer than half of Republicans — the party that claims to embrace free markets! — now have a strongly favorable view of capitalism. And 42% of them endorse a pretty Bernie Sanders-sounding sentiment about our “rigged” economy. A company that bears Trump’s name and owns his social media company is selling early access to his social media posts for up to $100,000 per month. Early access to the posts, which have moved markets when they announce tariffs or other policy decisions, give subscribers who can afford it — likely to be Wall Street firms and high frequency trading outfits — a leg up on a public who can’t afford access. Family members technically control his business empire, but they have made no secret of the fact that they see the profit potential in his presidency, both for his businesses and their own. Just one example: The Trump administration wants to spend a lot more money on defense and has asked Congress to approve $1.5 trillion for the Pentagon for the coming fiscal year, up from about $1 trillion in the current fiscal year. Two of his sons, coincidentally, invested in defense tech startups, as the Washington Post documented . Whatever kind of economy it is becoming, it is far from the free market ideal people learn about in economics class.

At a time when no American celebrity seems immune from the country’s many divisions, Dolly Parton was a crossover icon who stayed neutral in the culture wars while still speaking her mind. Her style was adopted by the LGBTQ community and is celebrated in drag shows. She starred in a feminist comedy and became an icon for feminists, but didn’t use that word to describe herself. She preferred “woman in business.” She laughed about her plastic surgery and said the joke was on the public . She talked about her deep faith and lent her name to a wholesome family-friendly theme park in her home state of Tennessee. She did all of this without seeming to offend anyone. Country music fans, pop music fans, Republicans, Democrats, presidents, faith leaders and drag queens all genuinely mourned her passing Tuesday. President Donald Trump announced after her death that flags will be lowered to half-staff to mourn her passing, an honor he has denied to perceived enemies. “There has never been anyone like her, and never will,” Trump said in a statement posted on social media. Former President Barack Obama seemed shocked when he was asked by then-“Late Show” host Stephen Colbert in 2020 why he hadn’t given Parton a presidential medal of freedom. “I’m shocked,” Obama said. “ That was a screw-up .” He assumed she’d already been honored with the nation’s highest civilian honor. Parton worked hard to appeal to everyone. When it was erroneously reported she had endorsed Hillary Clinton against Trump in 2016, she issued a clarifying post on social media , saying that while she supported having a woman in the White House, it was not a nod to Clinton. “I try not to get political but if I am, I might as well just run myself ‘cause I’ve got the hair for it, it’s huge, and they could always use more boobs in the race,” she wrote, adding. “But seriously, I have not decided who I’m voting for, but no matter what we’re gonna be suffering from PMS, Presidential Mood Swings.” That doesn’t mean she wouldn’t take any positions. When access to bathrooms for transgender people was in the news in 2016, she suggested to CNN that people should be able to use the restroom where they felt comfortable. “I try not to get too caught up in the controversy of things,” she said, adding, “I hope everybody gets a chance to be who and what they are.” But then she added the kind of plain-spoken Dollyism that pierced through the debate. “I just know if I have to pee, I’m going to pee. I don’t care where it’s going to be.” Her popularity was exceptional. When the University of Massachusetts Lowell and YouGov surveyed 1,000 people in April about their views of a random assortment of people with global fame, Parton had, by far, the strongest net favorability of +65%, a figure that included strong majorities of both liberals and conservatives. The next most popular person on the list was Obama, with +14%. Trump was in negative territory, along with former President Joe Biden. “I have as many Republican fans as I do Democrats,” Parton told USA Today in 2020. “I don’t want to offend anybody, I have a right to myself.” That kind of professional political agnosticism, perhaps partly a function of her home base in the heartland and her start as a country artist, might seem like a cop-out in today’s political climate. But it’s also true that much of the country, like Parton, doesn’t talk about politics every day. She brought an earnest smile and an infectious giggle into any conversation. Her music was more focused on the sad songs, love ballads and duets that sold in the ‘70s and ‘80s. Today it’s breakup albums that get plays and attention. “Jolene,” sung from the perspective of an unnamed narrator whose man would leave her for the more beautiful Jolene if he could, comes across as a plea and a lament. If a similar theme were addressed today by another country/pop crossover artist, it might come off more like a beef track. Parton came from a time when division wasn’t necessary to build an audience. And she built the widest audience possible. “Dolly was raised in her grandfather’s church. She knew the Bible. And one of her favorite verses was judge not, lest you be judged,” her biographer Martha Ackmann told NPR in 2025. Parton lived by that principle, Ackmann said. The big hair and makeup might have created a persona upon which others placed their own expectations. But beneath it all, Ackmann said, Parton was best described by the word “decency” — “that hardcore decency that respects other people and treats others with compassion and openness.” This story has been updated with additional details. This article’s headline has been updated.

Donald Trump’s presidency rests on the premise that he and the United States are so powerful that allies and enemies alike must submit to his will. His break with decades of US foreign policy doctrine is laced through his speeches and national security strategies. It was best explained in January by top aide Stephen Miller , who told CNN’s Jake Tapper that “iron laws” dictate a real world that is “governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power.” But the philosophy faces its most serious tests in deepening showdowns with Iran and Canada . Iran has defied the might of the US military for six months in a war Trump started but has been unable to end. Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney, who shut down trade talks with Washington, has meanwhile argued more forcefully than any other Western leader that the US under Trump “has changed.” He told his country Saturday that Trump was using “economic integration as a weapon.” It is a commentary on the extreme disruption of the Trump era that Canada, one of America’s most loyal friends, has found itself in a similar state of economic warfare with the US as Iran, one of Washington’s worst foes. But the Trump administration left no doubt Monday what it wants as it fights a trade war with Ottawa and a shooting war with Tehran. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an “economic onslaught” against Iran’s global financial connections, drawing an analogy with the D-Day invasion that turned the tide in World War II. Trump, meanwhile warned on social media that “The U.S.A. will always be far bigger, richer, and stronger than Canada.” He added: “Someone should get these clowns to ‘fall in line.’” The administration’s rhetoric Monday suggests that Trump is now sending the US economy to war. Trump hopes to chalk up a lopsided trade deal with Canada and to finally bring about the downfall of Iran’s regime. But the way forward is uncertain on both fronts because the president often backs down when the economic consequences of his attempts to assert his authority become clear. Any prolonged US effort to prevail over Canada and Iran — and third-party nations sanctioned in his bid to shut down Tehran’s financial networks — could trigger retaliation that causes energy and food price hikes for US consumers. It could also rattle US markets at a time when some investors fear a bond crisis . If Monday’s threats are the precursor to more TACOs (“Trump always chickens out”), the president will undermine his own power and the nation’s, and slip closer to lame-duck status as difficult midterm elections loom in November. Bessent’s announcement was the latest US effort to find a new way out of the war with Iran. But the D-Day analogy seemed tonally off, given the terrible sacrifices made by American soldiers to liberate Europe. And unlike Bessent, allied commander Gen. Dwight Eisenhower didn’t spent days in 1944 previewing a massive attack only to follow through with new threats of sanctions and no timeline. Still, administration skeptics often ignore the genuine power that Trump could wield by clever use of economic warfare. A truly global effort to cut off Iran’s pathways to finance and trade could inflict extreme damage on an already devastated economy. “It can work if we can get the buy-in of our partners,” Max Meizlish, a former senior Treasury official, said on CNN News Central Monday, specifically referring to Bank Melli, an Iranian commercial bank controlled by the government that operates in France, Germany and elsewhere and is a cog in Iran’s efforts to evade sanctions. Kenneth Rogoff, a former IMF chief economist who is now a Harvard University chair, told CNN’s Richard Quest: “Fundamentally, sanctions work if you can get most of the world behind you. But if they’re not, it’s very hard.” Trump might have had more success with such an approach before alienating US allies with a war many regard as unwise and illegal. And the White House may be misreading its capacity to influence events inside Tehran. Signs of disagreement between pragmatists and hardliners over the economy are encouraging. But Washington has for decades over-read such tea leaves and assumed regime collapse would follow. Most damagingly, the Trump administration is sending signals that it may not be serious about its own policy. There was no immediate action against an array of Chinese banks that facilitate Beijing’s trade in cut-price Iranian oil. China has already said it will defend its interests — code for potential retaliatory reaction against the US that could further raise prices and anger US voters. It showed last year in threatening to curtail rare earth mineral exports critical to the US defense and tech industries that it can counter Trump’s power. And the US leader also has a big date circled on his calendar — the state visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping next month. It’s hard to see him souring the atmosphere before then. In a revealing moment, Bessent only reinforced doubts about the administration’s staying power. He was asked why he was not immediately imposing secondary sanctions on entities that deal with Iran. “Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior; why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” he replied. The administration is less wary of sanctioning the manufacturers of Canadian hockey sticks than Chinese banks. And cross-border rhetoric is increasingly toxic. “We have to remember, Canada is a state. Sorry, Freudian slip. That was actually an accident,” Vice President JD Vance said Monday. Ontario Premier Doug Ford said at a news conference that “I have a lot of real estate on my ass, so (Trump) has a lot of room to kiss my ass.” Venting can sometimes create political room to relaunch talks. But Canadians believe they are embroiled in more than a trade dispute. Drew Dilkens, the mayor of Windsor, Ontario, just across from Detroit, explained the damage inflicted by Trump’s 51st-state claims. “When you say it the first time, perhaps you can laugh it off, but it was the doubling down and certainly continuing to reinforce that,” he told CNN’s Brianna Keilar. Ottawa said that, among other disputes, Carney ended trade talks after the US sought to water down its constitutional guarantees of bilingualism. Printing packaging for products sold in Canada in French as well as English is an inconvenience for US firms. But it’s a validation of the cultural and linguistic diversity that keeps Canada whole. Carney also implied Washington sought to restrict trade deals that his government could make with third countries. “We will not allow any nation to dictate our future,” Carney said Saturday. As the smaller economy, Canada would suffer the most harm in a trade war with the US. But it can challenge American power. A long tariff duel could result in the mutually assured destruction of the auto industry on both sides of the border. And the growing impact of Canadian boycotts could weaken Republicans in key contests in border states Michigan and Maine, which could decide who controls the US Senate next year. And in seeking to impose his dominance, Trump may have revealed another iron law of power that Miller did not mention back in January. When people see their sovereignty and independence threatened by a hostile greater power, there is almost no price they will not pay.

The cartographer in chief is at it again. Calling Canadians “nasty people,” President Donald Trump signed an executive order Thursday ordering the renaming of Lake Ontario as his frustration grows that a longtime friend he’s turned into an adversary won’t cave to his terms in a trade war . The gesture doesn’t change much — Trump has no control over how international bodies or other countries refer to the lake, though he can require the US government to refer to it as “Lake America.” The same issue applies to his renaming of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America last year. His move — while apparently designed to punish Canada and show his power — will nevertheless be seen as something of a cover for failure after Ottawa walked away from talks and decided to match his own sharply rising tariffs, arguing that he was trying to encroach on its sovereignty. “‘Lake of America’ was something I’ve been thinking about for a long time,” Trump said, surrounding by maps of the Great Lakes in the Oval Office. “We have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.” America’s bulldozer president also threatened this week to raze the Kennedy Center if courts continue to block his attempt to renovate the nation’s premier arts center. Such actions might appear petty and in the case of Canada, a kind of tin-pot colonialism. But they epitomize a driving impulse of Trump’s second term: the belief that nothing can stand in his way. And when reality doesn’t please him, he invents his own. The twin episodes also raise the glaring question of why Trump fixates on such trifles even as his war in Iran grinds on and Americans despair at high prices for food, fuel and housing ahead of the midterm elections. Is this really what the country voted for in 2024? But the trolling is Trump at his most authentic. It shows how he wields the politics of spectacle to outrage elites, confound establishments and ignite media storms. It’s all a way of burnishing his outsider image and uniting his populist coalition. There’s almost no institution that he won’t try to disrupt — or destroy, if it resists his power. No building, natural landmark or historic artifact is safe from the branding maestro’s eye. Courts, the Constitution and US allies be damned; Trump seeks to leave a mark on the landscape and the map to ensure the world remembers him. But while the president sees openings for unaccountable power, his extreme reactions this week also hint at growing impotence. His legal team is threatening to demolish the Kennedy Center only because the courts have confounded his plans to renovate it — and, perhaps not incidentally, to put his name on the front . And renaming the vast inland sea between Ontario and New York State seems a poor substitute for what he truly covets: to make Canada the 51st US state. Trump’s latest threat to the Kennedy Center emerged in legal documents related to a court attempt to thwart his bid for control. His team warns that if renovations don’t happen, the center may need to be replaced by an open-air amphitheater. Most immediately, Trump is trying a familiar device by adopting an apparently outlandish legal argument to game the judicial process. Judges have previously ruled that the president lacks the authority to change the building’s name or to authorize major structural work. That power resides with Congress — not the presidentially appointed trustees he’s lined up to empower his takeover bid. But the saga is also remarkable for Trump’s obliviousness to the optics of taking over a living memorial to an assassinated president who staved off nuclear war in the Cuban Missile Crisis. Perhaps he’d like to deal an insult to a great American and Democratic dynasty that still enjoys the historic recognition that he seems to crave, but that so far eludes him. It’s hard to argue that — for all Trump’s showbiz nous — his interest has been anything other than disastrous for the Kennedy Center. The Washington National Opera and the National Symphony Orchestra have left home. The Washington Post reported on Tuesday that ticket sales and donations plummeted after Trump’s board voted to put his name on the building. Farcical scenes followed, with a tarp covering the facade after the president was ordered by a court to erase his name from alongside that of the 35th president. Critics will likely see the new threat to destroy the center altogether as yet another act of revenge, or an attempt to cover up another embarrassing Trump project, along with the botched renovation of Washington’s Reflecting Pool . Trump, however, insists he’s beautifying a capital that has been left to decay in recent times. And it’s true that cleaning up fountains, parks, statues and some public buildings has been in many cases an aesthetic improvement. Meanwhile, another legal showdown threatens to halt construction on the ballroom that is replacing the White House East Wing, which he tore down in another legally questionable power grab. And his proposed towering arch that would overshadow the capital’s sacred sight lines is seen by many as a future memorial to presidential hubris. But there may be political mileage for Trump in the Kennedy Center imbroglio even if he loses the legal fight. Turfing the capital’s cultural deep state out of their palace of the arts is hardly likely to harm Trump’s populist credentials. The president’s Great Lake renaming ceremony was a gesture of mockery and contempt toward a loyal neighbor that has long been sending its sons to die in America’s wars — sacrifices Trump ignores. Trump loves trolling. His most viral posts often create outrage in the political establishment, among his foes and in traditional media. This serves to please his base and right-wing media. His proposal to Make one of the Great Lakes Great Again is not even a new move. It mirrors his renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as Gulf of America, announced during his inaugural address last year. When he did so, Hillary Clinton, his vanquished 2016 opponent, couldn’t contain her giggles. For Never-Trumpers it was a moment of ridicule. But the episode turned out to be a glimpse of an incoming president with a habit of redrawing maps to suit his monarchical whims. A few weeks ago, Trump mused about declaring the Strait of Hormuz, which is under an Iranian stranglehold, US territory. A president can’t just declare a foreign waterway he doesn’t control part of the United States. But the troll delighted conservative pundits and for a little while turned attention away from his failure to end a war he claimed that he’d won after a few days last winter. All presidents use naming rights as a tool of political power, to reflect their ideology and to try to define their age. But Trump takes it to another level, fittingly for a serial brander who made his fortune putting his name on hotels and golf courses, steaks and sneakers. His administration has renamed military bases, warships and mountain peaks to empower what it sees as its anti-woke crusade. It hauled out the old name for Mount McKinley in Alaska, for example, which had been renamed Denali by President Barack Obama after its historic Native American title. And CNN reported last week that the Pentagon — under its testosterone-fueled new moniker the Department of War — is considering renaming an aircraft carrier under construction, potentially for Trump. It had been slated to honor Black Pearl Harbor hero Doris “Dorie” Miller . Justifying his move on Lake Ontario, Trump said this week that there was no need to mention the province because two-way trade with the US would soon peter out. But of course the troller in chief can himself be trolled. “Let’s just call it Lake Natalie so we know you’ll start protecting our Great Lakes,” Democratic Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan wrote on X, in an arch reference to White House executive assistant Natalie Harp , the president’s ubiquitous aide. This article and headline have been updated with new developments.

Russia’s harrowing history has bred a dark sense of humor in its citizens. CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s hosts therefore surely appreciated the irony when he flew into Moscow this week, reportedly to tell the Russians that they are losing their debacle of a war in Ukraine . Russian spy chiefs might have pointed out that President Donald Trump, like President Vladimir Putin, is also embroiled in a war — in Iran — that he can’t win and can’t end . Two leaders in two different conflicts face a similar dilemma: They can’t achieve their war ends. But they can’t walk away and save face. Each launched hostilities after apparently underestimating the tenacity and capacity of adversaries whose militaries were dwarfed by the conventional power and matériel of US and Russian forces. Both Putin and Trump saw their tactical military advantage undermined by unconventional asymmetrical tactics by Ukraine and Iran that pioneered cheap new technologies like drones and a new era of warfare. In its report describing Ratcliffe’s visit, the New York Times noted a concern long shared by many in the Washington foreign policy community that Putin is not getting honest assessments of the war’s trajectory. Many observers wonder whether Trump’s sunny assessments of US victory in Iran mean he’s also poorly served by an inner circle unwilling to give him bad news. Washington and Moscow are no strangers to costly foreign entanglements; both, for example, were humbled by wars in Afghanistan. Russia’s disaster in Ukraine in some way recalls the US defeat in Vietnam. Still, the parallels between two strongman leaders now stuck in wars they started, while apt, only go so far. Trump has not copied Putin’s grave error of pouring ground troops into a quagmire — a decision that has left more than 1.4 million young Russians dead, injured or missing, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies . Putin, a true authoritarian leader, is less constrained than Trump by domestic dynamics. Such a toll would be politically unsustainable in the US. And while Putin is raining terror and death on Ukrainian cities and power plants with missile and drone raids, Trump has largely avoided deliberately targeting civilians and civil infrastructure in his war. He has declined, however, a full public accounting of a missile strike that hit an Iranian school in February, killing nearly 200 children and adults, which apparently resulted from the use of outdated intelligence. Ratcliffe’s surprise visit to Russia came at a moment of flux and somber omens in international relations as the wars in Ukraine and Iran destabilize the wider Middle East, entangle the world’s great powers and raise fears of widening geopolitical conflict. The CIA chief had a broad agenda. He warned Russia against any overt or covert attacks on NATO territory amid growing fears in Europe that Putin might test the alliance’s defenses, two people familiar with the matter told CNN. Ratcliffe also used his meetings with Russian espionage officials to encourage Russia to cut off economic and military support for Iran. His mission could offer a measure of relief to US allies who’ve long fretted about Trump’s commitment to NATO and its security guarantees. And a fresh US attempt to end the Ukraine war would be widely welcomed, even if the president’s downgrading of military aid to President Volodymyr Zelensky’s government raises suspicions about his motives. Trump still hasn’t followed through on an apparent offer this summer to allow Ukraine to license the production of Patriot anti-missile systems . Trump once predicted he could end the war in Ukraine in 24 hours, but his peace efforts have gone nowhere. His repeated claim that Putin wants to make peace is incessantly disproved by events. The United States has been an arm’s-length player in the Ukraine war since the start. Russia has its own over-the-horizon role in the Iran war. US missteps in Iran are especially in the spotlight this week because the war has hit its six-month mark as the administration turns from military action to all-out economic warfare . Russia may have little strategic interest in easing Trump’s plight in Iran. Any quid pro quo involving Ukraine would founder on the US president’s previous failure to browbeat Kyiv into territorial concessions. CNN reported in March that Russia has provided Iran with intelligence about the locations and movements of American troops, ships and aircraft, according to multiple people familiar with US intelligence reporting on the issue. Much of the intelligence Russia has shared with Iran has been imagery from Moscow’s sophisticated constellation of overhead satellites. Putin’s anti-Western posture means Russia is constantly combating US and Western influence in the Middle East and elsewhere. He’s likely playing a longer game than Trump, whose term ends in two-and-a-half years. Still, Washington could use the help of Moscow — and Beijing — with its new policy of utter economic isolation for Iran. “For the economic pressure to bear fruit, (Trump) has to be able to get some cooperation with the Chinese, the Russians, and other regional actors that are the main trading partners for the Iranians,” Firas Maksad, Eurasia Group managing director for the Middle East and North Africa, told CNN International on Thursday. “I think he’s going to have a real hard time getting the Chinese to cooperate … It’s a similar situation with Russia.” As the implications of Ratcliffe’s trip sunk in Thursday, the Washington Post reported that his visit was preceded by fresh US intelligence suggesting the Kremlin sees the US as weakened by the Iran war. Trump’s failure to decisively win the conflict has not only bruised US credibility; it has also depleted munitions and strained naval and air forces. It would not be surprising therefore if US adversaries like Russia and China question Washington’s capacity for or interest in responding to any crisis in Europe or Asia. “Because Donald Trump decided to go to war against the Iranians, without a strategic goal, without a plan, without a timeline, without a way out, and now he is stuck — yes, sure, that helps the Russians,” Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona told CNN’s Brianna Keilar on Thursday. “And by the way, the Russians are helping the Iranians.” Trump, however, argues that his friendly relationship with Putin makes the world safer. He insisted on Thursday that there was no danger of Putin taking any action that could cause a conflict with the West. “I’ve had good talks with him. He’s not going to be attacking a NATO territory,” he told CNN’s Kristen Holmes in the Oval Office. Still, multiple layers of intrigue surrounding Ratcliffe’s trip to Moscow represent a fascinating new twist in the extraordinary relations between two leaders who face a common strategic conundrum that may define their legacies. The Iran war may not be as existential for Trump’s political and personal survival as the conflict in Ukraine is for Putin. But like his friend in the Kremlin, he’s cornered by his own war.

Imaginations run wild at what President Donald Trump and his allies might yet do to interfere in the coming midterm election. He’s already done quite a bit. This is the man who alleged widespread voter fraud even in the two elections he won and who tried to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election he still won’t admit he lost. There’s no evidence of any such fraud. Asked in recent months about some more extreme possible actions he could take in November or after, Trump has stayed coy while leaving ample room to stoke conspiracy theories, even as his top aides have continued to raise unsubstantiated concerns about voting machines and noncitizens voting. Some of these extreme possible measures — which have been the subject of either speculation or direct lobbying by Trump allies — include seizing ballot boxes, declaring a national election emergency, or deploying troops or ICE agents to polling places. When Trump in July gave an address to the nation on election integrity, he did not promise to do any of these things. But speculation has persisted, particularly on the political left as it tries to get out the vote in November. “Trump is throwing stuff out there. People are biting on it, and it makes the country as a whole more nervous, and is a self-perpetuating cycle,” said Ben Ginsberg, a longtime Republican election lawyer. But he also said the country — and election workers — needs to be ready for the unexpected. “Because the rhetoric is there and (Trump) has shown a singular ability for asymmetrical warfare starting on January 6. If you’re an election official, you have to be preparing,” he said. But that preparation must come, Ginsberg said, with the knowledge that “the creation of a climate of fear is maybe a goal in and of itself.” When a reporter asked in February, Trump seemed surprised and said he didn’t know anything about a push by election deniers for him to declare a national election emergency and seize broad and unprecedented control over how states run elections. But this month, when the idea was explained to him by conservative commentator Wayne Root, Trump didn’t reject it, but also didn’t endorse it. “Let me just say that stranger things have happened, OK? I’ll leave it at that,” Trump said . The idea for declaring a national emergency dates back to Trump’s first term, although it was never employed. More recently, as the Washington Post first reported , supporters have been pushing an executive order , written last spring, that would declare a national emergency to enact new federal powers over elections. The draft EO claims meddling by China justifies the president seizing control over elections from states — even though US intelligence suggests Iran and Russia have more actively tried to meddle in US elections. Trump never signed the order. Shortly after those first reports, in March, Trump did sign a different executive action that sought to put new limits on mail-in voting and to direct the Postal Service against the use of mail-in ballots. That order is still the subject of multiple lawsuits and seems unlikely to be implemented before November. Allies like podcaster and former Trump aide Steve Bannon are still pushing for a national emergency declaration soon because it could, they say, unlock power for Trump to do some of what’s listed below, such as dispatching federal agents to polling places or seizing ballots or voting machines to guard against supposed Chinese interference. Opponents like Norm Eisen, cofounder of Democracy Defenders Action, a group that has repeatedly sued the Trump administration on a variety of issues, said US elections have taken place during wars and pandemics without national security declarations and lawyers are standing by to challenge Trump if he tries to declare one in the coming weeks. “There’s no power to declare emergency relating to our elections to seize ballots or do anything else. Courts are going to slap it down. We’re ready to go fast,” Eisen told reporters Thursday. The argument from Trump allies and those worried about election integrity is that agents could be used to deter undocumented immigrants from casting ballots. It is already illegal for noncitizens to vote or register to vote, and there are protections in every state to make sure each vote corresponds to a voter registration and for votes cast provisionally to be verified. A Republican candidate for governor in Maine has promised to request ICE agents at polling stations. Elections are run by state and local governments, so it is their job to provide security. Laws vary from state to state, but it is illegal under federal law for anyone – including law enforcement – to intimidate voters. The law also prohibits “troops or armed men” from polling places unless they are repelling enemies of the US. Bannon has also pushed for ICE agents at polls. CNN’s Gabe Cohen unpacked all of this back in March. Top Trump aides have repeatedly declined to say that ICE agents will not be sent to polling places, but they have also not outlined plans to send them. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin gave a somewhat convoluted answer to CNN’s Kasie Hunt back in June when she asked if the administration would dispatch ICE agents to polling places. He said agents would not go on their own to verify the immigration status of voters, but rather to help local law enforcement respond to things like bomb threats. “We wouldn’t show up on our own,” he said. “We would be getting asked to show up, but not for immigration purposes.” In the meantime, however, Mullin has been tasked by Trump with rooting out instances of noncitizens on state voter rolls, a process which has so far yielded few federal charges and far less evidence of potential illegal voter registrations than initially suggested by Mullin. CNN’s Gabe Cohen has pored over the data . In Nevada, a state of more than 3 million people, DHS teased that more than 15,000 ineligible noncitizen voter registrations were discovered, but, according to communications reviewed by CNN, only “confirmed” 185, and didn’t give Nevada officials enough data to follow up, according to the state’s election leaders. A recent release claiming tens of thousands of noncitizen voters were found using Census data was equally vague and impossible to verify. Experts quoted in CNN’s report called the use of Census data a “ hijack by the White House .” He regrets not doing it before. When the New York Times asked in January if he considered ordering the National Guard to seize ballot boxes in 2020, Trump said, “Well, I should have,” before qualifying that he doesn’t think Guardsmen are “sophisticated enough” to do that particular job. It’s worth noting here that the administration has this year seized ballots and machines related to the 2020 election, although that’s years after the fact. Trump was once the subject of criminal cases related to his efforts to overturn election results in Georgia in 2020. Those cases essentially went away after he was reelected in 2024, but the administration has tried to flip the script. Trump’s previous director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, was present when federal agents seized 2020 ballots in Fulton County, which includes Atlanta, in the swing state of Georgia. CNN recently reported the FBI has detailed 260 staff members to a resulting investigation, although no charges have been filed and no specific evidence of wrongdoing has been provided to dispute the results of the election Trump lost, which was the subject of multiple recounts, and which was overseen by Republican officials in Georgia. Any effort to seize ballots or machines after the coming election — before the outcome was known, contested or litigated — would be the subject of immediate court action. Courts have so far rejected Trump’s efforts, across multiple elections, to dispute results. That doesn’t mean the administration will not use its power to suggest there are issues in elections where it disagrees with the outcome. The question will be whether the system can withstand those inquiries. Democrats have flagged that a longstanding Justice Department memo dating back to 2017 that made it US government policy not to seek election materials until after an election had been settled was removed from the agency’s website. In any event, Trump’s DOJ can be expected to put a much more circumspect eye on elections in places where Trump does not like the outcome. It seems far too late to attempt decertifying voting machines before November’s elections. Doing anything this close to an election would sow major chaos; voting machines are utilized in the vast majority of the nation’s more than 95,000 voting locations. This year they will be essential to count potentially 150 million or more votes. Republican election officials are among those who will generally tell you most Americans already use a paper ballot and the voting machines are more accurate at counting them than humans. Conspiracy theories about voting machines have persisted for years, but they have had consequences. Fox News agreed to a $787 million settlement for a defamation lawsuit for lies it spread after the 2020 election about Dominion Voting Systems, then the largest manufacturer of voting machines used in the US. Dominion’s products are still prevalent in US elections, but the company was bought in 2025 by a former Republican election official from Missouri and rebranded as Liberty Vote. The new owner, Scott Leiendecker, acknowledges that Trump lost the 2020 election. But voting machines have been a major issue for Trump – and questioning them has long been high on his list of complaints about the US system. After he lost the 2020 election, Trump was presented with a plan dreamed up by supporters outside the White House, according to The New York Times , to seize voting machines in key states where his supporters alleged there was fraud. No compelling evidence of fraud was ever produced, and courts rejected challenges to the election results. Trump was told by officials at the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security in 2020 that he lacked the authority to seize machines without probable cause. Election deniers are in some key roles at the White House and the Department of Homeland Security during Trump’s second term. And top leaders have been more pliant to his whims, which opens the possibility of more active federal oversight in areas where Trump does not like election results. But the results of an election would have to be known before Trump could dispute them. The machines have a paper trail and can be audited. Those facts would not change. Plus, there would be lawsuits if the administration tried to take machines. The DNI under Gabbard examined voting machines in Puerto Rico for vulnerabilities in 2025, although the government has not found any evidence that voting machines were compromised. CNN’s Sean Lyngaas reported this month about backlash and an alleged smear campaign against the small cybersecurity firm tapped to investigate the machines when it found no evidence of fraud. Reuters reported last year that Kurt Olsen, a spreader of election conspiracy theories who works in the White House, had pushed the idea of a nationwide ban on voting machines produced by Dominion Voting Systems. The plan went nowhere, but is indicative of how the administration views voting machines. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that because three companies that produce voting machines utilize some parts made in China, the machines cannot be trusted. Mullin has also proposed holding federal security aid states rely on unless they hand count a certain percentage of ballots. It would be difficult since states certify their own election results. Trump has a history of trying to stand in the way of certification of results he disagrees with and there are election deniers in some key posts around the country. Every election is subject to real-time observation by representatives from both political parties. There have been periodic concerns raised that partisan election watchers could seek to disrupt elections, although that has not occurred in a way that has affected how people vote. But if an election board or election officials refused to certify election results, it would be the subject of lawsuits and both state and federal courts have historically shown little interest in letting challenges linger. Tammy Patrick is a former Maricopa County, Arizona, election official who now oversees election programs at the Bipartisan Policy Center. She said there is a multilayered system that makes sure US elections go smoothly and are certified. “So far, the checks and balances of our system have held,” Patrick said. There are horizontal checks, she said, where Republicans and Democrats observe what’s happening in real time and after the election. There are also vertical checks, where state officials check the work of local election workers and election boards. There is a fringe theory — Jeffrey Toobin laid out the fever dream in the New York Times — that House Republicans could refuse to seat new Democratic members of Congress. It would be an unpopular redux of January 6, 2021, to say the least, and run afoul of the 20th Amendment . Relying on some parliamentary trickery and the complacency of the unelected official known as the clerk of the House, it would rely on Trump declaring there had been rampant fraud after the election in a Hail Mary attempt at blocking the new Democrats from being seated. Widespread outrage, including from many Republicans, could be expected. It seems too far-fetched to focus on at the moment. Patrick said election workers game out potential scenarios before Election Day. “Election officials are planners,” she said. “They have tried to think through ‘What would happen if __?’ and then fill in the blank.” One thing they have encountered increasingly in recent elections is bomb threats or the discovery of suspicious substances. Bomb threats mailed in from addresses with Russian email domains, for instances, were sent to multiple polling locations in key states in 2024 . Although none of those threats disrupted voting at the time, she said local officials will be expecting more of that type of shenanigans. For all the conjecture about what might happen, it’s worth noting that the White House and Republicans have already undertaken an unprecedented effort to sway the election in their favor. With singular focus in his second term, Trump has already tried to use the power of his presidency, and his influence both in congress and over his allies in states to alter how, when and in what districts Americans will vote this year. That influence campaign is at odds with the Constitution, which leaves the “ times, places and manner ” of holding elections to the states. And results so far have been mixed. The GOP clearly won the first round of a redistricting war Trump started in Texas and which spread to other states. The redrawing of congressional maps this cycle could net Republicans up to 10 new seats , if voters do as map-drawers predicted, before votes are cast in November. That effort got an assist from the Supreme Court’s gutting of protections for minority voters in the Voting Rights Act, which means the war will continue into future elections as a lasting effect of Trump on US democracy. His calls for a new proof-of-citizenship law don’t even have the votes needed to get a simple majority in the GOP-controlled US Senate. Courts, so far, have stood in the way of his efforts to use executive power to target mail-in voting, particularly in blue states, but court cases continue. While the Supreme Court did not immediately dismiss his effort to use the USPS to make states jump through hoops for mail-in voting, it’s not clear that effort will come to pass for the midterms in November. The first mail-in ballots will be sent to voters in North Carolina in early September. Each state has different rules and policies for mail-in ballots (and their elections in general). Trump has also tried to use the power of the federal government against states. His DHS has demanded state voter rolls, something even some red states have fought. They’ve also hobbled and sidelined the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, CISA , which is charged with coordinating responses to foreign election interference at the same time intelligence suggests foreign governments have tried to meddle in US elections. That’s what has already happened. There is plenty of fear about other things Trump might do — and what his allies have encouraged him to do — that’s giving election-watchers heartburn even as they project confidence in an American election system that is decentralized, complicated, which makes it impossible to rig.
