Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who walked away from US trade talks last week due to what he said was American intransigence, now wants to get negotiations started again. But he suggested Tuesday the Americans are too busy trolling. “When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” he said, lamenting “It’s not constructive. But that’s their democracy.” What Carney means is that rather than making any visible efforts to end the trade war with Canada, American leaders are trying — and sometimes failing — to own the Canucks. Meanwhile, the 50% tariffs the US imposed on a host of Canadian goods and dollar-for-dollar response tariffs from Canada continue. Carney didn’t mention that Ontario Premier Doug Ford has also trolled Trump, and a Canadian city council is considering renaming a street currently named for Trump with a deliberately taunting moniker. But much of the new material from top officials is coming from the US. When the White House posted an image of a bald eagle appearing to hold down a Canada goose — something it has posted before — Canadians pointed out photos showing the same goose getting the better end of the fight . https://t.co/OYaldd4UhI pic.twitter.com/7jQXwWW26K After Trump renamed Lake Ontario, he then called Apple to make sure the change showed up on maps. It does in the US, but not in Canada. And interest surged in Mapquest in App stores after it refused to change the name of Lake Ontario for US users. While Trump has focused on nomenclature, his aides have been belittling the Canadian military. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Canada is “a country that doesn’t have a military.” That’s not true, obviously. Canadians have fought and died alongside American allies in multiple wars. Insults do not seem to come as naturally to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who does not have a background in reality TV or at Fox News. But Bessent tried to land one on the neighbors to the North. “I mean, we’re not at war with Canada. How are we going to be at war with Canada? They’re going to take their two set submarines from the Edmonton Mall and sic them on us,” Bessent said Monday during an interview on CNBC ahead of a G20 finance meeting he is hosting in Asheville, North Carolina. Apparently there used to be a submarine attraction at a mall in Edmonton. Sick burn, Scott! But Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who prefers to be called secretary of war, was clearly trying to be mean Monday on X, when he posted a photo of two women in Canadian military uniforms. He included a Canadian flag emoji and added, “(this is real).” Maybe he was trying to say something about how the Canadian military is not as macho as he’s tried to make the US military. In any event, at least one of the women in the photo may have been part of a cadet program for young Canadians. It is arguably poor form for a high-ranking US official to be trying to make fun of a young Canadian, particularly one who may be considering a move into public service. Canadians remain American military allies. They responded when the US was attacked after 9/11. Hegseth has sometimes been on the other side of internet trolling, for example, his form doing pull-ups and bench presses in the workout videos he frequently posts have been mocked online. That’s also rather harsh, since a man deep in his 40s who can do any number of pull-ups should be celebrated. But Hegseth doing pull-ups won’t help to end the war in Iran, which has gone months longer than Trump initially promised and warped the world economy. Pull-ups also aren’t going to help rebuild the upper ranks of the Army. The same day Hegseth was trolling the Canadian youth, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, just before resigning, apparently went to the White House and told Trump that Hegseth’s leadership had left the Army with key leadership positions unfilled. Some of Hegseth’s picks for top generals may not have the bipartisan support to get confirmed. And he should also know better than to criticize cadets interested in the military. The US has been able to meet recruiting goals the past two years in part because of pre-enlistment programs meant to get American recruits in shape to pass fitness tests. But Hegseth isn’t about to sanitize his insults. He leans into criticism of diversity efforts. Appearing at an event in support of a Republican Congressman at the Iowa State Fair over the weekend, Hegseth used an epithet for transgender people, whom he has tried to boot from the military. And yes, when a partisan US official makes an appearance at the Iowa State Fair it often means they’re considering a run for president. Hegseth says he’s not. All of these men have arguably better things to do than troll Canada. Hegseth has a war the US has yet to win. Bessent could spend some more time on the squirrely bond market, Duffy could be focused on gas prices, say. If the trolling was meant to help build support for the US in the trade war, they have so far failed. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found a majority of Americans oppose both renaming Lake Ontario and the imposition of tariffs on Canada. This headline has been updated.

It is not news, or surprising, that Americans are worried about government corruption. They twice elected Donald Trump, who twice promised to drain the “swamp” of Washington, DC. “We are transferring power from Washington, DC, and giving it back to you, the American People,” he said in his first inaugural address. In his second inaugural address, Trump promised to liberate the country from “a radical and corrupt establishment” that “extracted power and wealth from our citizens.” On that promise, there’s striking new evidence that Americans believe he has failed to deliver. It should be of some concern to the White House — and to every American, really — that 89% of Americans said “yes” in a Gallup poll when asked, “Is corruption widespread throughout the government in this country, or not?” Gallup isn’t alone on this. The University of Massachusetts at Amherst is also out with a poll Tuesday in which 97% of Americans — nearly everybody — says there is some corruption in government. A smaller portion, 75%, said there is “a great deal” of corruption in the UMass poll. Decades of polling has found widespread frustration with and mistrust of government, but the new data from Gallup is notable for two main reasons. Gallup is still collecting data from all 38 countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) for 2026, but the preliminary indication is that the US is now in a class of its own in terms of how its people view government corruption. The US already outpaced other OECD countries in Gallup’s polling, but while the average corruption perception has been below 60% since 2022, it has now shot up for the US, which has been above 70% since 2010. In 2025, the US was tied with Colombia at 79%. What changed? Usually, as Gallup notes , when power changes hands, those who favor the winning party are less likely to see corruption. That expected drop has not happened. Instead, the 83% of Republicans who see widespread corruption in the most recent poll is broadly in line with the 87% who said corruption was widespread in 2024, the final year of President Joe Biden’s administration. At the time, Republicans worked very hard to portray Biden’s family, particularly his son Hunter, as corrupt, which the Bidens vehemently denied. In the meantime, while Republicans have not abandoned their perceptions of corruption, 91% of Democrats and 90% of political independents see widespread corruption. Very few issues see such cross-party agreement. And lawmakers are not doing much to counter the trend. In the UMass poll, respondents were asked to rank four governmental institutions from most to least corrupt. Most people — 53% — listed the president first, compared with 18% who listed Congress first. Forty-one percent listed Congress as the second most corrupt branch of government. Fewer pointed to courts and the federal bureaucracy first or second. After accusing Biden of trying to enrich his family through the presidency, Trump’s family has adopted a YOLO attitude toward wealth acquisition during Trump 2.0. The dollar figures the Trumps appear to be bringing in could dwarf what Hunter Biden was paid to sit on corporate boards. In the UMass poll, 77% said the president should not or definitely should not be profiting from business ventures that could be affected by the policies and decisions of his administration. One Trump-aligned company, Trump Media, is selling early access to his social media posts , giving Wall Street firms who can afford up to $100,000 a month possible early looks at some of his policy decisions. Trump’s sons both have interests in defense contractors at a time when President Trump is pushing for a gobsmacking $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget , which would be an increase of nearly $500 billion in one year. Overseeing their father’s assets, sons Eric and Don Jr. founded a firm, World Liberty Financial , along with the son of his Mideast and Ukraine negotiator Steve Witkoff, to capitalize on the craze around cryptocurrency. All of this is happening at a time when President Trump is taking a hands-off approach to regulation. Trump made more than a billion dollars from cryptocurrency ventures in first year back in office They are pursuing overseas deals at a time when their father is seeking trade deals. “I found out that nobody cared,” he told the New York Times back in January, suggesting he feels entitled to mix business and politics. He said he tried to separate the two during his first term and “got no credit.” Don Jr. and Eric Trump say they do not discuss business with their father. The sons of other top Trump administration officials, including Witkoff and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , are also working business angles that touch their wealthy fathers’ public jobs. Lutnick, pressed on CNBC about the perception of a conflict in a mining deal that benefits his family and Trump’s, dismissed “silly questions” and a “waste of time.” The president also apparently does not have direct control over his stock portfolio, so it is at least possible he does not know about the 1,000-plus recent stock trades made on his behalf by third-party financial institutions, including in energy companies affected by his war on Iran. The trades were disclosed in government-mandated disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics. Trump isn’t the only politician playing the market. Tracking the trades of members of Congress, including wealthy Democrats such as Reps. Nancy Pelosi and Ro Khanna of California, has become an investment strategy for people who want to buy the same stocks as lawmakers from either or both parties. It has also led to growing bipartisan calls, but no concrete action , for a ban on members of Congress and their direct family members trading stocks. A large, bipartisan majority of Americans support passing such a ban . Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who prefers to be called secretary of war, was critical, before his nomination to join the Trump administration, of generals working for defense contractors. But he notably declined, when pressed by Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, to pledge not to work for a defense contractor for 10 years after he leaves office. “I’m not a general, senator,” Hegseth told Warren at his confirmation hearing. More recently, he and Warren tangled at a congressional hearing over whether the Pentagon should be doing anything to investigate well-timed oil market bets before Trump launched the war in Iran. Warren’s own one-percenter wealth — divulged when she released tax returns during a 2020 presidential run — could be construed as antithetical to her progressive bona fides, although her wealth was built through her and her husbands’ healthy salaries as professors and her book deals rather through than stock trades. Many of the people who are elected to office are wealthy. (And simply having money in index funds would have inflated anyone’s bottom line in recent years.) That is clearly different from using knowledge or access to gain an upper hand. A larger issue than the money made by lawmakers in their private pursuits may be how the government spends money at a time when the national debt has eclipsed $40 trillion . Trump’s administration has sounded the alarm about government spending, but then cut revenues with massive tax cuts that will only generate more revenue far down the road, if ever . Elon Musk, the world’s richest individual, was brought in as a special government employee early in the Trump administration with directions to cut government spending and whittle down the bureaucracy. But it’s not clear what, if anything, he actually accomplished other than making wild, frequently unfounded accusations about fraud and corruption in social safety net programs. Musk ultimately left government to return to his companies, which benefit from government contracts, and briefly became the world’s first trillionaire. He’s still doing OK. The nearly $300 million we know about that he spent helping get Trump elected in 2024 can be viewed as a solid investment. How much of Musk’s wealth comes from government help? Virtually all of it At the same time, the increasing murkiness of US election spending means we don’t know exactly who is spending what to get candidates elected. Trump has also made wild and unverified claims about fraud throughout government and repeatedly alleged corruption in US elections. All of these claims could appeal to his political base, which identifies with his claim that the system is rigged against them. And Democrats have alleged that his moves are a threat to democracy and the right to vote is under threat. Take a step back, and the vast majority of Americans just see corruption. This headline has been updated.

A plain reading of the law about presidents on coins says the face of a living president should not be on currency. And yet President Donald Trump’s is, after his Treasury Department exploited a different law related to commemorative coins. The law says a president must not commit the US military into hostilities for longer than 60 days without congressional approval . The US has been in a conflict with Iran for more than six months, although the administration says it has taken time-outs in the war. Previous presidents from both parties have danced around this requirement , but nothing on the level of Trump’s war on Iran. Chief Justice John Roberts called it “ likely unlawful ” for Trump to tear down part of the White House and build something else. And yet construction is happening around the clock to get that White House ballroom done for Trump to enjoy. Laws would seem to require Congress to approve the construction of a triumphal arch adjacent to Arlington National Cemetery. The administration isn’t waiting and the Department of Interior appears primed to start excavation shortly. The law says suspected criminals should not be put to death without a trial . And yet the US military has taken out numerous alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific. The law says Congress creates agencies of the federal government, like USAID , the US Department of Education and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau . Trump has tried to end some of them anyway, either through starvation or outright deletion. The law says Congress decides where money should go. That didn’t stop Trump’s administration from cutting research funding and aid money it simply disagreed with. The law says the government should not be entering people’s homes without a judicial warrant . But Immigration and Customs Enforcement has utilized that power. The law says the Federal Reserve should operate independently, but that isn’t stopping Trump from trying to pressure the Fed to lower interest rates — most recently via a threat to cease trade with top partners . The list goes on, and with it the complicated legal arguments the Trump administration has made – in those instances when it has had to make them. Even when faced with setbacks in court, Trump’s administration has brazenly looked for end-runs. A judge ruled Trump’s administration can’t ignore the law and put his name alongside John F. Kennedy’s on the Kennedy Center. But the administration plans to add it to the building anyway, by adding an inscription giving Trump credit for the rehab job. And if the administration can’t put the name on the building, it threatens to tear the whole thing down . The tearing-down of buildings the president should not be able to tear down is an apt analogy for this whole presidency. Once something is gone, it’s gone. It doesn’t matter if getting rid of it was illegal. Roberts sided with liberals on the court to argue – in an unsuccessful dissent – that Trump’s East Wing project should be halted because it was “likely unlawful.” In his dissent, Roberts quoted Winston Churchill during World War II. “We shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us,” Churchill had said. Roberts didn’t mention that Churchill made those comments to argue the British House of Commons should be rebuilt as it had stood before it was destroyed by Nazi bombs. Churchill wanted to rebuild it as a monument to the British form of government. Trump saw the White House East Wing as a tear-down project — a (likely) illegal tear-down in Roberts’ eyes. But Trump’s monument to himself – one of many — is getting built nonetheless. Asking Congress for the taxpayer money to help with the project came only after the walls were torn down. It has become a pattern during Trump’s second term that the president does something; Congress shrugs; and the Supreme Court allows him to proceed, regardless of whether what he’s doing is, strictly speaking, legal. A week before Roberts’ historical lament, the liberal Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson blasted the court’s conservatives, including Roberts, for allowing Trump’s executive order meant to cut down on mail-in voting to proceed, again on a technicality. The White House has a “Catch-Me-If-You-Can approach,” Jackson said. In the case of disrupting mail-in ballots, Trump may ultimately get caught; the executive order still faces lawsuits and a new injunction that make it seem impossible to impose, at least for this election. Trump also got caught on birthright citizenship, where justices rejected his attempt to set aside the Constitution’s 14th Amendment. And on tariffs, they said no, he could not exploit national emergency laws to upend the economy. He’s still looking for ways around that decision. But on so many other issues, Trump’s administration has picked the laws it wants to follow, diverted funds here or there, and said little in public about what it’s up to. Congress has shrugged. Courts have had trouble keeping up, and the Supreme Court has preferred to let Trump go about his business while things get sorted out. That dynamic seems likely to change, at least somewhat, come next year if Democrats win control of either the House or the Senate. They will try to restrict funding for Trump’s goals. But it will be an interesting question for Democrats who want to replace Trump in the White House in 2029. Should they spend even more taxpayer money to tear down the East Wing behemoth he’s building? They won’t be able to go back and take the coins with his face out of circulation. They can’t un-deport people who didn’t get a hearing . And it will take time and effort, if the next president is so inclined, to rebuild the system of scientific and medical research funding the Trump administration cut back. On so many of the things Trump has done, catching up may not even be an option.

Sen. John Fetterman is lashing out at former aides who accused him of showing indifference toward his work and of routinely skipping constituent meetings, dismissing them as “disgruntled staffers” pushing “smears” to tarnish his reputation. The first-term Pennsylvania Democrat broke his silence this weekend after The Wall Street Journal published text messages and cited former staffers who contended Fetterman has grown more keen on ingratiating himself with conservative media than on the critical work expected of a United States senator. Now, former Fetterman staffers have created an anonymous account on X and are threatening to share further unflattering details about the senator, who is facing sagging approval ratings within his own party amid battles with the left over Israel, Iran and immigration — all as he stares at a potential run for reelection in 2028. The senator bluntly warned in July that he would leave the Democratic Party if it adopts an anti-Israel policy — one of his most direct threats yet. Facing an extraordinary rift with his own staff, Fetterman went public in a statement to CNN this weekend after he didn’t reply to requests for comment from The Wall Street Journal. He called the article “the third hit piece from disgruntled staffers” who have gone after him. “Per usual — lies, half-truths, innuendos, smears and anonymous,” Fetterman said, later adding: “No matter how many smears or stories, I’m proud to continue to deliver for Pennsylvania.” In the statement, Fetterman responded to three of the leaked text messages in The Journal’s report, arguing they were “stripped of any context and circumstances.” In one text message from last September, The Journal reported, Fetterman asked his staff why he had to “keep having to meet” with officials from the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, known as CHOP. “Because they’re worried about Medicaid cuts,” the aide said. Fetterman responded: “Well, I’m not.” In the statement to CNN, Fetterman called that comment a “dumb joke, and for that, I sincerely apologize.” But the senator added that he’s met with the Philadelphia hospital officials “virtually and in person,” pointing to a photo he posted on X . “My office and I always have, and always will, advocate for CHOP, support their requests and any other needs that we can assist with,” he said. The Journal report also revealed that Fetterman skipped a funeral for three police officers killed near his hometown of York last September, citing a text message in which the senator griped at the service’s three-hour length. “This may be a nonstarter,” Fetterman wrote in the text, according to The Journal. In the statement to CNN, Fetterman said he took steps to express his condolences and meet with the family members affected. “On the day of that tragedy, we privately ordered flowers to be delivered for their families and expressed my condolences publicly,” he said, citing a post on X expressing his grief . “In June of this year, I privately attended a Tunnel to Towers fundraiser in York for the families. I met with their chief and the family members directly to express my personal condolences.” Fetterman, according to The Journal, also skipped a planned meeting with three paralyzed Pennsylvania veterans to discuss healthcare legislation. The paper reported that after Fetterman’s staff told the veterans he wasn’t feeling well, he showed up about an hour later in his office appearing fine and then conducted an interview on Fox News. “It was my intention to meet with the group,” Fetterman said in the statement to CNN. “Prior to the meeting I was at home throwing up, so I asked my staff to continue with the meeting which they did. Hours later, I felt well enough to continue the day as scheduled.” Pennsylvania’s other senator, Republican Dave McCormick, defended his colleague on Sunday and vowed to continue working with Fetterman on bipartisan measures together. “These stories are the latest example of outrageously disloyal staff and forces on the Left using anonymous leaks to cancel my friend John Fetterman,” McCormick said on X . “They hate that he is an independent thinker who refuses to fall into line so they want to silence him.” The Journal report is not the first to cite aides raising alarms over Fetterman’s behavior. Last year, New York Magazine reported on a 2024 letter from Adam Jentleson, who had served as Fetterman’s chief of staff, raising concerns over his behavior and mental health. The senator was hospitalized for depression in 2023 for about six weeks and has been open about receiving treatment. At the time, Fetterman had a similar response, telling CNN in May 2025 that the story cited “disgruntled staffers” with a “weird grudge.” Jentleson said on X last week that the recent Wall Street Journal report cited “an entirely new group of staff who have rotated in and apparently find themselves horrified at Fetterman’s behavior.” This story has been updated with additional details.

A man later found to have weapons on him allegedly pushed through a crowd toward Ohio Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton on Sunday and injured multiple people at a fair in Canfield, a campaign spokesperson and the local county sheriff said. “While attending the Canfield Fair, an armed individual lunged at Dr. Acton, injuring multiple people,” Acton spokesperson Addie Bullock said in a statement. “Dr. Acton and Eric are grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured.” Mahoning County Sheriff Jerry Greene identified the individual as 38-year-old Patrick Havas. He is expected to face two charges of assault and one count of disorderly conduct after two older adults were knocked down during the incident, Greene said. The extent of injuries to those knocked down isn’t clear. Greene said law enforcement found two firearms and a pair of brass knuckles on Havas after the incident, though neither of those weapons were brandished during the alleged attack. Havas, of Canfield, allegedly entered the Mahoning County Democratic Party tent, using his cell phone to record Acton as she was speaking to a crowd, and started pushing his way through before being knocked to the ground by Acton’s security detail, according to Greene. “Dr. Acton’s security detail, which was made up of Ohio State Highway Patrol Troopers confronted Havas, and as that was happening, two people were knocked to the ground,” Greene said in a statement. Acton commented publicly on the incident for the first time at a campaign appearance Monday and thanked those who had come to her aid. “We had a rough day yesterday,” she recalled. “I’m so thankful to our first responders and our state highway patrol and everyone who helped out the people who were injured and our prayers are with them.” Acton, the former director of Ohio’s Department of Health, is running against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in a closely watched race for the governor’s office. With political violence in the country an increasing concern, news of the alleged attack rippled through social media on Sunday, with commenters expressing both anger and relief that the incident wasn’t worse. CNN has reached out to the Acton campaign and the Canfield Police Department for more details. According to a Mahoning County inmate listing, Havas does not yet have an attorney representing him. Former Democratic Rep. John Boccieri said he witnessed the incident while standing in the tent. He told CNN that a very “large individual, white male, came barreling through the tent, and started pushing people to the ground as if he was trying to rush her.” He had been holding a phone camera up, Boccieri noted. Two elderly adults standing in front of Acton were knocked to the ground in the rush, and one of them appeared to fall and hit his head on the table right in front of her, Boccieri said. After Havas was subdued and taken into custody, Boccieri said, he helped pick up the individual who had seemingly hit his head and Acton began “assisting and administering care” to him, before her security team returned and escorted her out of the tent. This incident comes in an era of political violence with multiple assassination attempts on President Donald Trump over the last few years and near the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative political activist Charlie Kirk. Ramaswamy’s campaign denounced the incident in a statement on Sunday evening. “Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence,” communications director Connie Luck said. “What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope that no one was hurt.” Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, who had appointed Acton to lead the state health department during his administration, said he was thankful Acton wasn’t hurt and condemned the act of violence. “Fran and I are thankful Dr. Amy Acton was not hurt, and we send our thoughts to those who were injured. We spoke to Dr. Acton this afternoon and she said to share with Ohioans that she is ok,” DeWine said in a social media post . “Violence or the threat of violence at political or public events is always unacceptable.” Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly from Arizona, whose wife, former Congresswoman Gabby Giffords was seriously wounded in an assassination attempt after meeting with constituents in 2011 said he spoke to Acton on Sunday and called her, “tough.” “There’s no place in our society for political violence. An issue that unfortunately Gabby and I are very familiar with. I want to thank law enforcement for stopping this attack. Perpetrators of political violence must be brought to justice,” Kelly said in a social media post. This story has been updated with additional developments. CNN’s David Wright contributed to this report.

President Donald Trump’s administration on Sunday again asked the Supreme Court to allow the US Postal Service plan for mail ballots to take effect immediately, a mostly procedural move that nonetheless underscores the president’s desire to restrict mail voting during the critical midterm elections. In its emergency appeal, the Postal Service noted that mail ballots for the November midterms are already being sent in one state, North Carolina, and that other states will soon follow. The USPS asked the high court to quickly allow it to implement its rule, setting up one of the most significant election cases on the court’s quick-turn docket in years. The Supreme Court was already considering an emergency appeal filed by the USPS on Sept. 3 that urged the justices to allow the agency to implement the new ballot rule ahead of the November elections that will determine which party controls Congress. In that appeal, the USPS asked the Supreme Court to stay a temporary restraining order from US District Judge Indira Talwani in Massachusetts that barred the agency from moving forward for two weeks. On Friday, a day after the Justice Department filed that appeal, Talwani ruled again, handing down a preliminary injunction. That subsequent order blocked the USPS plan indefinitely. It is that second, indefinite block on the plan that the administration appealed to the Supreme Court on Sunday. Shortly after filing the second appeal on Sunday, the administration withdrew the first case. Trump asks Supreme Court to OK sweeping changes for mail ballots In a letter to the court on Sunday, the Justice Department said it had filed the new appeal out of “an abundance of caution” and that it withdrew the first case “to simplify proceedings.” For voters and states, the difference between the cases will make little or no difference. The high court is being asked to rule with an extraordinarily quick timeline on an effort by the administration to give the USPS an unprecedented role in elections. North Carolina has already begun mailing out ballots. Alabama will begin doing so on Sept. 9. At least five additional states will begin mailing ballots on September 13, according to the Justice Department. “Once those ballot envelopes enter the mailstream, there is no retrieving them,” the Justice Department told the Supreme Court in its filing on Sunday. “And while the injunction allows the Postal Service and the states to continue taking steps to ensure that their envelopes satisfy the rule’s requirements, each day the injunction is in place risks sowing confusion and chaos because the injunction makes those preparatory steps voluntary, rather than mandatory.” The USPS rule would require state and local election officials to upload lists of their mail voters to a portal. It would also require election officials to use special barcodes on the envelopes to ease tracking of that mail. Many election officials have argued that it’s already too late to implement those requirements. The administration has argued that the changes are needed to secure the ballots and ensure that only eligible voters receive one. But a coalition of 23 Democratic-led states and voting groups have described the effort as a power grab by a president who has long falsely alleged widespread voter fraud in mail ballot systems, even as he has frequently voted by mail himself. “With fewer than 60 days to go before the November election, there is not a shred of evidence that states could comply with it without disenfranchising voters who rely on mail ballots,” said Sophia Lin Lakin, director of the Voting Rights Project at the ACLU, part of the legal team challenging the USPS proposal. In the appeal on Sunday, Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued that, “Contrary to the claims of the district court and respondents that the Postal Service is trying to federalize the rules for mail-in voting, the Postal Service’s final rule imposes only modest envelope-design and addressee-information requirements for federal-election ballots sent via US mail.” The Constitution empowers states and Congress to set the rules for elections, not the president nor the Postal Service. That was a point that Talwani stressed in her latest decision on Friday. “The Constitution’s elections clause tasks the States with the role of election administration, subject only to Congress’s superseding legislation, and the executive has no inherent authority in this joint endeavor,” she wrote. The new appeal is unlikely to change the timeline of the high-profile case very much. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, who handles emergency appeals rising from the Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals, had required the states to respond to the first appeal on Tuesday. On Sunday, Jackson ordered the states and voting rights groups challenging the USPS to respond to the new appeal on Wednesday, instead. This story has been updated to include new details.

President Donald Trump on Sunday appeared to suggest that New Mexico should be called “New America,” posting a photo of the state with the new name days after he signed an executive order to change Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” The image posted on Truth Social, which was reshared by the White House on X , shows the outline of the state with the word “Mexico” crossed out in red and replaced with “America.” There was no explanation shared alongside the image. The White House has not announced an effort to rename New Mexico. CNN has reached out for more details. While Trump has the power to rename what geographic landmarks, such as bodies of water, are called in the Geographic Names Information System, he doesn’t have the constitutional ability to legally rename states — that process would need to happen within the state. In addition to the renaming of Lake Ontario in the system late last month, Trump also used an executive order to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America in January 2025, on his first day back in office. In response to the post, New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat, accused Trump of trying to distract Americans, insisting that “New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate.” “While the President tries to distract Americans from his disastrous war in Iran, gas prices keep soaring,” she said Sunday on X. “While the White House wastes time coloring on maps, Nuevo México is busy doing the work.” Democratic Sen. Martin Heinrich also pushed back on Trump’s post. “Three things I will always call by their actual names,” he said on X. “The Gulf of Mexico. Lake Ontario. New Mexico.” The state’s name predates the founding of the United States back to the 16th century, according to a fact sheet on the origin of state names from the Bureau of Indian Affairs. Trump has frequently touted his desire to rename landmarks in a show of his presidential power. His move to rename Lake Ontario has come in the midst of tense trade war with Canada. Shortly after signing that executive order, he also teased potential plans to change the name of one of the oceans on either side of the United States. “We have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both,” he said.

The hair gel mostly withstood the Low Country’s sticky sweat. Between events in South Carolina, now fully enshrined as Democrats’ first presidential primary state, Gavin Newsom acknowledged last week’s trip was indeed part of feeling out a campaign. “Obviously, it’s an early calendar state, but, you know, my state of mind was here before,” the California governor told CNN during an interview in the staff kitchen of a cultural center after his session with voters here. “I’d be lying,” he admitted, if he denied 2028 was a factor in the visit but insisted it was further down the list of motivations for his fourth trip to the state in as many years. South Carolina Democrats are in such rough shape that their big aspiration is just winning enough statehouse seats to break the GOP supermajority. But Newsom said he’s truly committed to the state, explaining that he chose to come back to where he campaigned for both Joe Biden and Kamala Harris and traveled on his book tour, because of the relationships he’s cultivated with state party leadership. Chair Christale Spain, for example, chose to celebrate her 50th birthday on Thursday by driving in a van ahead of Newsom’s small motorcade to introduce him at events and touted the $370,000 he’s raised as having literally helped them keep the lights on at party headquarters. (Newsom arrived with a present of a tiara and a birthday sash for her at one stop, and boxing gloves at another.) As staffers set up extra chairs and the temperature rose in rooms not used to that kind of turnout, there was clearly interest in a very California governor in this very different part of the country. But even before this trip, Newsom’s team already knew that he would have work to do connecting with Black voters — who tend to make up over half of the Democratic primary electorate in South Carolina — if he goes forward with a presidential run (or, what some aides have taken to calling “the next thing”). He says that’s part of why he started his Southern swing touring the racial injustice Legacy Museum in Alabama, just down the street from the state capitol where Jefferson Davis was sworn in as president of the Confederacy. It’s the kind of poetic juxtaposition that tends to grab the 58-year-old. “If you’re a Democrat, you’ve got to come back to the South, you’ve got to connect with what’s going on in this country,” he said. For a party in a never-ending neurotic twist over whether they’re talking too much about what the president is doing or not talking about him enough, Newsom is trying to straddle the continental divide: by segueing from recounting how he fought back against Trump through California’s retaliatory redistricting ballot proposition into how that showed him Democrats need to fight differently now. In front of crowds of over a hundred mostly retirees, peppered with California transplants, each in Hardeeville and St. Helena Island, in Summerville and West Columbia — all spots picked by state Democratic Party leaders because they’re trying to scratch out wins far from the traditional Democratic population centers — Newsom delivered a confrontation call to action against the “invasive species” of Trump. In a free-associating stump riff that carried aspirational notes in the style of Bill Clinton or Barack Obama, he told a story of a country battered but resilient. Democrats, and really most Americans, he said, need a hug, giving one to a younger woman in one audience who held a bright yellow “HOLD ME” sign for Newsom to see. He described Trump’s crackdown on diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives as anti-Black and how “capitalism as we know it isn’t working,” but mostly focused on ticking through detailed breakdowns of how he said Americans are paying the price for Trump’s crypto-coin profits and upgrades to the Qatari-gifted jet and more, often eliciting gasps from audiences. But who was and wasn’t in those crowds was hard to miss at Aiken’s Center for African American History, Art and Culture, in a building constructed in the late 1800s to educate Black children, but where the audience for Newsom was predominantly older and White. “I was saying to my wife—where are we? Are we not part of the Democratic Party anymore?” said Bradley Taylor, recently retired from the Savannah River nuclear waste site, looking around for other Black attendees ahead of Newsom’s remarks. Taylor said he wasn’t convinced about Newsom but has his eyes on former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg for his “human connection.” Pete Buttigieg returns to first-in-the-nation South Carolina with a fresh appeal to Black voters His wife Jacqueline Taylor, a registered nurse, was more open to the California governor: “Watching him troll Trump — that kind of turns me on.” After listening to Newsom’s 20-minute routine, Taylor told CNN she felt inspired hearing about California’s redistricting effort, and the way he tied it to Democrats more broadly needing to “draw the line” in what they’ll allow Republicans to do. “I am so thankful for him. If you want to gerrymander and cheat… you’ve got to fight fire with fire,” Taylor said. She said Newsom made her think of what could be done to help her grandchildren: a truck driver trying to make a living with diesel costs high, another in the Army. Listening, her husband amended his initial reaction — “He pretty much said everything I already knew”— to say his wife convinced him. “He’s just saying things that touch us,” said Bill Clyburn, the 85-year-old longtime state representative and a cousin of the state’s power broker congressman, Jim, who helped deliver the Black vote in South Carolina for Biden in 2020. If Newsom runs for president, Clyburn added, “He can do about as well as expected.” Asked what, in fact, would be expected of Newsom’s performance in the state, Clyburn left his comment at a small chuckle. An hour away on Friday afternoon, 25-year-old congressional candidate Zyon Khalifa listened to Newsom’s rundown in West Columbia, liking the feel of a younger politician energetically working a room, and the way he talked explicitly about Black people being targeted. “You don’t hear him trying to code-switch,” Khalifa said. “Instead of trying to sugarcoat it, say it in some way that all audiences would be OK with, he’s just saying what’s happening.” Khalifa, like the Taylors and Clyburn, took a photo with Newsom. Asked if he would use that in his campaign against Republican Rep. Joe Wilson, he scrunched up his face and admitted, “probably not.” Jermaine Johnson, the Democratic nominee for governor, made the opposite calculation, having Newsom headline a fundraiser for him on Thursday evening and then join him for a fireside chat at the historically Black Allen University in Columbia on Friday afternoon. By Newsom’s last event on Friday in Lancaster, a higher proportion of Black faces were in the seats. “I don’t need big crowds, I don’t need to give a speech. I love this connection, I love the human connection, I love the granularity. I like reading between the lines, I like these small groups of people that we’re meeting,” Newsom told CNN. “I learn a lot.” Sen. Jon Ossoff almost didn’t run for reelection. Now some Democrats want to draft him for 2028 The strength of Newsom’s appeal to Black voters is already driving some internal deliberations, advisers say, as they look at Black support among potential primary opponents ranging from Harris to Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff , whose reelection ads often get played on airwaves over the state border. Newsom said he wasn’t worried about the crowd makeup this visit, explaining that he’d been told that was the downside of scheduling events while many people are working. “You come on the weekends, completely different,” he said. “By the way, last time we were here was almost exclusively African-American audience.” When a traffic accident Thursday afternoon delayed Newsom’s remarks in a country hall reception room by an hour, Spain, the state party chair, vamping for time, asked people to shout out which other politicians they’d like to see come through. Ossoff and Buttigieg, who was in South Carolina last month, followed by Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, who’s been through and is spending part of Labor Day weekend campaigning in New Hampshire. When another suggested Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro , she said she’d been told he wouldn’t come until January. Another mentioned Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who’ll be in the state in early October for his book tour. Josh Shapiro couldn’t avoid the questions about him. He decided he doesn’t want to But they waited for Newsom, and lined up for photos after, some in the $5 “Newsom 2028” buttons and $30 “Gavin 2028” hats sold by bootleg vendors who followed him around to every stop. “Of course I’d look at all the options, but I think he’s viable,” said Keri Whitaker, a recent retiree, after posing for a photo with Newsom in one of the bright blue caps bearing his name and the California bear. Most potential 2028 candidates will have a day job during the run-up to the election. But Newsom — like Buttigieg — is an exception: Come January, he’ll be out of office for the first time in a 30-year run from San Francisco supervisor to mayor to lieutenant governor to governor. While that means, as he noted to CNN, that he’s had to start figuring out health insurance for his family, it also could allow him to fill his weeks with events like these —building connections beyond core Democrats who already know him from TV or his social media team’s endless mockery of Trump. State Sen. Margie Bright Matthews said seeing him in person has already surprised her. “I thought he was just a tall glass of sweet tea,” she told the crowd in a church meeting room in Jasper County. “I realized he’s more than just a good-looking face. He’s got moxie.” Taking on Trump over the immigration crackdown, federalizing the National Guard and redistricting is what put Newsom on the minds of so many of the Democrats who turned out to see him. Sitting in South Carolina, he previewed how he’s going to keep that going once his time as governor is up. That effort was on display as he delved back into his late-night June 2025 phone call with the president as immigration enforcement officers faced off with protesters in Los Angeles. Newsom has called the president a liar for claiming to have berated him in the conversation, and he retold his version of the story several times in South Carolina, most extensively in Aiken. The call began with Trump bringing up the 2024 race against Harris, Newsom said, claiming to have won their debate and arguing that “it was a four against one” set-up with the hosts, cameramen and Harris set against Trump. Presented with this account, White House communications director Steven Cheung did not directly dispute it, but told CNN via email: “The only liar here is Gavin who continues to fail his state and gaslight the public instead of helping his state that is suffering under his radical policies. The president called Gavin Newsom to tell him to get his ass in gear, but Gavin decided to disgustingly side with the violent rioters instead of protecting Californians. He is a loser of the highest order and continues to beclown himself on a daily basis.” Newsom, anticipating such a response, said that he has already submitted his contemporaneous notes of the call to House Oversight Committee chair Rep. Jim Comer of Kentucky, and they’re also part of his defamation lawsuit against Fox News, now entering the discovery phase, regarding the outlet’s coverage of the phone call. Fox has denied wrongdoing and vowed to fight the allegations. “I’m in this for the long haul,” Newsom said. “They can say whatever they want. These facts are well established in the court of law and in Congress, and not a word has been said to refute those assertions and facts. And I’ve done them on the penalty of perjury.” An aide to the governor declined to provide a copy of the notes to CNN. Comer did not respond to a request for comment. But he kept his focus on South Carolina, even as a few protesters showed up at some of the stops to lackadaisically hold up signs like “Barking up the Wrong Palmetto Tree” and “Bless Your Heart, Gavin,” or GOP gubernatorial nominee Alan Wilson posting “Don’t California My South Carolina” ahead of his arrival. Pressed by CNN to respond, Newsom tried to weave his record as governor and attacking Trump together with some of what will likely be his more specific, forward-looking pitch if he’s back in South Carolina for the next phase of a campaign. “Minimum wage, universal health care, subsidized childcare, lowering cost of prescription drugs, making sure families are supported or getting Medicaid — I imagine those are not popular, according to (Wilson), which is kind of remarkable,” he said sarcastically. CNN’s Annie Grayer contributed to this report.

The left wing of the Democratic Party flourished this summer as fed-up liberals in key races across the country have eschewed traditional, more moderate candidates in favor of hard-charging progressives. But behind the scenes, ultra-progressive House members and candidates are pushing their own party leaders to reflect more of that mood — arguing that Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and his allies are, so far, failing to grasp the demands of far-left voters who showed up in droves this summer. Those liberals watched in alarm in recent weeks as Jeffries publicly disavowed their marquee “Medicare for All” bill while a pro-Israel Democrat was elevated to a key foreign policy role within the caucus. They also argue his allies were working to undermine a pair of progressive candidates in Michigan and California. “I was very confused and surprised by that,” Rep. Pramila Jayapal, a senior progressive and author of the House’s “Medicare for All” bill, told CNN about the leader’s comments about her signature bill. She added that she has been having “direct” conversations with Jeffries about it. The emerging frustrations on the left offer a preview of some of the pressures that await Jeffries if the party can flip the chamber next year, particularly as a new crop of far-left progressive candidates threaten not to support him for leader post-election. “I think what we’ve seen around the country is that people all over are dissatisfied. They’re not happy with the administration. They’re not happy with the current leadership in the Democratic Party — and are looking for a change,” Dr. Adam Hamawy, a progressive candidate who is likely to win a deep blue seat in New Jersey this November, told CNN. Hamawy is among several candidates fresh off primary victories who have not decided whether to back Jeffries. “Most Democrats, I think, agree that the current leadership is failing to face the moment,” Hamawy told CNN when asked if he’ll support Jeffries. “I have to see what the choices are and what the situation is.” Tensions have long simmered within the Democratic Party, including in its fractious House caucus, where many centrists are privately pleased with what they see as Jeffries’ effort to distance the party from a far-left agenda ahead of a critical election. But the rise of the democratic-socialist wing of the party has drawn new urgency to a major question now facing Jeffries: How much should the party embrace its insurgent left when it’s also trying to win dozens of seats in GOP turf in November? Nearly all progressives who spoke to CNN said Jeffries is still on track to become speaker next January if Democrats flip the chamber, according to conversations with more than a dozen Democrats. Privately, Jeffries has already met or made plans to meet with five of those insurgent Democrats: Hamawy in New Jersey, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York, and Melat Kiros in Colorado, according to people familiar with the discussions. Still, the recent frustrations on the left illustrate the challenge for Jeffries and his leadership team as they navigate the anti-establishment midterm mood within their party. The dissatisfaction goes beyond the upper echelons of leadership: there are preliminary internal discussions among current progressive members about challenging committee leaders and, possibly, instituting term limits for key roles, multiple people told CNN. “Defeating 10, 30-year incumbents should be a wake-up call to the Democratic establishment that the base is moving underneath them,” Usamah Andrabi, a spokesperson for a group helping to power the far-left wins, Justice Democrats, told CNN. (This cycle, nine of the group’s endorsed candidates won primaries, its biggest year to date.) Andrabi specifically pointed to Jeffries’ comments on “Medicare for All” – in which Jeffries recently said he did not support the legislation : “Unfortunately, it often feels that the Democratic leadership and establishment don’t even want to acknowledge the ground is moving.” Progressives, including Hamawy and Avila Chevalier, made clear in interviews with CNN they are coming to Washington to make real progress on an ambitious agenda on affordability and anti-corruption — not to simply antagonize leadership. “We’re not really going in to fight, we’re going in to deliver on what people want,” Hamawy said. Inside the fight for the Democratic Party Yet even Jeffries’ allies acknowledge the challenge awaiting him in January: navigating an intraparty battle over the party’s ideological future. While an emboldened left wing is pushing for a major shake-up in Congress, Jeffries could also face an expanded centrist bloc that humiliated leadership last week when some of its members showed they were willing to defy the party line on key priorities — even if it meant helping Republicans. That centrist rebellion has since triggered a messy internal feud among House Democrats. Privately, Jeffries and his team are discussing ways to crack down on any of their members voting for procedural motions that hurt the party – a proposal that has infuriated the left and centrists alike, according to Democrats from both factions. A tense debate has since unfolded over whether party leaders should create new rules for next year to punish members who defy leadership. In a closed-door meeting on Wednesday about leadership’s push, Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar of Texas pushed back firmly, arguing that members need to be able to voice dissent, according to multiple people familiar with the discussions. But he was immediately confronted by others, including Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz of Florida, who argued Democrats shouldn’t be willing to go rogue on the floor. Those dynamics will be on full display starting with the speaker’s vote in January, if Democrats win the majority. Avila Chevalier, a community organizer who shook New York City politics by unseating a long-time incumbent this summer, told CNN that she recently had a “positive” conversation with Jeffries. But she said she hasn’t “come to any final decisions on that yet,” when asked whether she would support Jeffries as party leader, adding: “It’ll be the first vote I make. It’ll set the tone for the kind of representative that my district will have, and I want that vote to mean something to my community.” Even if many of the far-left incoming Democrats ultimately do support Jeffries, it’s to their advantage not to show their cards just yet – creating what could be powerful leverage to negotiate for their priorities when they first arrive in Congress. Asked more broadly about her agenda for next year, Avila Chevalier offered a range of “day one” priorities such as ending the sale of weapons to Israel, the Green New Deal for Public Housing and abolishing super PACs – as well as other ideas that are widely backed by the party like universal childcare and raising the minimum wage. “It’s time that folks who are in DC or elsewhere who might be comfortable with the status quo to recognize that the vast majority of the people of this country are hungry for something different,” she said. Many liberal Democrats are careful not to openly criticize their own leadership just ahead of a must-win midterm election. But privately, progressive members and candidates remain concerned by Jeffries’ comments publicly disavowing “Medicare for All” and saying he does not support the Democratic Socialists of America agenda in an interview last month with NBC’s “Meet the Press.” Asked if he supports the bill, Jeffries said: “No, as you indicated, I haven’t cosponsored the ‘Medicare for All’ legislation that has been introduced over the last several years,” adding: “I do think we need to figure out how to fix our broken health care system and then build something better.” Jeffries’ allies said his comments also reflect one of his long-time beliefs — that House leaders should not support major bills until there’s broad support in the caucus. Other progressives are concerned that party leaders are not adequately responding to the movement’s vocal pro-Palestine push. They are, in particular, concerned about the recent elevation of prominent Israel supporter, Rep. Jared Moskowitz of Florida, to a Foreign Affairs subcommittee post that could give him influence over foreign policy next year. Multiple Democrats told CNN that Jeffries was not involved in the move – saying instead that it was arranged by Rep. Brad Sherman, another Israel ally, who inherited the role after a colleague’s resignation. Moskowitz, who’s facing a tough reelection, asked Sherman if he could have the spot on the panel to help him with pro-Israel voters back home, those people said. Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, dismissed the left’s criticism, calling the hand-off “standard committee procedure.” He added that Moskowitz had already held an important role on the committee – the top Democrat on the oversight subcommittee, which has since been passed off to Rep. Jonathan Jackson of Illinois. “I don’t know what the left’s problem is,” Meeks said, adding that he believes his committee is “very balanced” on the issue of Israel. Still, the rise of Moskowitz has emerged as a major flashpoint among progressive lawmakers and candidates, especially after Jeffries had appealed to the left earlier this year by declaring that “American policy in the Middle East must change” after he opposed cutting taxpayer aid to Israel during a landmark vote earlier this year. Then there are party leaders’ recent moves on the campaign trail. In California, progressives are furious that their state’s delegation leader, Rep. Zoe Lofgren, tried to tank a left-wing candidate in a bitter fight to fill the seat of former Rep. Eric Swalwell. Progressive candidate, state Sen. Aisha Wahab, won the state party’s endorsement and secured the most votes in two separate primaries for the seat (including a special election) – though she failed to top the 50 percent needed to avoid a runoff. Ahead of that August 18 runoff, Lofgren, a leadership ally, released a video statement questioning Wahab’s fitness to serve in Congress and instead endorsed a more moderate candidate for the upcoming runoff. The drama began after Lofgren and others, including No. 3 House Democrat Rep. Pete Aguilar, argued that California Democrats needed to fill the seat as quickly as possible and should install a “placeholder” Democrat to the seat temporarily. But progressives argued Lofgren was simply trying to keep Wahab out of the role, giving the more moderate — and AIPAC-backed — candidate a better chance of winning a full term for the seat in November. (A person familiar with the subject said the congresswoman wasn’t opposing her due to her progressive policy stands, but rather because of Wahab’s refusal to back the push to install a “placeholder” Democrat to the seat through January.) Wahab still won and was sworn into the House last week. But the cost, progressives say, was millions of dollars in spending in the election that could have gone toward defeating Republicans. Wahab has since spoken with both Lofgren and Aguilar and they congratulated her on her win, she told KCRA 3 News . But one of Wahab’s most vocal supporters, Amar Shergill, a prominent progressive activist in California, told CNN that he still blames party leaders for allowing such a “shocking” intervention against the candidate endorsed by the state party. “I’ve never seen anything like it, it was unprecedented,” Shergill said. “Lofgren leads the largest congressional delegation in the country. When she makes moves behind the scenes, everybody hears about it. It’s impossible for DC leadership not to know what she’s doing.” “It was a tough primary but we’re looking forward to everyone coalescing around her and putting the primary behind us,” said Evan Brown, executive director of the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC. Meanwhile, in Michigan, progressives are fuming that the House Democrats’ campaign arm has refused to publicly promote left-wing Democrat, Will Lawrence, roughly a month after he won a nasty three-way primary there. At issue: The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has so far declined to add Lawrence to a coveted list of their priority House candidates, in part out of deference to leaders of the Congressional Black Caucus, multiple people involved in discussions about the issue told CNN. The CBC has yet to endorse Lawrence after their public battle with him during the primary over his 2024 comments criticizing Black political leaders. Lawrence, a White climate activist who recently let his DSA membership lapse, came under fire from senior Black Democrats, including Jeffries and Meeks for saying Black political leaders “ defang the White left .” Lawrence, in previous interviews with CNN, has apologized for his “choice of words” in that statement. And some House progressives are “absolutely apoplectic” that party leaders have not yet backed him, according to one of those people. “We’re working on a path forward when it comes to being able to support him,” a Black Caucus strategist with knowledge of the situation told CNN. The list, run by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, is effectively seen as a “stamp of approval” from party leaders — a flashing sign for party groups and donors to put their support behind the strongest candidates. Lawrence’s absence, progressives say, is depriving him of a big fundraising boost to help defeat GOP Rep. Tom Barrett. The flare-up in Michigan comes after party leaders did get behind a slew of other progressive candidates in key races - including some who defeated party-preferred candidates - such as Randy Villegas in a pivotal California swing seat. The DCCC and Lawrence’s campaign declined to comment. But one person familiar with the inner-workings of the DCCC told CNN that the group has been “working every day” with Lawrence’s team to defeat Barrett in November. Meeks, who runs the Black Caucus’s PAC, said he’s had “good conversations” with Lawrence over the phone and is looking forward to sitting down with him in Washington soon. “We’ll talk. I think we’re going to get that resolved,” he said. “If you look at him, compared to who he’s running against, we want him to win.”

With less than two months to go until this year’s midterm elections , Democrats are becoming increasingly unnerved about the possibility of President Donald Trump deploying federal immigration officers or troops to polling places. Messaging from the Trump administration about that potential has been mixed. While some, like Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, have largely dismissed the notion of a poll deployment, others have left open the possibility of troops or officers being at the polls under specific or exigent circumstances, despite federal laws that prohibit such activity. Trump himself has been noncommittal. But while he has not explicitly come out to say he would take this step, several of his past actions and comments have worried those who believe he might overstep his authority, or that the implied threat might be enough to keep people away from the polls altogether. “If there is someone in the administration foolish enough to order them to be there, that will be stopped immediately,” said David Becker, the executive director of the nonprofit Center for Election Innovation & Research. “The states are prepared; they will go to court,” he said. “But it may be that there are members of the administration, and perhaps even the president himself, who would like to inspire in some voters the fear that that might occur, and get them to decide themselves not to show up rather than have to go through the trouble of trying to physically suppress their votes.” Here is what top officials within the administration or the military have said about the potential of sending troops or federal officers to polling locations: Concerns about immigration authorities being dispatched to polling places partly stem from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s decision earlier this year to deploy Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers to airports during a government shutdown. While immigration authorities have long had a presence and enforced immigration laws at airports, the large-scale deployment of ICE officers to assist with security and lines was a new development. It also spurred concern about whether polling places could be next , especially given the administration’s broader crusade against what it claims — without evidence — is widespread voter fraud by immigrants in the country illegally. “These are all tools of how the president is trying to think about a much larger plan, which is, if you cannot hold onto power through democratic elections, then adjust democratic elections,” Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a Democrat, told CNN in March. Asked by reporters last week whether ICE officers could be sent to polling locations in November, Mullin left open the possibility that they could be under specific circumstances. “The only reason why we would be at polling places, if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” Mullin said. He later added: “If we’re serving a warrant, we will be where we need to be.” But federal law prohibits “any troops or armed men” being sent to “any place where a general or special election is held.” Exceptions are provided for if they are actively voting. “I hope someone in his office has made him aware of 18 U.S.C. § 592,” Becker said. “That is illegal, and anyone who orders anyone to do that is committing a federal crime.” A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement Friday that ICE “is not planning operations targeting polling locations.” But the spokesperson added certain officers, “if called upon” by local law enforcement, could be poised to “rapidly respond to an incident if necessary.” Mullin’s comments this week echo a response he gave to a similar question during his confirmation hearing. “The only reason why my officers would be there is if there was a specific threat for them to be there, not for intimidation,” he said in March. Caine has denied any plans for active US military troops to be deployed to polling locations in November. In a letter responding to Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a Michigan Democrat who asked military leaders to commit to not sending troops to the polls, Caine wrote the military has “no plans” to send federal military personnel or federalized National Guard troops to voting locations. “Likewise, the Joint Force has no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material,” wrote Caine, who is the nation’s highest-ranking military officer. Trump has not specifically laid out any plans to deploy troops or federal officers to polls this year. But the president has constantly undermined the results of elections he lost or which went poorly for his party, and has made several suggestions or attempts to exert federal control over elections or undermine voters’ confidence in their security and reliability. In January, the FBI raided the election office in Fulton County, Georgia — a state that had been the centerpiece of Trump’s false claims of fraud in the 2020 election, and where the president and his allies previously tried to overturn the results. The raid stemmed from an investigation into allegations of voter fraud in the 2020 election. Tulsi Gabbard, the then-Director of National Intelligence, was at the raid , and her presence generated controversy given that her typical purview is coordinating overseas intelligence operations and not domestic law enforcement. Days after that raid, Trump called on Republicans to “nationalize” future federal elections. That would run contrary to provisions in the Constitution that give states, and not the federal government, primary control over their own elections. After he lost the 2020 election, some Trump aides urged him to enlist the military to seize voting machines. Trump told the New York Times in an interview earlier this year that he regretted not doing so. The president has also signed a pair of executive orders aiming to boost proof of citizenship requirements for voting and seeking to limit mail-in ballots. The former executive order was permanently blocked, while the administration is asking the Supreme Court to review the latter. The Department of Justice has also attempted to undertake a nationwide campaign to acquire states’ voter roll data. Those efforts have been consistently blocked by judges. Trump refused to rule out sending National Guard troops or federal officers to the polls when asked about it earlier this year. He said he would “do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections.”

CNN will host a California gubernatorial debate later this month, just weeks before Election Day as voters in the nation’s most populous state decide who will succeed Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom. The one-hour debate between Democrat Xavier Becerra , who served as health and human services secretary during the Biden administration, and Republican Steve Hilton, a former Fox News host, will be held on September 30 at 9 p.m. ET (6 p.m. PT). CNN anchors Jake Tapper and Dana Bash will moderate the event, which will take place in the Los Angeles area. To qualify for the debate, candidates had to meet the requirements outlined by the California secretary of state; raised, contributed or loaned at least $1 million for their gubernatorial campaign; and received at least 15% support among registered or likely voters in two polls conducted by polling organizations whose methodology meets CNN’s standards for reporting. Hilton and Becerra emerged among a crowded field of contenders in the primary election in June. The race is likely to be a challenge for Hilton, as he seeks to become a governor aligned with President Donald Trump in a state that voted against Trump by more than 20 percentage points in 2024. California hasn’t elected a Republican governor in 20 years. It was 2006 when voters gave Arnold Schwarzenegger a second term. In an effort to sway voters, Hilton has seized on affordability issues and blamed Democratic leadership for high costs in the state. He’s also vowed to reduce bureaucracy. Meanwhile, Becerra, who also previously served as California attorney general and a US congressman for the LA area, has emphasized his years of experience in governmental roles and argued that only someone who has managed crises could fix California’s problems. Early voting and ballot drop-off locations for the general election on November 3 will be coming October 5, according to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber. CNN’s Kaanita Iyer and David Wright contributed to this report.

On Friday, Sen. Roger Marshall took a rare step for a Republican incumbent running in Kansas: launching an attack ad against his Democratic rival. When pastor Adam Hamilton launched his campaign for the seat four months ago, the odds seemed long. The state has not sent a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century, and President Donald Trump has won it by at least 14 percentage points in all his campaigns. But as the traditional post-Labor Day sprint to the midterms begins, Hamilton is optimistic. “People are very frustrated,” Hamilton said in an interview, recalling a recent conversation with a 79-year-old man who handed him a receipt for diesel for his truck and told him, “This is why I’m voting for you.” From the suburbs of Philadelphia to California’s Central Valley, such stories are fueling Democratic hopes that they can not only flip the House but also capture the majority in the Senate by running strong campaigns in GOP territory. If successful, Democrats would both provide a consequential check on President Donald Trump for his final two years in office and begin to repair their party’s tattered brand as they prepare for the next presidential election. ‘One person kind of controls our fate’: Republicans confront growing midterm peril due to Iran war Republicans acknowledge they face historical headwinds as the party in power two years after winning the White House and capturing unified control of Washington. And Trump has not helped by starting a war with Iran that has exacerbated a cost-of-living crisis that was already on the top of voters’ minds. But with November’s midterm matchups largely set, the GOP sees cause for optimism in their financial advantage, Trump’s increasing efforts to galvanize the party’s base and the rise of democratic socialists across the country, whom they hope to make a liability for Democrats writ large. “The issues are going to be the same in my race and everybody else’s,” Rep. Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin said in an interview. “People are waking up to the fact that the Democratic Party is no longer the Democratic Party – it’s the Democratic Socialists of America party.” The GOP push ramped up this weekend as the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc. began tapping into its $400 million-plus war chest for the midterms, a highly anticipated moment for vulnerable Republicans. Starting Wednesday, Republicans are set to gather in Dallas for an unusual midterm convention that is expected to be dominated by Trump. He is scheduled to speak on both nights, and the Republican National Committee chairman, Joe Gruters, has hyped the gathering as “Trumpapalooza.” Democrats are not letting the Republican ramp-up go unanswered. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is sending a delegation of House Democrats to Dallas to counter the convention. And Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, is also heading to the city to help Texas Democrats push back, according to a Pritzker spokeswoman, Leah Hurwitz. Building off the convention, Trump has promised to spend the final 30 days of the election crisscrossing the country for his party, targeting 35 races that he believes will determine control of Congress. Trump’s emergence as a main character in the midterms, despite his unpopularity across the country, has excited Democrats and left Republicans in competitive districts weighing how closely to tie themselves to him. “It’ll be spectacular,” California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom told reporters Saturday in North Carolina, sarcastically praising Trump’s midterm plans. “He’s an historic president – historically unpopular.” “President Trump is not on the ballot,” GOP Rep. Tom Barrett of Michigan, who does not plan to attend the convention, said in an interview. “I’m on the ballot and my opponent is on the ballot, and that’s the choice people are going to be faced with.” Democrats need to flip a few seats in the House to win the majority, while their path to controlling the upper chamber is harder. They would need to net four seats, including some in Republican-leaning states, while defending a few competitive seats they already hold. Democrats generally agree their best opportunities to pick up Senate seats are in Maine, North Carolina and Ohio, and then in tougher territory including Alaska, Iowa and Texas. The 9 Senate seats most likely to flip in 2026 “Democrats have six core offensive opportunities and we are still expanding the map, forcing Republicans to scramble to defend deep red states as we head into November with multiple paths to win the majority,” Devan Barber, the executive director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, said in a statement. The map is not without its challenges for Democrats. In Michigan, Democrats nominated progressive Abdul El-Sayed over the opposition of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who saw Rep. Haley Stevens as more electable. And in New Hampshire, Democrats are playing defense against a strong and well-known GOP candidate in former Sen. John E. Sununu. And while Democrats are encouraged by the strength of Sen. Jon Ossoff’s reelection campaign in Georgia, he is still seeking another term in a state that Trump won by 2 percentage points in 2024. In the fight for the House majority, Democrats continue to add redder and redder districts to their target list. But they still have to defend more seats won by President Donald Trump in 2024 than Republicans have to hold on to seats he lost. “They’re operating on our turf,” said Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee. The nationwide redistricting effort that Trump spent months waging has also given Republicans hope they can stem their losses. But Democrats, seeing a political landscape that has revolted against Trump, believe even some of the redrawn seats are in play, such as those that Republicans reconfigured in predominantly Latino South Texas. In a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll , voters said they favored Democrats over Republicans on the generic congressional ballot by 5 percentage points. They disapproved of Trump’s job performance by a 25-point margin and his handling of the economy by even more. For Democrats, the strategy for the midterms is simple: speak to the mounting economic frustrations of voters, including those who took a chance on Trump in 2024 but now feel betrayed. “The word that I hear almost daily is ‘drowning,’” said Democratic Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan. “Families in my district are drowning, and it is so much worse for them now than it was two years ago.” McDonald Rivet’s district in Central Michigan is a traditional battleground district, voting for Trump by just 2% in 2024. But Democrats are also finding opportunity in places such as Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, which supported Trump by 15 points. The Democratic nominee there, former federal prosecutor Zach Dembo, said the issue of affordability is “hyperfocused” in the Central Kentucky district.
