Kentucky raises the most cattle east of the Mississippi River, he noted, making it especially impacted by Trump’s recent decision to lower tariffs on foreign beef producers . “Really this race is not a Democrat versus Republican,” Dembo said in an interview. “It’s about change versus the status quo.” In many competitive races, Democrats know they need to separate themselves from a national party brand that often polls worse than the GOP and has now become equated, in part, with democratic socialists such as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani . Hamilton, for example, said he is for “strong and secure borders,” calling former President Joe Biden a “disaster” on the issue. “When people in Kansas think about national Democrats, they think about the DSA,” Hamilton said. “I’ve been asked, ‘Are you a socialist or communist?’ My answer is, ‘No, I’m an independent-minded Democrat.’” The Democratic brand is especially under pressure in a handful of races where independents are running strong campaigns for Republican-held seats. In some of those contests, the Democratic nominees have stepped aside to give the independents a better shot. Nebraska is a prominent example. During their first debate last week, GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts repeatedly labeled his independent opponent, Dan Osborn, as “Democrat Dan” as Osborn insisted he would not caucus with either party if elected. The economy is a far more sensitive issue for Republicans, who have to sympathize with voters’ concerns while grappling with Trump’s insistence on continuing the war. Trump said Wednesday he was “not affected” by the midterms when considering an end to the war. Republicans have mostly remained united behind Trump on the war, though their impatience has shown at times. House Speaker Mike Johnson recently said that it would be “great” if the war would end before the midterms, but if not, Republicans “can explain why that was necessary, why we had to complete the job.” Van Orden, a retired Navy SEAL, said the consequences would be disastrous if Iran were to obtain a nuclear weapon. “When I explain that to folks, they’re like, ‘Oh, I got it,’” said Van Orden, who is set to speak at the midterm convention. “And I also remind them, especially my Democratic colleagues and many people in the media, that we’re still not paying as much money for a gallon of gas as we did under Biden. We’re not.” A few Republicans in competitive races have distanced themselves from the war by supporting resolutions to limit Trump’s war powers. Among them is Barrett, who said he is “very sensitive to the nature of prolonged war” as a 22-year Army veteran. “I haven’t budged and this is something I feel very strongly about and I’m going to vote my conscience,” Barrett said. Trump, who has a penchant for punishing intraparty critics, has largely held back as some Republicans in tough races have sought daylight with him. And Vice President JD Vance suggested Thursday that he understood if some candidates wanted to skip the convention to focus on “local” matters. The White House would much rather make the midterms a referendum on Democrats who they say have lurched too far to the left. In some key House races, Democratic voters picked nominees that national groups worry are too liberal to win in the general election. Barrett’s opponent, Will Lawrence, is one of those candidates – and CNN reported Friday about hundreds of deleted social media posts where he backed the abolition of police and prisons, among other things. Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, said he no longer supports defunding the police and regretted some of his past remarks. ‘F**k you…hurry up and die’: Swing-seat Democratic House candidate’s deleted tweets show far-left record Republicans are also drawing optimism from a larger stockpile of money in their national committee accounts. The Republican National Committee ended July with $130 million cash on hand, while the Democratic National Committee had $16 million in the bank, along with $18 million in debt. That money is more relevant than ever after a Supreme Court ruling in June that struck down limits on coordinated spending between party committees and campaigns. The National Republican Congressional Committee has already taken advantage of the ruling by reserving coordinated ads for at least 20 candidates, while the NRCC’s Democratic counterpart has been slower to capitalize. Up until this weekend, however, it was unclear whether Republicans in battleground seats could also count on MAGA Inc. to come to the rescue. But the super PAC began answering that question Saturday when it disclosed $10 million in spending on the Texas Senate race where Democratic nominee James Talarico has vastly outraised Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton by nearly $60 million. Trump suggested Friday he had almost $1 billion in outside money at his disposal and planned to spend as much as half of it on the midterms. “We’re going to spend a lot of money because we don’t want to lose our country,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. Republicans also hope Trump’s increased activity on the campaign trail reactivates his 2024 voters, even if it puts vulnerable incumbents in an awkward position. At a recent meeting of the Republican Jewish Coalition, the GOP nominee for Senate in North Carolina, Michael Whatley, estimated that his state had as many as 250,000 voters who have turned out for Trump in presidential elections but sat out the midterms. “That turnout is absolutely essential,” Whatley said. One Republican strategist working on a battleground House race agreed that Republican turnout is a major issue but said the solution to the problem has to be “much deeper” than Trump hitting the road. “I think there has to be more optimism that things are getting better” economically, the strategist said, adding that the White House lacks a “clear message” about when that will happen. The Trump factor is not the only major variable heading into the final two months before the election. Both parties are scrambling to respond to voters’ rising anger at data centers and the resources they consume. In the blockbuster race for governor in Nevada, GOP incumbent Joe Lombardo and his Democratic opponent, Attorney General Aaron Ford, have traded TV ads accusing one another of being too cozy with the industry. “Data centers are raising our costs, but Joe Lombardo doesn’t care,” Ford says in one ad that replays Lombardo saying in May that he is “wholeheartedly in support of data centers.” (Lombardo, like many GOP governors confronting the issue, has demanded data centers take responsibility for not straining local resources.) Candidates will also spend the coming weeks haggling over whether to debate — and if so, how much. While Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson appear set for four debates in October in their all-important race in Maine, there is more uncertainty in other contests, such as the contest for Ohio governor, where Democrat Amy Acton indicated Wednesday she was not interested in debating Republican Vivek Ramaswamy . And, in another open question, while much of the recent speculation about outside spending has focused on pro-Trump groups, super PACs aligned with Israel supporters and the cryptocurrency and artificial intelligence industries are still sitting on hundreds of millions of dollars that could shape races. Voters can also expect to see more of potential 2028 candidates in the coming weeks, especially Democrats, as they work to show their usefulness to the party and build new allies in Congress. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg is scheduled to visit at least six states in September alone. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro is expected to continue campaigning heavily to flip four House seats in his state as he runs for reelection himself. And former Vice President Kamala Harris is expected to step up her travel for candidates, even as some in GOP-leaning territory have said they would not welcome her support. Harris shrugged off their snubbing in a TV interview Thursday, telling MS NOW, “I support them in doing whatever they need to do to win.” Addressing reporters Thursday, Vance, widely seen as the de facto frontrunner for the GOP nomination in 2028, urged all Republicans to focus on the midterms as some of them, such as Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, have stirred buzz about their White House ambitions. McDonald Rivet said she was taking nothing for granted in the final stretch, even after Republicans in her district nominated a relatively unknown candidate, Tom Smith, over a Trump-backed rival. “I think that this is going to be closer than most people think,” she said. “I think that we are going to have to work for every single vote and run hard all the way through November.”

Lonnie Bunch III said he will retire as the head of the Smithsonian Institution, a role that placed him at the center of President Donald Trump’s efforts to reshape the world’s largest museum organization. “It is with very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude that I announce my retirement from the Smithsonian,” Bunch said in a statement on Tuesday, adding, “I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.” Bunch, 73, said in multiple interviews that his retirement was not related to pressure from the Trump administration to make changes to the institution. It still comes as the Trump administration has increased pressure on the institution, including saying in an August 28 letter that federal agencies may stop working with the Smithsonian if its leadership does not change. The letter cited an earlier report that accused the Smithsonian of moving “toward an extreme political activism that seeks to transform our country.” CNN has reached out to the White House for comment. “Secretary Bunch has pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story,” Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, who is also chancellor of the Smithsonian, said in a statement, adding, “We look forward to working with him in the coming months to ensure a smooth transition for his successor.” Bunch, who has been in the role since 2019, had defended the organization’s independence amid the administration’s intense scrutiny and efforts to assert control over the 180-year-old institution’s content. However, he has also tread a fine political line, complying with the White House’s request to hand over extensive documents about museum exhibitions. In a July interview with CNN’s Christiane Amanpour, Bunch said, “It’s our job to tell an accurate, complex and truthful history.” However, Trump has taken issue with the Smithsonian’s telling of the past, describing it as “woke” and tasking aides with rooting out what he considers a rewriting of American history at the museums. For example, in a July executive order, the president directed the National Park Service to install temporary signage near the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, warning of “inaccurate information.” Greg Werkheiser, an attorney involved in multiple lawsuits against the Trump administration over the president’s changes to Washington, said in a statement that Bunch’s departure should raise concerns. “Whatever words are used to describe his departure, it comes after an extraordinary campaign of political pressure on the Smithsonian and its leadership,” Werkheiser said. “The loss here is bigger than one extraordinary public servant. Americans should be deeply concerned whenever political power is used to make the people entrusted with telling our nation’s history fear for their jobs if they tell that history honestly.” The Smithsonian Board of Regents will choose the next secretary. In addition to Roberts, the board’s members include Vice President JD Vance and Republican and Democratic lawmakers. Some members of the public are also part of the board, and Trump signed an executive order last year directing Vance to seek the appointment of public members who are aligned with his priorities for the institution. Two of nine public regents’ terms have expired and two other spots will open up by the beginning of October, according to a term chart on the Smithsonian website . This could give Trump a chance to try to expand his influence on the board before the November midterm elections shake up Congress. New board members are appointed via congressional joint resolutions that the president must sign into law. Before becoming secretary, Bunch served as the director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American History and Culture for nearly 14 years, leading the site from when it was just a concept to its opening in 2016. He served at multiple museums within the institution since he first joined in 1978. He departed the organization for a few years to serve as the president of the Chicago Historical Society. Bunch has been widely recognized for his work at the Smithsonian, including by receiving multiple awards for his contributions to American culture and history. This story has been updated with additional information. CNN’s René Marsh, Piper Hudspeth Blackburn, Brian Todd, Michael Williams, Betsy Klein and Kit Maher contributed to this report.

A member of the Georgia National Guard assigned to the task force patrolling Washington, DC, is facing assault and gun charges after he was accused of pulling his firearm on a fellow soldier during an argument last month. Zion Mitchell, 21, faces charges of assault with a dangerous weapon and possession of a firearm during a dangerous crime. He’s being held in the DC Jail. Mitchell’s attorney, Gregory Copeland, did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment. CNN has also reached out to the task force for comment. According to court records, Mitchell and other soldiers were sitting in a van outside a Popeye’s on H Street Northeast on August 25 when an argument started about whether the soldiers’ hairstyles followed Army regulations. One witness told detectives that Mitchell told the soldier he was arguing with that he would “slap the Jackson 5 out of you.” It’s not clear what that comment meant. One soldier told detectives she heard a clicking noise after telling Mitchell to shut up and believed he had unclicked his holster. Other soldiers in the van later told police that Mitchell had drawn his weapon. One of the soldiers told detectives they saw Mitchell point his handgun at the solider he was arguing with. A year into the National Guard’s deployment in DC, has crime actually gone down? Mitchell initially said during an interview with detectives that he pulled a pistol magazine out of his vest and pointed it at one of the soldiers during a playful argument. He later recanted his statement and said he pulled out his pistol and pointed it toward the soldier, but said the gun was aiming downward and not at the soldier’s head, according to court records. A judge ordered Mitchell to be held in preventative detention without a cash bond due to the nature of the alleged crimes. His next court appearance is September 15. National Guard troops from several states have been patrolling Washington, DC for more than a year after President Donald Trump declared a public safety emergency because of what he described as an out-of-control crime problem in DC. Data showed, however, that violent crime reached decade lows in the city even before Trump’s deployment. The president also surged members of federal law enforcement to patrol the city alongside DC police officers. Eight hundred soldiers were initially deployed to patrol the capital — a number that has grown to the thousands. The soldiers have become a part of life in DC, patrolling Metro stations, tourist attractions and neighborhoods throughout the city. City crime rates this year are generally lower than they were last year. Total crime rates have fallen by 17%, homicides are down by 30% and robberies are down by 10%, according to data kept by the Metropolitan Police Department. There are some outliers to the lower rates. Rates of violent crime rates are slightly higher than last year at 6%. Another exception to the lower rates: reported incidents of assault with a dangerous weapon — the same crime Mitchell is accused of — are up 40% from last year.

Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas will face Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu in the race for New Hampshire’s open Senate seat, CNN’s Decision Desk projects. The battle for retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s seat could prove critical to her party’s hopes of flipping the chamber in November. Tuesday’s contests are setting several key midterm matchups that could test the status quo in New Hampshire, which has largely elected Republicans in the state government while sending Democrats to the US Senate and House of Representatives in recent years. At the top of the ballot, voters also picked nominees for governor, with CNN projecting that Republicans will renominate Kelly Ayotte for another two-year term while healthcare lawyer Cinde Warmington ran unopposed for the Democratic nomination. With Pappas vacating his battleground House seat, CNN projects that Democrat Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of New Hampshire’s senior senator, will face Republican businessman Anthony DiLorenzo in November’s general election for the 1st Congressional District. Here are the key takeaways: The Republican Senate race tested whether past criticism of President Donald Trump still carries a price in a GOP primary. Sununu, who held the seat from 2003 to 2009 and belongs to the state’s most established Republican family, defeated Scott Brown, the former Massachusetts senator and Trump ambassador who ran as an outsider vowing to break up a political dynasty. While Sununu described Trump as a “loser” in an op-ed backing Nikki Haley’s 2024 presidential campaign and said that he wouldn’t have launched the war in Iran , he still managed to secure Trump’s endorsement along with support from the national Republican establishment. On the Democratic side, Pappas, a four-term congressman from a battleground House district, defeated Karishma Manzur, a democratic socialist who sought to score the latest upset for an ascendent anti-establishment left-wing. Echoing Democratic primaries across the country this year that have wrestled with the issue of US support for Israel amid the devastation in Gaza, Pappas received criticism from his rival over his voting record in Congress and his relationship with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. But Pappas prevailed in the contentious race with a focus on affordability concerns, a vocal defense of safety-net programs, and a strong electoral track record, while also benefiting from about $4.8 million in outside spending, according to AdImpact data. His victory could give Democrats a more clear-cut path to holding onto the seat in November than Manzur would have. But Sununu’s strong name recognition and Senate record could prove troublesome for Pappas. Ayotte, a former US senator and state attorney general, is one of only two GOP governors seeking reelection this cycle in a state that former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024. She campaigned on tougher public safety policies, drawing on her experience as a prosecutor, as well as expanding affordable housing and combating new taxes. She defeated two primary challengers. In her time as governor, Ayotte has had an occasionally antagonistic relationship with New Hampshire’s legislature, despite the body being controlled by her own party. In the last legislative session, Ayotte vetoed 33 bills . Lawmakers overturned seven of the vetoes, clashing with the governor over issues like criminal justice and education. With Warmington running unopposed in her primary, Republicans turned their attention to the former New Hampshire executive councilor’s campaign early and sought to tie her to the opioid crisis . The Democrat previously worked for Purdue Pharma, which produced the highly addictive painkiller OxyContin, and in the early 2000s she fought against a state bill meant to make it more difficult to get a prescription for the drug. She has since said she was not aware of how dangerous the drug was at the time. While Harris won the state in 2024, Republicans have held a trifecta in the state government for several years. When Sen. Jeanne Shaheen leaves the Senate early next year, her daughter could be headed to the House of Representatives at the same time. Bolstered by support from local labor unions and New Hampshire’s other senator, Democrat Maggie Hassan, Stefany Shaheen defeated a crowded field of primary rivals to secure the Democratic nomination. In November, she’ll face Republican Anthony DiLorenzo for the Manchester-based swing seat, which Pappas has represented since 2019. But while she’s likely benefited from name recognition in her bid for New Hampshire’s 1st District, Stefany Shaheen has not been afraid to separate herself from the longtime senator and former New Hampshire governor. A healthcare advocate and entrepreneur, the younger Shaheen focused her campaign on the issue and publicly broke with her mother when the senator last year voted in support of a deal to end the government shutdown without the extension of Affordable Care Act subsidies. “Improving health care has been the cause of my life. It’s why I am running for Congress. So I cannot support this deal when Speaker Johnson refuses to even allow a vote to extend health care tax credits,” she said in a statement at the time. DiLorenzo is a first-time candidate endorsed by Trump. He leaned heavily on his experience in the private sector as a real estate developer and auto dealer during the GOP primary, funneling more than $1.7 million of his own money into his campaign. The longtime GOP donor was also bolstered by support from key members of Republican House leadership as they look to flip the 1st District and expand their razor-thin majority in the chamber. This story has been updated with additional projections.

Back-to-back court orders on Tuesday injected chaos into Missouri’s plans for this year’s midterms, with state officials and a group opposed to a GOP-friendly congressional map racing into multiple courts with less than two months before Election Day. A federal district court ordered Missouri to proceed with a congressional map for the November midterm elections that would benefit the Republican Party by giving it a chance to flip an additional seat, stepping into the case shortly after the US Supreme Court shot down an emergency appeal from GOP officials in the state. The unusual legal machinations left uncertain whether Missouri would head into the upcoming elections with a map that gives Republicans another seat favor as the party has attempted to retain its narrow grip on the House of Representatives . US District Judge Stephen Clark handed down a temporary order late Tuesday that would require the state to proceed under a map created last year that targets a Democratic district based in Kansas City. That decision came minutes after Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh denied a request from Missouri Republicans to use that same map. “Using a different map for the general election would wreak havoc on the fairness and orderliness of Missouri’s congressional elections, calling into question the candidacy of those nominated in the primaries and the votes of those who voted in the primaries,” wrote Clark, who was nominated to the bench by President Donald Trump. “Widespread voter confusion would inevitably follow.” Earlier Tuesday, the Supreme Court denied Missouri’s request to use that same map. The decision was issued by Kavanaugh, a conservative, who handles emergency cases rising from parts of the Midwest. Kavanaugh did not refer the case to the full court, a signal that he didn’t think the emergency appeal was significant enough to do so. He also did not explain his reasoning, and there were no dissents. Clark’s decision said that the plaintiffs in the separate case — led by Republican Rep. Bob Onder — had sufficiently argued that switching the maps between the primary and the general could represent an equal protection problem. The groups challenging Missouri maps have quickly appealed and began filing a series of emergency motions in an effort to pause Clark’s order. Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, a Republican, said that the state was “prepared to follow and comply” the newer, lower court decision. Time is of the essence because the state was set to finalize its ballots for the November election on Tuesday evening. “We maintain that changing the congressional map in between the primary and general elections is simply not feasible and profoundly unjust to Missouri voters,” she said. The Supreme Court’s ruling was the first of several quick-turn election cases the court is expected to decide in the coming days just weeks before the midterms. The justices are mulling a far more significant case dealing with President Donald Trump’s effort to change how mail ballots are sent to voters . And earlier Tuesday, the Trump administration asked the high court to reinstate a controversial citizenship records system his administration has sought to wield for sweeping reviews of state voter rolls. Missouri moved to the 7-1 Republican map under pressure from Trump, who has inspired an unusual mid-decade redistricting war in Republican and Democratic states. “Today the law won,” Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, the group that challenged Missouri’s map said after the Supreme Court decision. “The Missouri constitution is clear as was the Missouri Supreme Court.” If Missouri’s map is ultimately blocked for this year, Republicans would gain a net of nine seats in the US House of Representatives because of those redistricting efforts in other states. Missouri’s new map, which was enacted last year, was used in the state’s primary election in August. But the state’s highest court ruled last week that officials in Missouri wrongly dismissed a petition with more than 300,000 signatures to let the state’s voters decide on the map via a referendum before it took effect. The map targeted the 5th Congressional District, held by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, by breaking up its Kansas City base and stretching it into rural and Republican-leaning parts of the state. Missouri officials had raced up to the US Supreme Court, arguing that the state court decision would create a “federal-election-administration disaster” and “unprecedented chaos.” Organizers of the referendum who sued over the use of the map countered that if there was an election emergency it was Missouri’s own making. Opponents of the map had submitted their petition for a referendum late last year, but state officials waited until August 4, the last possible date, which happened to be the day of the state’s primary, to declare that the state constitution’s right for voters to weigh in on legislation doesn’t apply to redistricting measures. The state supreme court rejected that interpretation. The 6-3 conservative US Supreme Court has played a significant role in shaping the outcome of this year’s midterms. The court’s landmark decision earlier this year gutting a significant part of the Voting Rights Act led to new redistricting in several Republican states in the South. Meanwhile, the court allowed Texas to use a Republican-friendly map and permitted California to use a map that benefits Democrats. This story has been updated with additional details.

President Donald Trump on Tuesday honored the heroes who bravely ran toward the danger during the September 11, 2001, terror attacks as the nation prepares to commemorate the day’s solemn 25th anniversary. He also used the event near the White House in Washington, DC, to briefly plug some of his own priorities, including arguing for his war with Iran and comparing the danger officers faced during 9/11 to the threat of communism — one of his frequent digs at the Democratic Party ahead of the midterms. A crowd of first responders from New York, Washington, DC, and Pennsylvania, along with service members, Gold Star families and the families of fallen first responders gathered on the Ellipse, where a 21-foot, 13,900-pound steel beam recovered from the World Trade Center’s South Tower was on display. “When we see this steel, we’re reminded that no matter what threat or challenge comes our way, America will fight. America will endure, and America will prevail,” the president said. Trump, a native New Yorker, recalled his own experience that day: “I saw things that I never want to see again.” He described a trip to Ground Zero in the days that followed as “raw.” The steel beam, which has traveled from Lower Manhattan to key sites — including the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, and Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Sarasota, Florida, where then-President George W. Bush was reading with second grade students when he learned the second tower had been hit — is part of a broader educational effort to teach Americans about the service and sacrifice of the heroes of 9/11. And it’s a reminder — as more Americans grow up who were either too young to remember the fatal day or not born yet — to never forget. At the entrance to the event, images of more than 400 first responders who lost their lives provided a reminder of the sacrifice. Trump repeatedly praised the first responders, but also drew a comparison between the tragedy and the administration’s war with Iran, now in its seventh month. “We’re right now fighting because we have a certain nation that wanted a nuclear weapon. They were very close to getting it, and now they have no chance of getting it. They will never have a nuclear weapon. Iran will not have a nuclear weapon,” he said. Trump also posthumously honored Welles Crowther with the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Known as the “man in the red bandana,” Crowther, an equity trader and volunteer firefighter, made three trips to the South Tower’s 78th floor lobby to help guide people to safety before the tower collapsed. Trump quipped during his speech that the fallen hero had “become more famous than me. I don’t like it.” The president recognized some of the officials in the audience, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — who at the time of the attack was the president of Cantor Fitzgerald, which had offices in the World Trade Center and lost 658 employees, including Lutnick’s brother. Lutnick has come under scrutiny in recent days after the secretary falsely asserted in a CNBC interview that no Americans had died during the war with Iran. Trump preemptively sought to downplay the remark on Truth Social last week, and Lutnick later apologized for the comment. “He’s got some faults, but overall, he’s excellent,” Trump said Tuesday. The president’s speech also briefly veered political as he heralded the nation’s law enforcement, suggesting that they are responsible for protecting the country from threats — including communism, repeating a theme he’s used to attack Democrats on the campaign trail. “Our law enforcement holds our country together in light of some threats. We have some very real threats right now. We have people that want to go a different way, they want to go a communistic way. Well, that’s not going to work,” he said. Trump is not expected to travel to New York City on Friday for anniversary ceremonies at the World Trade Center, but will mark the moment at the Pentagon. Trump is not attending the World Trade Center ceremony in part because he wants to deliver remarks, people familiar with his plans said. Politicians have not been permitted to speak at the event in New York since 2012. CNN’s Alayna Treene contributed to this report.

The Roman Emperor Titus has one. Napoleon Bonaparte ordered up the world’s most famous example. And the Duke of Wellington’s iconic version is the gateway to London’s Hyde Park. Now, Donald Trump wants his own ceremonial arch. And his latest architectural passion project may tell history rather more about the 45th and 47th president than other examples of his second-term Washington makeover blitz. The Arch of Titus in Rome marks the capture of Jerusalem in AD 70. The Arc de Triomphe in Paris honors the dead of Napoleonic and Revolutionary wars and France’s subsequent fallen warriors. The arch honoring Wellington celebrates the French emperor’s eventual defeat. This history reveals one problem. Trump so far lacks the triumph to justify a triumphal arch. The US stalemate with Iran has revealed deficits in US power rather than demonstrated its dominance. And he recently dismissed the conflict as “ small potatoes .” To finesse this problem, the president billed his planned arch near Arlington Cemetery — which would obliterate sight lines for famed Washington monuments — as celebrating the Declaration of Independence, with a foot of elevation for each year since 1776. But Trump has admitted his building spree is an attempt to impose his persona on Washington in perpetuity. “Nobody will do it once I’m gone,” he recently confided to New York magazine . Even by his standards, the president’s decision to spend so much of his time on monuments is extraordinary. He’s flexing brazen power and revealing a sense of political impunity that midterm election voters might punish if they judge him indifferent to their economic plight. But Trump is not only trying to redesign Washington. This is about more than blinging up statues ; building a ballroom/drone launchpad that will overshadow the White House; or botching the renovation of the National Mall’s Reflecting Pool. Trump isn’t just into the trappings of empire. He wants the empire itself. His foreign policy — bristling with gunboat diplomacy, naval blockades, grabs for other nations’ resources , and a map fixation — recalls Victorian-age adventurism in which military might was matched with trade and finance dominance. Trump is also tapping into America’s own colonial heritage, copying his 19th-century role model President William McKinley’s tariff wars. And he’s expanded the 1828 Monroe Doctrine to lodge a US claim over the Western Hemisphere. Trump’s hardly a history buff. His foreign policy emerged through osmosis from a personality wired for confrontation, life lessons that monetary wealth equals power and a sense that the strong can bully the weak. But America First ideologues have also tried to encode his populist nationalism in documents like his administration’s national security strategy . Top White House official Stephen Miller notably argued on CNN that the “iron laws” of the world mean America must rule with strength, force and power. Of course, this is a stark breach with the US foreign policy creed based on alliances and international institutions that made the US the world’s preeminent power and prevailed over fascism, Japanese imperialism and Soviet communism. Trump aspires to a world of autocrats ruling geographic spheres of influence, with the ascendant US lording over lesser powers like Canada or the EU. This all raises some difficult questions. The sins of empires are embedded in the ideology of the left. And the West has for decades been trying to divert the question of what restitution is due to nations once under the colonial yoke. But does Trump have a point — albeit a politically incorrect one? Is this America First power play a reasonable approach to a world in which the postwar consensus was fraying well before he arrived? In the race with China for contested resources, could a more muscular US posture and a narrower, more nationalistic definition of American interests make sense? Or has Trump misjudged America’s power, and the willingness of foes and allies alike to wilt before it? And does his anachronistic worldview mean he’s fighting 21st-century geopolitical battles, including a growing bond crisis and a Beijing-Tehran-Moscow-Pyongyang axis — with a 19th-century approach? The White House is looking to the distant past to shape the future. Last year, with an eye on China, it appended a Trump corollary to the Monroe doctrine , updating the 200-year-old eviction notice for European colonialists in America’s hemispheric backyard. Its support for right-wing nationalists in Latin America and extrajudicial killings of supposed drug boat operators in the Caribbean and the Pacific are an implicit statement that Trump’s America is so powerful that no law or rival can stop it doing exactly as it likes. Empire vibes also cloud Trump’s deal with Venezuela to jointly exploit 17 oil fields. The plan is to fill depleted US reserves, lower gasoline prices and ease dependence on vulnerable Middle East export routes like the Strait of Hormuz. Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Sunday made clear who dictates Venezuela’s destiny. “We have a lot of leverage over Venezuela. We control the sale of oil outside of their country,” he told ABC News’ “This Week.” “So right now, they are forced to work in partnership with us and they are working in partnership with us,” Wright said. “It’s drawing billions of dollars in investment and it’s transforming that region from a region of conflict to a region of commerce.” But at what cost? Trump’s deal legitimizes the repressive election-stealing regime left behind when he ousted dictator Nicolás Maduro in January. It recalls empires that plundered resources from vassal states to swell their wealth. He’s hardly shying from the comparison, saying on September 1 that Venezuela’s oil was “unbelievable value.” “We’re going to be taking that oil out,” the president said. And Trump now poses as the distant viceroy who will decide when Venezuelans get to decide their own futures. Asked when elections would take place, he said, “I just don’t think they’re ready yet. You know, it’s very new.” Former Venezuelan oil minister Ricardo Hausmann told CNN’s Richard Quest last week the deal “is a scandal.” “I think this is criminal” Hausmann said. “I think this is abusive. I think this is the most imperialistic thing the US has ever done in its history.” Venezuela is critical to understanding the administration’s theory of power. The daring special forces raid that ousted Maduro left it hungry for new conquests. “Nobody is going to fight the United States, militarily, over the future of Greenland,” Miller told CNN’s Jake Tapper after the raid, stating that the US “should have” the vast island, an autonomous territory of Denmark. Such hubris also led the US into the kind of war Trump promised he’d never fight. Now in its seventh month, the Iran war flared up again this weekend with US strikes on Tehran’s tankers and reprisal attacks. Tehran’s conventional forces are shredded. Previous Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei is dead. Yet the revolutionary regime built on resistance to perceived US imperialism survived through asymmetric warfare and drones. Its resilience stretched US naval forces and challenged assumptions about Washington’s power beyond the Middle East. Who, for instance, now really believes the US could win a maritime war against China over Taiwan? The administration might have finally stumbled on a way to get oil through the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz and to choke Tehran economy. But perpetually shepherding tankers would be massively costly. Many analysts believe regime change in Tehran is a pipe dream. And reopening the strait would simply be restoring a pre-war status quo. Back home, Americans faced their highest-ever Labor Day gas prices . Diesel hit all-time highs Friday — hiking transportation costs and auguring yet more inflation. Consumer anger is deepened by another of Trump’s 19th-century fancies — tariffs, which haven’t revived US industry but have hit every wallet. These are hardly the triumphs to justify a Trump arch. The critique of Trump’s infatuation with empire is not that American might is worthless. It’s more about how he’s using it. American hard power — a military shield over Europe and Japan, and policing of the seas — has protected the industrialized world for 80 years. But it was matched with soft power like the Marshall Plan , which rebuilt Europe while Americans came as liberators rather than colonizers. “You know, the only thing America’s ever asked for, particularly after World War II, was no land, no empire, just give us enough land to bury our dead,” former Secretary of State Colin Powell often used to say — in a now-archaic Republican era. Trump is right that Europeans took advantage of America by investing in generous welfare states rather than defense. But by endlessly attacking US allies, he’s also loosening the foundations of American global power. A combined US-North American and EU trade front against China, for instance, would be far more effective than Washington alone. Meanwhile, the US struggles in Iran and what Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has called Trump’s “rupture” with the West suggest Trump’s imperial ambitions are built on caricatures. He’s wielding a big stick rather than understanding what made empires strong. Rome’s wasn’t built in a day; nor were those of Paris and London. It called for a mix of force and diplomacy, forging new alliances and the mastery of localized global politics. Alan Lester, a British historian and critic of the Empire, says Trump sees power “purely in terms of economic leverage or violent, military-force leverage — and sometimes that works.” Thus, in Venezuela, Trump’s regime replacement could yield profits for the US, no matter the moral compromises he’s made. Yet, in the long term, his imperialism is doomed, argues Lester, a professor at the University of Sussex. “Even at its peak, (Britain) was able to project power in so many places simultaneously because it rationed out its military force very carefully, and because of the framework of exactly the kinds of agreements with other powers that Trump finds anathema,” Lester said. Britain kept its grip by dodging wars that would drain its power, through alliances with the Ottoman Empire; via its use of the Indian army to project force; and because of the Royal Navy’s dominance, which the overstretched and under-shipped US Navy may not be able to emulate. Britain’s empire was only bankrupted by two world wars. Trump seemed to understand the peril of overreach after America’s post-9/11 quagmires, pledging in his inaugural address last year that his second term would be defined by “the wars we never get into.” But, stunningly, he fell into the same old trap, and his multibillion-dollar Iran conflict may have already squelched his imperial ambitions. So America’s excursion back to the 19th century may be short-lived. If so, Trump’s new arch may come to stand as not a shrine to personal power but a monument to presidential folly.

The Republican-controlled House last week adopted a resolution denouncing socialism “in all its forms.” But now the Trump administration is attempting something that even many on the right say sounds a lot like one of those forms of socialism. And it’s merely the latest example. Indeed, Trump wants to make socialism the GOP’s big boogeyman in the 2026 midterm elections. But he and his administration have repeatedly compromised that message by doing things that are getting more difficult for their allies to play off as anything other than, well, pretty socialist. The initiative, championed by Vice President JD Vance, would allow stay-at-home parents to collect childcare subsidies by taking the money from a program that assists working parents, according to The New York Times . So basically, the government would pay parents about $9,000 per child per year to stay home and raise their children. CNN has reached out to the White House and Department of Health and Human Services about the draft rule, which would still need to be finalized. The proposal got a decidedly mixed reception Monday morning on Fox News’ morning show, “Fox and Friends.” Co-host Rachel Campos-Duffy (who is married to Trump’s transportation secretary) called it her “favorite policy, like ever, that President Trump has brought.” But fellow co-host Lawrence Jones strongly disagreed. “I see what the president is doing, but I think it’s a terrible idea. It’s socialism,” Jones said. He added on X that “if we are going to defeat socialism, we need to nip it entirely in the bud.” And he’s not the only one. “ Agree with LJ !” conservative Washington Post columnist Marc Thiessen posted on X. “If only we offered a contrast to Democratic Socialists rather than an echo,” Marc Short, an adviser to Trump’s former Vice President Mike Pence, added . “I am old enough to remember a time when Republicans were against government entitlement programs,” said Meghan McCain. “This is welfare,” conservative commentator Dana Loesch said . “We tried this socialist program many times, and it failed. It utterly and completely failed when Viktor Orban tried something similar in Hungary, too.” (Orbán, the former Hungarian prime minister, attempted similar policies to raise his country’s flagging birth rates, but the project ultimately failed and he lost reelection this year.) Former GOP Rep. Bob Good of Virginia called Vance a socialist . Rep. Chip Roy of Texas warned the administration to “ Stay out ” of the issue. And the GOP’s nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, Bo French, agreed . The proposal does have its defenders. But tellingly, rather than argue that it’s good small-government conservative policy, they’ve largely argued that it’s a better way to administer an existing welfare program. “The principle here is simple: Government should not put its thumb on the scale against parents raising their own children,” said Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri. Conservative commentator Michael Knowles said the choice was between reforming the program and leaving it alone, because abolishing the welfare state is a goal “ no one even pretends to think is possible .” And in perhaps the most telling response, Heritage Foundation President Kevin Roberts — whose organization once carried the torch for Reagan-style, small-government conservatism — said Republicans should do what they can to use the money for what he cast as conservative purposes. “The welfare state already exists. The subsidies already exist. And conservatives do not have the votes to dismantle either,” Roberts said . “Until that changes, taxpayer dollars should reward family formation, not subsidize its decline. That is the conservative option.” Defenses like this are so telling because they betray a conservative movement that has largely set aside its ideals in favor of using big government to further its purposes. Over and over again, Trump has pursued ideas and policies that a recent former version of the party — i.e. the tea party version — would surely reject. But because Trump has so dominated his base, the internal criticism has been muted. Some of the more prominent examples: There was an instructive scene about all this last week at a House Rules Committee hearing. While debating the House GOP’s anti-socialism resolution, Democratic Rep. Joe Neguse of Colorado asked House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil whether it would be socialism for the government to take equity stakes in grocery stores. “That’d be a form of socialism, yeah,” the Wisconsin Republican said. But then Neguse asked whether it would be socialism if Trump took a 20% equity stake in the grocer Kroger, and Steil was less firm. “I’d want to see the details,” he said. This was a hypothetical example, but explaining away things Trump does — or outright ignoring them — has become a survival mechanism in a GOP where Trump has proven so successful at targeting his critics. The problem is that with each provocation that his small-government-conservative allies give him a pass on, he moves the ball. They repeatedly give him a few inches, and then he takes a mile. That’s the position the GOP finds itself in. The fact that even the Heritage Foundation is defending a policy like this says it all. And as the gloss has fallen off of Trump — and his excesses have jeopardized the GOP’s midterm hopes — it seems some conservatives are coming to the belated realization that Trump isn’t exactly the great conqueror of socialism, but arguably a participant in it.

President Donald Trump asked the Supreme Court on Tuesday to reinstate a controversial citizenship records system his administration has sought to wield for sweeping reviews of state voter rolls. Voter roll audits using the Department of Homeland Security data program known as SAVE (Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements) have been on hold in most of the country since a lower court found that the administration violated privacy law in how it beefed up the program for voter purges. Critics of the program argue that it produces inaccurate results wrongly identifying eligible voters as non-citizens and could lead to flawed purges that disenfranchise voters. What a Nile crocodile case means for Trump’s DC building projects Trump has made the program a central tool in his government-wide effort to find proof of non-citizen voting. For at least a decade, Trump has claimed that foreigners are tainting elections – allegations that have been debunked in numerous studies of non-citizen voting that have found it to be a rare occurrence. US Solicitor General John Sauer argued in the new filing that the “indefensible” ruling by the lower court “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections.” The new request the Supreme Court used comes after the Trump administration is already pressing the high court to also reinstate new US Postal Service mandates proposed by the president for mail voting for the midterms. Many Republican-led states have been eager to use SAVE to vet their voter rolls for potential non-citizens. But they acknowledge that additional investigation is needed of its results before voters are removed from the rolls. How the US voting system prevents fraud Voter advocates filed the lawsuit after the Trump administration expanded the program to make it easier for states to use for sweeping voter purges. DHS added new sets of data to the program – like Social Security records – and allowed states to upload their voter lists in bulk. Before the changes, states could only use the data program for individualized checks of a voter’s citizenship status. The legal challengers pointed to Texas’ experience using the expanded program last year, putting forward evidence that citizens were wrongly purged from the rolls because of the state’s SAVE review. US District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan, a President Joe Biden appointee, said in her June ruling blocking it that the “federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote.” The DOJ stressed in its Supreme Court filing Tuesday that the federal government was not to blame for any wrongful removals, arguing that the onus is on election officials to make sure that any purges prompted by SAVE audits followed voter registration laws. White House makes new appeal to restrict mail-in voting The Trump administration has tried to condition states’ access to DHS anti-terrorism grants on states’ use of SAVE, among other elections-related requirements. Trump also touted the SAVE system in his July speech on elections, claiming that states that had used it found thousands of non-citizens on their voter rolls. However, some states have said the figures DHS put out at the time were inflated and didn’t take into account how several of the voters tagged by SAVE as non-citizens were shown to be citizens upon further investigation. Currently, a handful of states have been able to continue to use SAVE because of separate litigation in Florida.

Chinese artificial intelligence firms are committing “industrial-scale” theft of their American counterparts’ trade secrets to save money and bring the coveted technology to market faster, US federal agencies alleged Tuesday. Major Chinese tech companies are using “distillation,” which involves training lesser AI models on more advanced ones, to “extract restricted proprietary functionalities and capabilities of U.S. frontier AI models,” the FBI, National Security Agency, and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency claimed in an advisory. Distillation can be a legitimate research technique, but American officials and AI executives have long complained that the volume and targeted manner of Chinese distillation campaigns against US firms amount to stealing. The new advisory puts more evidence behind those accusations and adds to the growing tensions between US and China over AI technology. President Donald Trump has said that AI will be among the discussion topics when he hosts Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington, DC, later this month “The sheer scale of these campaigns and their sophistication indicate that distillation is not a supplement to these companies’ AI model development, but the critical core of it,” the new advisory says. China-based AI firms “use a gray market of proxies known as ‘transfer stations’” to get around US AI firms’ geographic restrictions, safeguards, and terms of use, the US agencies said. They singled out several Chinese tech firms, including DeepSeek and Alibaba Group, as having conducted “high-volume knowledge distillation campaigns” against US AI firms. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened sanctions against Chinese companies that distill American AI. “When [People’s Republic of China] firms conduct covert, industrial-scale distillation attacks that cross the line into IP theft, sanctions and Entity List designations will be on the table,” he wrote on X. “The U.S. side’s hyping of the so-called ‘distillation’ concept is deliberate attack on China’s development and progress in the AI industry. China firmly rejects it,” a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, DC, said in a statement. On Wednesday, China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China’s AI development reflected its high level of self-reliance and strength in science and technology. The US, she said, should refrain from making “unfounded accusations against or smearing China.” “China and the United States are both major powers in artificial intelligence and should strengthen cooperation,” Mao said. CNN has requested comment from DeepSeek and Alibaba. Anthropic alleged that three Chinese AI labs had been behind an “industrial-scale campaign” to extract capabilities from Anthropic’s AI model, Claude. The Chinese labs “generated over 16 million exchanges with Claude through approximately 24,000 fraudulent accounts,” Anthropic claimed . Chinese open-weight AI models are growing in popularity since they are highly customizable, can operate off the cloud and tend to be less expensive. The global race for AI supremacy has put a bull’s-eye on American firms in other ways. Hackers of various stripes are “increasingly targeting AI assets,” Google’s Threat Intelligence Group said in a report released Tuesday. Hackers with a range of motivations have targeted “proprietary AI models and source code,” the report said. “This shift underscores that enterprise AI assets—from model weights to cloud compute quotas—are high-value targets for espionage, extortion, and resource theft.” This story has been updated with additional information. CNN’s Hadas Gold and John Liu contributed to this report.

In offices across the military and in the intelligence community, there have been recent quiet discussions about cutting the number of people and facilities typically stationed in the Middle East if the Trump administration succeeds in ending the Iran conflict, six sources say. If those cuts happen, it would mark another shift in how the US national security apparatus treats a region that successive presidents have sought to leave behind. In the wake of the September 11, 2001, attacks, the US exponentially expanded a constellation of permanent military and intelligence facilities to fight wars and conduct strikes in half a dozen countries: Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Iran, Yemen, Libya. But the recent fighting with Iran has laid bare deep vulnerabilities in the American infrastructure in the Middle East as many of those sites have become targets of repeated Iranian attacks in an unpopular war that has killed 18 American service members . Officials involved in the informal discussions in the military and the intelligence community indicated they are now acting at least in part to predict what might be acceptable to a mercurial president who sources say has articulated no clear strategy for a postwar future — and who, in the past, has staked his political identity on reducing American forces overseas. Those discussions are happening even as there are still 50,000 troops and a large number of military assets in the Middle East, including two aircraft carriers and more than a dozen guided-missile destroyers. CIA officers who were sent home during the hottest part of the fighting earlier this year are being sent back to the region, one of the sources said. The US military is also evaluating how to harden its defenses for those troops who are expected to remain in the region, even once the war ends. That includes by moving some installations underground to better defend against missile and drone attacks like those launched by Iran in the monthslong conflict, according to two sources familiar with the discussions. While the Pentagon has long discussed moving some bases in the region underground, the idea took on new urgency after the first weeks of war as Iran exposed how vulnerable they were to drone and missile attacks. “The vulnerabilities were always known, but the US never acted on it with urgency,” said one of the sources, a US official. The military has developed several potential courses of action for changing the US force structure in the Middle East as soon as next year, two of the sources said — noting it would not make sense to abandon those strategic locations for launching aircraft while the conflict is ongoing. The Office of the Secretary of Defense directed questions to US Central Command. After publication, a US official said the military would “not discuss internal deliberations and we will not speculate on future force posture for operational security reasons.” The Central Intelligence Agency declined to comment. In the background of today’s discussion are the repeated planned pivots out of the region: 25 years of military intervention in the Middle East since September 11 with cycles of promises to pull back. The US military started dramatically increasing its footprint in the Middle East in the years before 9/11, maintaining a presence of roughly 27,000 active-duty troops across the region starting in 1998 — significantly more than in the decades prior. That number would only continue to grow after the September 11 attacks, as US basing grew to support first the war in Afghanistan, then Iraq, then a metastasizing series of counterterrorism conflicts in hot spots around the region. Two years after the September 11 attacks, the US had an estimated 250,000 troops in the Middle East during the invasion of Iraq. Between 2007 and 2011, the number of Americans in the region fluctuated but never dropped below roughly 100,000, according to publicly available estimates. In 2011, then-President Barack Obama announced that “the tide of war is receding” in Afghanistan and that the US would begin drawing down tens of thousands of troops whom he had surged to the fight. The US would not withdraw fully from Afghanistan for another decade. That same year, Obama withdrew combat troops from Iraq in a bid to extricate the US from a war widely seen as a failure. But he was forced to return when the vacuum of American power arguably led to the rise of ISIS. Even as the total of US troops in the Middle East dropped in the years following 2011, it still hovered between 30,000 and 60,000. Throughout that time, the potential threat from Iran also loomed large in the mind of US policymakers, in particular proxy groups that launched fatal attacks on American service members in Iraq. Though planners are discussing options for potential cuts now, the US appears no closer to negotiating a settlement with Iran that would end the conflict. Iran continues to target US bases and forces deployed to the region, launching attacks against American installations in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates last week as the two sides exchanged fire for the first time in roughly a month. The damage has been substantial, US officials say: The CIA’s outpost in Riyadh , Saudi Arabia, for example, was effectively destroyed by an Iranian attack, according to one US official and a former intelligence officer. Although Pentagon officials have sought to downplay the impact, American military installations in Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait have all been struck by Iranian drones and missiles, and sources say the damage has been significant. For the CIA and the military’s elite special operations command, some officials have considered whether the same sensitive jobs can be done without permanent basing, according to two US officials: leave personnel and equipment stationed in the United States, send them to the Middle East for individual missions, then return home. In some cases, the US government may simply decline to rebuild assets that were severely damaged or destroyed by Iranian attacks — in part due to cost considerations, one official and two other sources familiar with the discussions said. Pentagon officials have publicly refused to say what they might rebuild. In April, Pentagon comptroller Jules “Jay” Hurst III told reporters it was not clear how much it would cost to repair bases and facilities damaged from the war with Iran, “and part of it is we would assess what our posture should be in the Middle East.” Hurst later added that the Pentagon does not “have a final number for what the damage is to our installations overseas,” and it depends “on how we decide to rebuild those, or if we do.” Senior Pentagon officials have privately made clear they want to scale back the US military’s troop presence in several Gulf countries as part of a broader effort to shift more of the defense burden onto regional partners, according to three sources familiar with the discussions. Sources said there was no official process or direct order to conduct what’s known formally as a force posture review. Officials within different parts of the military and the CIA are instead keenly aware that even as the military continues to escort ships through the Strait of Hormuz , launch attacks on Iranian infrastructure and threaten strikes against additional targets that would likely further escalate the conflict, President Donald Trump is known to change his mind quickly. “Is there an implicit task? Is there something coming down the pike where we need to be prepared to go, or are we sitting [forward] just in case?” said another US official, describing the tone of the discussions. The CIA was in search of a mission at the time of the 9/11 attacks, former officers and historians say: Its chief adversary, the Soviet Union, had fallen. There were analysts at the agency deeply steeped in terrorism and in the Middle East — but not many of them. Staff in the region probably numbered in the mere hundreds, according to Jeffrey Rogg, an intelligence historian at the University of Texas at Austin. After 9/11, that all changed. The agency recruited heavily and grew a much larger cadre of paramilitary officers who carried guns and worked closely with the US military to hunt out terrorists — a contrast to the traditional picture of a case officer, who was tasked with developing source relationships and gathering secrets. But both organizations lived through the ebbs and flows of a two-decade engagement in a region that presidents of both parties at times wanted desperately to leave behind. Obama sought to engineer a “pivot” of American military and intelligence resources to Asia; Trump’s administration in his first term ranked China as America’s biggest threat in his first national security strategy. But the word “pivot” became a running joke in national security circles as successive crises and policy decisions — including the unforeseen rise of ISIS and Trump’s first-term decision to kill top Iranian Gen. Qasem Soleimani — continued to suck the United States back into the Middle East. Top US military leaders have recently warned Trump that combat options for escalating the conflict with Iran are unlikely to achieve his stated objectives, CNN has reported , with the president instead opting to focus on ramping up economic pressure in hopes of crippling the regime. But there is no clear timeline for how long that strategy may take to produce results, and many analysts believe that Iran’s current leadership may be willing to endure months of economic pain and is unlikely to capitulate in the near term. Broadly, Pentagon officials expect to maintain some of the large, permanent military bases in the region, but rebuilding those installations may depend on the host nation’s willingness to contribute to the cost, which would likely be in the billions of dollars, one of the sources told CNN. The source added that many were originally constructed and paid for by the country in which they reside. In the short term, US troops and bases in neighboring countries will almost certainly face continued attacks from Iran. The Navy’s top admiral said last week that personnel would not be returning to Bahrain, the traditional home of the 5th Fleet, “anytime soon.” “We’re not getting back in there anytime soon,” Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle said. “I just want to be completely honest with that.” The story has been updated with additional reporting.

The Trump administration took sweeping actions against Iran’s airline industry on Tuesday as part of its pressure campaign on Tehran. The latest sanctions hit 27 Iranian airlines and nine service providers and sales agents accused of providing services to Mahan Air, which has been sanctioned since 2011. Mahan Air is a private Iranian airline accused of providing key support to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. The service providers and sales agents sanctioned Tuesday are in Turkey, Malaysia, Kazakhstan and the United Arab Emirates. “These jurisdictions have been on notice for some time, and now we’re moving quite directly to essentially cut off those operators from the Western financial system,” a Treasury official said Tuesday. It is not the first time the administration has targeted operators in other countries for allegedly supporting Mahan Air. In addition, the US Treasury Department is “effectively today terminating all licenses that related to aviation,” the official said, including “payments for overflights of Iranian airspace, authorizations that have allowed non-US airlines that were flying US export-controlled airplanes into Iran.” “We’ve also pulled back on a general license for safety and other emergency aviation support,” they said, noting they could consider such licenses on a case-by-case basis. “Essentially, we’re taking the entire aviation sector of the Iranian economy out of the market,” they said. The latest measures come as the administration seeks to cut off Tehran’s financial lifelines and stop its ability to fund the ongoing war. Administration officials like Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have raised the prospect of regime change in connection to the sanctions. Richard Nephew, a former US deputy special envoy for Iran, said the new airline sanctions “could be meaningful but mostly as a way of making it hard to engage in clandestine procurement and similar given the blockade” the US has maintained in the Strait of Hormuz. “Tourism has dried up, not surprisingly, so this mainly hinders business and cargo transfers,” he told CNN. “If we take the next stop and threaten airports providing services, (it) could reduce overall transit.” Still, experts and diplomats have questioned the overall impact the new sanctions campaign, dubbed “Operation Economic Outcast,” will have on Tehran, which has withstood decades of economic pressure. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi scoffed at the latest sanctions efforts by the US. “After 47 years of sanctions, the US went to war with Iran on behalf of Israel. The fallout has been disastrous for America, including its standing worldwide,” he wrote on X. “After failing to achieve its aims through sanctions or war, Washington’s ‘novel’ solution is…more sanctions. Seriously?” The Treasury official on Tuesday claimed there are a “number of different economic indicators” and “a number of different anecdotes that we’re seeing that sort of suggest and sort of show the effect that this is having.” There has also been deep skepticism from experts and diplomats that the US will take meaningful action against key Iranian partners like China. “We have more in common with the Chinese on Iran than we disagree with them on,” Bessent said at an event on the sidelines of the G20 Finance Ministers meeting last week, referencing nuclear weapons and freedom of navigation. Asked about conversations and possible points of agreement with Beijing, another Treasury official said Tuesday that Bessent has “had a number of conversations with lots of foreign counterparts about these issues, and some of those conversations are best kept private.” “Just know that there is a level of progress being made, even if you may not see it publicly,” the official said without specifically referring to China.

At least seven oil tankers have been struck in and beyond the Persian Gulf since Tuesday evening local time, as the United States and Iran step up tanker attacks in what could mark a dangerous new phase in the war. The escalation led global oil prices to rise briefly above $100 per barrel for the first time since July. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, rose 2.3% before falling back slightly. Late Tuesday, the US military struck five Iranian tankers, sinking one, after Iran fired ballistic missiles at a US Navy warship. Four crude oil carriers in the Gulf of Oman and one near Kharg Island – a hub for Iranian oil exports in the Persian Gulf – were struck, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said. One of the ships, identified as the M/T Riesco, is seen on fire and sinking in the Gulf of Oman in a video posted to X by the military. US forces instructed the crews of the vessels they targeted to abandon ship prior to striking, CENTCOM said. Iran retaliated by firing a barrage of missiles toward regional US ally Jordan, saying it was targeting Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, a key facility used by US forces. The barrage was ineffective in face of integrated air and missile defenses, a US official told CNN. The Jordanian army said its air defenses dealt with 20 ballistic missiles, 18 of them successfully destroyed, with two falling in unpopulated areas. Global oil prices hit $100 per barrel as Middle East conflict roils markets On Wednesday, two tankers in the Gulf were struck by drones. One was off Dubai’s coast, the other in Iraqi waters. A seafarer was killed in an incident involving the Gibraltar-flagged oil products tanker Hercules Star while at anchorage ⁠off Dubai, the vessel’s charterer, Peninsula, said on ⁠Wednesday. It gave no cause of death. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade ⁠Operations (UKMTO) center said earlier that a vessel in the same area was seen listing, indicating that it could be taking on water after an attack from an “unknown projectile. Further north, a Panama-flagged tanker was struck by an unknown source in Iraqi waters, causing damage to the vessel’s hull, according to the Iraqi Ministry of Transport. The incident caused no casualties or injuries among the crew, the ministry said. There’s been no claim of responsibility for the attacks on the two tankers. But Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had warned “all crews aboard oil tankers in the vicinity of ports in Kuwait and Bahrain – which host these (US) terrorists and are partners in their hostile actions – to immediately leave their vessels, whether they are at anchor or docked at the ports, as the vessels will be targeted.” The US strikes were in response to Iranian attempts to attack a US Navy ship over the past two days. The US ship evaded the missiles and was continuing to patrol regional waters, CENTCOM said, adding that “no American personnel were harmed.” The exchange of strikes comes as the US has focused its strategy on ramping up economic pressure on the Tehran regime, while conducting escort operations for commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz and maintaining its naval blockade on Iranian ports. Over the weekend US forces hit three Iranian crude oil carriers in response to an Iranian attempt to attack a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer. Iran’s repeated attempts to attack US warships and the increased “quality and quantity” of the missiles it fired at US targets in the region showed “a pattern of gradual escalation,” said Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, on X . US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, during his trip to Colombia , warned Tehran that the US would respond every time Iran targeted its naval ships. “Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships and for every time they do that, or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” he told reporters in the city of Barranquilla. Iran has also announced that it will expand its maritime restriction zone in the Persian Gulf region. ‘Surge in construction’ at suspected Iranian nuclear site, analysts say, as US considers ways to strike deep underground A spokesman for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), General Hossein Mohebbi, said the expanded zone would start “approximately from the direction of Chabahar,” an Iranian port city on the Gulf of Oman, and would include “another part of the Arabian Sea along the route leading to the Strait of Hormuz.” Exact coordinates would be announced later, he said. Tehran has sought to maintain leverage over transits through the strait as a way to keep oil prices high and put pressure on the Trump administration. Gasoline prices in the US climbed to a fresh three-month high above $4.15 a gallon on Tuesday. This story has been updated with additional information. CNN’s Eleni Giokos, Eyad Kourdi, Thomas Bordeaux and Yasha Saebi contributed reporting.

EDITOR’S NOTE: Peter Bergen is a CNN national security analyst, a vice president at New America, a professor of practice at Arizona State University and the author of the just published, “ All the Presidents’ Wars: Twenty-Five Years of America’s War on Terror ,” from which this piece was, in part, adapted. Friday marks the 25th anniversary of the attacks of September 11, 2001 . Since 9/11, US presidents have expanded their power, step by step, to wage war anywhere, anytime, as they please. With Operation Epic Fury in Iran, President Donald Trump reached a new peak in the war-making powers claimed by the US commander in chief. Trump launched his war of choice on Iran — in his words, “the world’s No. 1 state sponsor of terror” — without any congressional authorization, the support of NATO allies or a UN resolution. There was also scant buy-in from the American public for what was at its outset the least popular war of the modern era, nor was there anything resembling an imminent threat to the United States. Nor had Trump bothered to learn anything from past American wars, and he did not have a real plan for the “day after” hostilities commenced. The US military has long been adept at breaking things and killing people, but when its tactics were not aligned with a clear strategy, the United States ended up in the quagmire of Vietnam, or the sectarian civil war in Iraq that eventually birthed ISIS, or precipitating a possible global economic recession caused by the Iran war. Trump’s predecessors also laid the groundwork for the Iran war. The “war on terror” morphed over time in the months after 9/11, beyond the war in Afghanistan against the Taliban and al Qaeda that was backed by the UN and NATO allies. It then grew to encompass President George W. Bush’s doctrine of “preventive war” that justified the 2003 invasion of Iraq. That invasion led to a civil war during which an estimated 200,000 Iraqi civilians died. The war on terror expanded to include President Barack Obama’s prolific use of armed drones in countries such as Pakistan and Yemen that were not at war with the United States; attacks that killed thousands of suspected terrorists and a sizeble number of civilians. With UN and NATO support, Obama also ordered the campaign to remove the Libyan dictator Moammar Gadhafi from power in 2011, but Obama didn’t seek approval from Congress. The overthrow of Gadhafi precipitated a civil war in Libya that lasted a decade, and the country continues to be divided, ruled today by two governments. Obama later said that not planning for the “day after” Gadhafi’s fall was his greatest failure as president. During the “global war on terror,” the United States cycled through a variety of strategies and tactics, some of which backfired spectacularly. Those include Bush’s Iraq invasion and the bipartisan fiasco of the US withdrawal from Afghanistan more than a decade and a half later, an agreement negotiated under Trump and executed under President Joe Biden. The US pullout from Afghanistan predictably resulted in the Taliban taking over the country. The debacles of the Iraq War and the Afghanistan withdrawal signaled that the US superpower had little idea what it was doing when it came to foreign policy, which undercut its position around the world. There were some real American operational successes during the war on terror: The CIA became an effective paramilitary agency hunting and killing terrorists; Joint Special Operations Command transformed from a barely used counterterrorism force to an industrial-level killing machine; US Special Forces partnered adeptly with Afghan and Iraqi ground forces; and the National Security Agency skillfully penetrated enemy communications. All these developments played important roles in eventually decimating the leadership of al Qaeda and ending the geographical “caliphate” of ISIS. As a result, there were no large-scale lethal attacks by foreign terrorist groups in the United States following 9/11, which was a major national security goal of the four post-9/11 presidents. Last fall, Trump dramatically expanded the ambit of the war on terror when he claimed that he could kill suspected Latin American drug cartel members at will on the grounds that they were “narcoterrorists.” This resulted in dozens of American strikes on boats transporting drugs in the Caribbean, and when US Joint Special Operations Command captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in early 2026, Trump asserted he was a narcoterrorist. Encouraged by what he termed the “brilliant” operation to remove Maduro from power, Trump soon issued the order for Operation Epic Fury. This echoed the way the relatively quick war to overthrow the Taliban after 9/11 emboldened Bush to launch the war on Iraq a year and half later. A lesson that the United States never learned after 9/11: Make real plans for the “day after” the war appears to be won, or you will likely lose the peace.
