The Bush administration didn’t negotiate a peace agreement with the Taliban after the group was utterly defeated in December 2001 when many of its leaders were looking to cut a deal, which could have avoided many years of war. The many failures to plan for what followed the fall of Saddam Hussein’s regime in Iraq were well known, and yet only eight years later the Obama administration also made no plan for what happened after the overthrow of Gadhafi. The confusion about what constituted American strategic success and merely tactical US wins was particularly evident during the Iran war when the many military victories against the theocrats in Tehran did not produce any meaningful change in the regime. As Trump himself admitted during the first days of the conflict: “You go through this, and then in five years you realize you put somebody in who’s no better.” This grim prediction would come true in only a matter of weeks. The United States’ dismal record of regime changes in the post-9/11 Middle East also did not inspire confidence that America’s regime decapitation project in Iran would have a happy ending. Meanwhile, the Iranian regime has wielded its newfound control of the Strait of Hormuz to inject great turmoil into the gas and oil markets that fuel the global economy. Twenty-five years after 9/11, the United States, which once prided itself on being the guarantor of global order, is now its chief disruptor.

Brandon Herrera, the Republican nominee for a key Texas congressional district, has repeatedly made vulgar sexual statements and derogatory comments about the appearance and intelligence of women, according to a CNN review of his videos, social media, and podcasts. Herrera downplayed his controversial comments, which he made as a right-wing online personality known as “The AK Guy,” by describing them as jokes. But the remarks surfaced by CNN underscore the uncomfortable position top Republican leaders face as they embrace Herrera in a district where the incumbent GOP congressman resigned over sexual misconduct allegations – and where Herrera’s Democratic opponent is a woman. In the videos and other material reviewed by CNN, Herrera compared feminists’ weight to whales and nuclear bombs, joked that he was irresistible to “fat b*tches” after rubbing ranch dressing on his body, and described liberal women discussing guns as “both fat and wrong.” He also lobbed sexually explicit insults at a gun safety advocate and her children. Herrera, who has an audience of more than 4 million subscribers on his gun-focused YouTube channel, is seeking to replace GOP Rep. Tony Gonzales, who resigned in April amid a House Ethics Committee probe into his relationship with a former senior aide. He now faces Katy Padilla Stout in a Republican-leaning district where Democrats believe his controversial past could give them a path to victory. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee recently added the seat to its “target” list and sent funding to Stout, a former teacher and attorney who has sought to capitalize on Herrera’s past comments. Republican leaders, meanwhile, including House Leader Mike Johnson and President Donald Trump, have spoken up for Herrera, with Trump promising voters on Truth Social that “HE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” Beyond the political consequences, one expert in online speech who reviewed CNN’s findings described Herrera’s statements as representative of Internet misogyny and said such content can result in real-world damage. “I think if we want a safer society overall, we should also be worried about candidates like this who help normalize things that we know are reliable predictors of political violence,” said Cynthia Miller-Idriss, who oversees the Polarization & Extremism Research & Innovation Lab (PERIL) at American University. Miller pointed to research her lab has done suggesting that spreading misogynistic statements can fuel extremists willing to commit real-life violence. Herrera, in a statement to CNN, characterized his past comments about women as jokes and pushed back on Miller-Idriss’s assertion. He also criticized Stout’s legal work last year on behalf of a father seeking to restore parental rights after a domestic abuse allegation. “It’s disappointing that CNN would allow someone to allege that jokes about feminism lead to violence when Stout is fighting to return children to the parent convicted of abusing them,” Herrera said. Stout’s campaign, in a statement to CNN, said that she was appointed by the court to represent the father in an appeals case and that her “ethical obligation was to represent her client,” adding that “there is simply no comparison to the career Katy has dedicated to serving children and families, and the career Brandon Herrera has made mocking them.” Herrera, 30, is a co-owner of Firearms Direct Club, which sells members weapons at wholesale prices. A self-described Second Amendment “absolutist,” he has also amassed millions of YouTube subscribers by reviewing gun memes, re-enacting historical shootings, and testing and building firearms. He also posts comedic clips performing gun-related gags, like stuffing food into a rifle. The same edge that made Herrera an online conservative star, though, has dogged him as he’s sought to shift into elected office. When he challenged Gonzales in a primary in 2024 – arguing the incumbent was weak on gun rights for backing a safety bill passed after the school killings in Uvalde, Texas – Herrera’s online jokes about Nazis and veteran suicides emerged as liabilities. Herrera described the comments, including a video where he called a Nazi-era gun “the original ghetto blaster,” as part of his comedic persona, posting on X that “I am not, nor have I never been a neo-Nazi.” But the Republican Jewish Coalition condemned him in the 2024 race, referring to him as “a goose-stepping extremist,” and he narrowly lost a runoff with Gonzales. This year, Herrera again challenged Gonzales, beating him in the first round of the March primary. Soon after, Gonzales dropped out amid the House Ethics probe. In his voluminous online content, Herrera took frequent aim at women he politically disagreed with – especially feminists, whom he often refers to as “blue hairs,” and gun safety advocates. At a 2024 event with former Rep. Matt Gaetz, Herrera said that the weight of the world’s population was equivalent to about two dozen feminists, according to the San Antonio Current and other outlets in attendance. Earlier this summer in a YouTube video, he said “when a blue hair on the news says that a semi-automatic AR-15 is an assault rifle, she is both fat and wrong.” Herrera also denigrated feminists’ intelligence, saying in a 2023 video that a gun range dummy’s empty head was “full of mush – much like the average Austin feminist.” In one video from 2023, Herrera said that Cold War-era nuclear bombs weigh “approximately four times as much as the average Austin feminist.” In another 2024 video, Herrera compared the weight of “angry blue-haired” feminists to killer whales and elephants. He also joked in a podcast appearance that “there’s no ugly women in Norway” because “the Vikings didn’t take the ugly ones.” He went on to say that “is why all the women in Siberia are built like f*cking refrigerators.” Herrera also made sexually explicit jokes aimed at women’s weight. In a video from 2021, Herrera suggested his audience was “manning the harpoons” – online slang for sleeping with overweight women after a night of heavy drinking. In another video, Herrera shot at bottles of ranch and rubbed dressing onto his arm, saying it would “make me irresistible to the fat bitches.” Miller-Idriss argued that the comments went beyond attempts at humor – particularly Herrera’s comparison of women’s weight to animals, which she described as a “way to put women in their place, to diminish their power, their authority, to belittle or degrade.” She added, “If you’re referred to as an animal, you’re not actually even fully human, right?” Herrera also employed crass sexual language when discussing women, according to the content reviewed by CNN. Over the summer, Patriot Takes, a social media channel dedicated to posting old videos of Republicans, resurfaced a 2022 clip of Herrera denigrating gun-safety advocate Shannon Watts by using offensive sexual slang to describe Watts and then saying that her being a mother “doesn’t mean I have to give a shit about your political opinions.” He also used a vulgar term to describe her children – an action he bragged about in a follow-up tweet. When a reporter from the Austin American-Statesman asked him about the comments earlier this summer, Herrera doubled down — and his campaign responded with a joking photo referring to the vulgar remarks. Watts and her group Moms Demand Action faced other insults from Herrera, CNN found. Earlier this year, Herrera referred to the women in the group as “M’s” and not “MILFs,” a slang referring to sexually desirable mothers. In an interview with CNN, Watts said that the online abuse she faces on both sides of the aisle is “worse than it’s ever been” – amplified by social media feeds rewarding inflammatory content like Herrera’s statements. “When I started Moms Demand Action, I had no idea I would receive threats of death and sexual violence,” she said. “What I noticed right away was the attacks on me were much different than men who supported gun safety. It was obviously very gendered and misogynistic.” In his videos, Herrera also shared sexually explicit content of women inappropriately using guns, like when he shared a story of an adult content creator who accidentally shot herself in the vagina. In another video, he told his audience that he named a gun after the adult film star Stormy Daniels, explaining that it’s “because it’s been through so much hell and abuse and we’ve run the shit out of it to just abuse it thoroughly.” In a separate video posted a few months later, he bragged that his team has buried, blown up, and generally “been an asshole” to the gun, again calling it by the Stormy Daniels name. Herrera also repeatedly referred to “thots” – a slang term meaning “that ho over there.” In one video from 2019, Herrera said he wore a wedding ring despite being unmarried as “thot repellant.” During one of his “meme review” videos, Herrera responded to a picture of a cartoonishly sexualized young model inside of a gun safe by dramatically shouting “be gone, thot.” He added that “she’s probably got diseases I can’t pronounce.” And although Herrera at times talked about his respect for female gun owners, he also belittled “gun bunnies” – online slang for scantily clad women who post content with weapons. In videos reviewed by CNN, he joked several times that they would do anything for gun discounts and attention. In another video, he shared an online post saying that “gun bunnies” wore masks to hide herpes. As he pushes toward the midterm election, Herrera said he expects his online commentary to continue to be an issue. “For better or worse, my entire life is on the internet. So, I am an open book in that regard,” he said in a recent LA Times interview, arguing that voters will care more about his stances in favor of broader gun rights and tighter border security. Cognizant of the razor-thin margins needed to maintain congressional control, the GOP has largely coalesced around Herrera, with major figures like Speaker Johnson rallying with him in San Antonio earlier this summer. In his endorsement of Herrera, Trump wrote on Truth Social that “Brandon is strongly supported by many Highly Respected MAGA Warriors in Texas, and Republicans in the US House.” But some other conservatives have continued to push back – including the Republican Jewish Coalition. The group continues to criticize him, with a spokesperson telling Politico it “has a longstanding policy of speaking out against those who traffic in Nazi ideology, and this is another case.” Democrats are aiming to turn his work as “The AK Guy” into an electoral liability. “Brandon Herrera’s disturbing history of extremism … and antisemitic rhetoric puts this open Congressional district squarely in play,” said DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene after announcing her group would financially back his opponent. Watts, the gun-safety advocate who has sparred with Herrera online, told CNN she hoped his comments about women would resonate with voters. “The idea to me that this would be a man who had the power and control to take away women’s rights… That should be terrifying to all women,” she said. These days, it’s easier than ever to conduct some form of polling and as difficult as it’s ever been to get it right. Completely faked numbers like a phony “poll” of the Los Angeles mayoral race that made waves last month are thankfully rare. That said, even real polls can have serious flaws in the ways they’re conducted or an agenda behind their release. And the most rigorous polling doesn’t come with any guarantees. But if read carefully, high-quality polls can still tell you a lot about how this year’s midterms are shaping up – and keeping a few simple questions in mind can help you sort through the overwhelming and sometimes overblown deluge of data. At CNN, we ask pollsters to answer more than a dozen questions about their work before we cover it, from revealing who paid for the poll to sharing the technical details of their sampling and weighting. Even if you’re not an expert on methodology, there are a few things you can look for to get a sense of whether a poll is worth your time – and to get the most information out of its results. Here are some of the most important questions to ask: As a starting point, look for pollsters who are transparent about what they’re doing. If there aren’t many details available about who conducted and sponsored the poll, how they carried it out or what questions they asked, that’s your first sign to be skeptical. For an idea of what that methodological information might look like, you can read more about how CNN conducts its own polling here or find detailed explanations of how outlets like the Pew Research Center or The New York Times conduct their surveys. The American Association for Public Opinion Research also has a helpful guide to the information you should be looking for . Fundamentally, polls work by talking to relatively small groups of people who are selected to be demographically representative of a much larger universe (say, “adults in the US,” or “people who are likely to vote in the next election”). How do pollsters choose which people to talk to? In past decades, many did so by calling a randomly selected set of phone numbers. These days, very few polls are conducted by interrupting Americans’ dinners with calls to their landlines. Instead, pollsters are trying to reach people however they can, whether that’s through cell phone calls, text messages, postcards in the mail, panels of people who’ve agreed to answer surveys or a combination of all these approaches. What’s critically important across these methods, though, is that the people taking any individual survey are selected by the pollster, not the other way around. Feel free to ignore “polls” that let anyone answer, which can’t reflect the opinions of anybody beyond those who happened to answer. When looking at the sample size of a poll, keep in mind that a relatively small but representative sample is better than a very large, unrepresentative one. But a small sample does increase the margin for error, particularly among subgroups of people – like young voters, or those from minority groups – that make up only a smaller share of the population. Polls shouldn’t come out of nowhere. Look for polls that are transparent about the people who conducted them, and the precise survey companies or tools they used to carry them out. If the pollster has a track record of previous work – or if they’ve never released polling before – that’s helpful context, too. It’s also important for polls to disclose who, if anyone, funded their surveys, whether that’s a media outlet, a think tank, or a campaign. Anyone putting in the time and effort to conduct a survey has a reason for doing so. Sometimes, that’s simply to inform the public. But campaigns are often selective in releasing only internal data that supports the narrative they want to share, or that might drive fundraising and engagement, and advocacy groups are often trying to shape a conversation around the policies they support. The way a poll question is framed can have major impacts on the results of the poll, particularly around unfamiliar candidates or complicated topics. So can the order that questions were asked in – for instance, a neutrally worded question about a choice between two candidates can still be thrown out of balance if voters were first asked a series of questions about controversies facing one candidate. Look for polls that share the exact wording of their questions, so that you can evaluate whether those questions seem balanced and get the clearest sense possible of what the people taking the survey actually meant by their answers. Pretty much any data point is more useful in context. When looking at new data, it’s helpful to know whether it’s broadly in agreement with other polling, or whether it’s saying something new – or if there isn’t much else out there to compare it to. Just because a poll is an outlier, of course, doesn’t mean it’s necessarily wrong. But sometimes, the variation between polls can tell you something. For instance, if minor changes in wording produce very different reads on an issue, that’s probably a topic where public opinion isn’t very settled. While surveys can capture how voters are feeling at a given point in time, they can’t predict the future. This can pose a particular challenge in races like primary elections that often see multiple candidates, varied turnout and a lot of movement - see the Democratic primary in Michigan, where polls may have misread the composition of the electorate , and in Wisconsin, where polls also overstated the eventual support for the progressive candidate but accurately reflected that the race remained highly in flux. Polls also aren’t meant to be precision instruments, which means that in a tight race, they may not be able to reliably measure which candidate is ahead – merely that the race is close. But even in an election year, most surveys also ask questions beyond whom voters are planning to support. These questions can provide a sense of the dynamics behind the race: For instance, measuring anti-incumbent sentiments, highlighting voters’ ongoing concerns with cost of living, or tracking big partisan shifts . That’s often more illuminating than the horserace itself.

The critical Senate contests in both Maine and Michigan feature tight races with no clear leader, according to new CNN polls conducted by SSRS. But voters in the two states see their choices through two very different lenses. In Maine , the race centers more on likely voters’ broadly negative views of incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and President Donald Trump than on their impressions of the late-breaking Democratic nominee, Troy Jackson. Many voters are still getting to know Jackson after he replaced Graham Platner following allegations of sexual assault that Platner has denied. Michigan voters are more focused on the candidates’ issue positions amid an open-seat campaign featuring one of the most progressive Democratic candidates of this cycle in Abdul El-Sayed against former GOP congressman Mike Rogers. Fifty percent of voters say El-Sayed’s positions are too liberal, compared with 42% who say that Rogers is too conservative. Roughly two-thirds – including broad majorities of both candidates’ supporters – think El-Sayed would try to change things a lot in Washington, while just 20% say the same of Rogers. But both Collins and Rogers face political headwinds driven by economic concerns and negativity toward Trump. The people most likely to vote in each state say that they would prefer to see Democrats win control of the Senate after this fall’s midterm elections. Trump is deeply unpopular in both Maine and Michigan, with about two-thirds of voters in each state disapproving of his performance as president. The share of voters who say they are dissatisfied or angry with the way things are going in the country far outpaces the share who are satisfied or enthusiastic. The economy and cost of living is far and away the top issue in each state, and by a better than two-to-one margin, likely voters say they are worse off rather than better off compared with two years ago. Most also view the increased tariffs on Canadian goods with skepticism: less than 15% think the tariffs are a good thing and about two-thirds in each state – both of which border Canada – view the tariffs negatively. Even among likely voters, Democrats in both states are far more motivated to vote than their Republican counterparts, mirroring a trend seen nationwide in this year’s midterm polling. Among the most motivated voters, Democrats lead handily in both states. In Michigan, likely voters split about evenly between El-Sayed at 47% and Rogers at 44%, a margin that lands within the poll’s margin of sampling error. Rogers has broadly unified Republican likely voters in the state: 97% back him. Among Democrats, 90% support El-Sayed, while just 3% say they back Rogers. Independents break toward El-Sayed, 48% to 32%, with about one in five not supporting either candidate. About a quarter of Michigan likely voters overall haven’t yet firmly decided who they will support in the race for Senate. That number hits 40% among Black voters and voters younger than 35, and it stands at 36% among independents who are likely to vote. Most voters who have picked a side say their vote is more in favor of their chosen candidate than against his opponent, but there is more negative sentiment among Rogers’ backers. About 4 in 10 who support Rogers say their vote is against El-Sayed while 31% backing El-Sayed say their vote is an anti-Rogers one. Nearly half of Michigan likely voters say that the candidate’s positions on the issues are their top factor in deciding whom to support, while fewer, 31%, say that partisan control of the Senate is their top consideration and 22% cite the candidates’ character and experience. Although El-Sayed’s positions on Israel were a point of contention in the Democratic primary, a scant 3% of likely voters statewide say US policy toward Israel is the top issue in deciding their vote. Most, 54%, say the US is doing too much to help Israel. El-Sayed’s backing is strongest among younger voters. He carries a majority of likely voters younger than 45 while trailing among those 45 and older. He holds a 9-point lead among women while men split more evenly, 48% for Rogers to 44% for El-Sayed. White voters in the state break narrowly in Rogers’ favor, while Black voters broadly back El-Sayed, 77% to 10%, with about 14% opting for neither. El-Sayed’s primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, performed strongest in the August primary in counties with significant Black populations. The new poll suggests many Black voters haven’t yet formed opinions on El-Sayed: 66% say they have a favorable view, 2% an unfavorable one, and 32% aren’t sure yet. Roughly one in five say they don’t have an opinion of each candidate. El-Sayed’s favorability is an even split, 40% on each side. Views of Rogers break negative, 42% unfavorable to 35% favorable. In the race to replace Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, current Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson leads the Republican Rep. John James 50% to 41%. In Maine, 48% of likely voters are currently backing Jackson with 45% supporting Collins. That’s inside the survey’s margin of sampling error and a considerably tighter race than the state’s gubernatorial contest, where Democrat Hannah Pingree leads Republican Bobby Charles, 52% to 39%. Roughly 18% of likely voters say they could change their mind about whom they support for Senate, or that they haven’t yet picked a candidate. Jackson’s supporters stand out from other voters in either state polled for their close focus on the national implications of the race. A 53% majority say that party control of the Senate is the top consideration in their vote, and nearly half cite the state of US democracy as their top issue. Roughly 7 in 10 of Jackson’s backers say they’d be casting their ballot more out of opposition to Collins than support for him, while only a quarter of Collins backers are motivated by their opposition to Jackson. That may in part reflect Collins’ status as a better-known quantity. While likely voters’ impressions of both candidates are negative on balance, nearly a quarter don’t yet have an opinion of Jackson, while just 8% haven’t formed an opinion on Collins. And while Maine voters in both parties largely say they’re satisfied with their choice of candidates in the race, nearly 4 in 10 Democratic-aligned voters, compared with about a quarter of those who side with the GOP, say they’re unhappy. Maine voters are about equally likely to call Jackson too liberal and Collins too conservative – and most reject both characterizations. But Jackson is seen as relatively likely to shake things up in Washington, with 42% saying he’d try to change things a lot if elected, compared with just 14% who think Collins would do so if given another term. This is the first time Collins has stood for reelection since the Supreme Court overturned Roe vs. Wade, an outcome owing in part to her support for the confirmation of Justice Brett Kavanaugh. Four years later, almost two-thirds of Maine voters say they feel negatively about the 2022 Dobbs ruling, including about half saying it makes them feel angry. Those who remain angry are largely backing Jackson, while those who feel less strongly are largely behind Collins. The CNN polls of Maine and Michigan likely voters were conducted online and by phone August 31-September 6, 2026. Registered voters were randomly sampled from both registered voter lists and a probability-based panel. Results among likely voters include all registered voters in the poll weighted for their predicted likelihood of voting in this year’s election. Results among 880 likely voters in Maine have a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points; it is 4.1 points among the 843 likely voters in Michigan.

A suspected Iranian nuclear site buried under granite has seen a flurry of construction work this year as the war with the US has transpired, according to a group of analysts who reviewed six years of satellite imagery. The Pickaxe Mountain site, located near the Natanz nuclear complex roughly 140 miles south of Tehran, has been the subject of steady discussion by intelligence agencies which view it as a likely location for Iran to protect future nuclear program efforts. According to a new satellite imagery analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank, shared exclusively with CNN ahead of its publication , there has been “a clear surge in construction activity” this year. The underground facility is “likely” designed to be a safe haven for Iran’s nuclear program, according to the CSIS analysts. Israeli intelligence has suggested that Iran may be seeking to move centrifuges to the location as part of uranium enrichment efforts, and President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike the site. “We may hit Pickaxe very soon,” Trump told reporters last week, adding that “we know everybody that’s moving” at the site. The granite mountain, however, presents a difficult target to even the Pentagon’s “heaviest non-nuclear” bombs, the CSIS team reported. And It’s not the only Iranian nuclear facility feared to be out of reach for current-generation weapons. But there are signs the US is working to devise some means of striking those sites, even as US forces have largely focused on other types of targets during the six-month conflict with Iran. Four days before the US launched Operation Epic Fury, a program manager at an obscure Pentagon agency charged with combating weapons of mass destruction signed an emergency $1.2 million contract justification to repair a “unique subterranean test facility at White Sands Missile Range” in New Mexico for a “live-fire test designed to validate classified capabilities against rapidly emerging threats.” The document from the Defense Threat Reduction Agency was uploaded to a federal database on February 27 — the day before the war started. The memo said the “rapid test prep,” as another database labeled the contract awarded to Pate Construction, needed to be complete within two-to-three weeks due to “a time-sensitive national security directive.” The plans for the test were connected to the Iran war, three sources familiar with the matter told CNN, and the need to develop a way to target Iran’s deepest-buried underground facilities and, likely, simulate US strikes against specific nuclear facilities. The US previously struck nuclear sites in June 2025 as part of what the military called Operation Midnight Hammer. While the strikes successfully destroyed some key locations linked to Tehran’s nuclear program, a top US general told lawmakers last year that the deeply buried Isfahan nuclear site only had its entrances buried because the Pentagon believed its bunker-busting bombs — known as the Massive Ordnance Penetrator — could not knock it out. The military is working to develop a “next generation penetrator” bomb to succeed the current MOP and potentially hit targets even more deeply buried. A contract to begin work on a prototype was awarded in September 2025, and the Air Force solicited defense industry sources for the new weapon in June. Satellite imagery reviewed by CNN shows that between February 16 and February 18, excavation work began at a remote DTRA and US Strategic Command-operated site at White Sands intended to test the effects of weapons on deeply buried targets. The timing aligns with that of the emergency contract: Pate Construction provided an estimate for the test work on February 17 and received the deal the next day, according to federal contracting records. Work at the remote location, known as the Alternate Seismic Hardrock in Situ Test Site, continued into mid-March as a pile of excavation dirt gradually grew. The round of activity appeared to halt then, according to the imagery. Similar to Pickaxe Mountain, the DTRA test site in White Sands is also carved into granite, according to an environmental assessment . CNN could not independently verify whether the test occurred, nor could CNN confirm the purpose of the work at the DTRA test site observed via satellite imagery. The Pentagon did not immediately reply to questions from CNN. Pate Construction did not return calls from a CNN reporter. The US military maintains operational plans for strikes against Pickaxe, and it was part of a target package that was under consideration earlier this summer when Trump was threatening to escalate the conflict with Iran, according to a source familiar with the matter. The strike plan for Pickaxe involved using some of the largest bombs in the US arsenal, though it remains unclear if those munitions can penetrate deep enough underground to destroy whatever Iran may have moved there, the source added. Efforts to develop plans for decisive strikes against underground facilities continue; a source familiar with the matter told CNN that elements within the Defense Department recently held a “planning sprint” on the topic. The facility at Pickaxe Mountain is “likely” designed for one of three purposes, all related to Iran’s nuclear program, according to the CSIS analysis. It could be a centrifuge assembly facility, an enrichment facility, or a safe haven for other “nuclear weapons-relevant” work such as uranium metal conversion. In their report, the CSIS analysts argued the construction at the site “has shifted from active excavation toward probably internal construction and continued exterior reinforcement.” Pickaxe Mountain in 2026 has seen “more road activity” than ever before, and additional work has included “raising and hardening of the (tunnel) portal accesses, paving of the internal road network, reinforcement around access areas, and the flattening and removal” of dirt excavated while building its tunnels, the report said. The CSIS analysts cautioned that the “continuous construction” they’ve observed at Pickaxe Mountain, among other factors, suggests the site “is not yet capable of enrichment work, if that is the intended purpose.” CNN’s Tal Shalev contributed to this report. Republicans will gather in Dallas this week for a midterm convention that’s a version of the type normally held in presidential election years. President Donald Trump, party leaders, and battleground candidates comprise the 109 planned speakers who are there to set their agenda and rally voters, with the post-Labor Day sprint to Election Day underway. The program starts at 4 p.m. Eastern on Wednesday and Thursday. Here’s a look at some of the notable speakers and attendees. The midterms convention features speaking slots for a series of 2026 candidates from safe red seats to the most competitive battleground races. It’s a calculated risk for the battleground contenders, who could benefit from national exposure, presidential favor, and fundraising support, but risk alienating swing voters by appearing at what Republicans are calling a “Trump-a-palooza.” Among those banking on the upside of attending are Reps. Mike Lawler (NY-17), Derrick Van Orden (WI-03), Monica De La Cruz (TX-15), Ryan Mackenzie (PA-07) and Rob Bresnahan (PA-08). In addition, representing the Senate battlegrounds are five Republican candidates set for some of the most competitive, high-profile races of the fall – Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Georgia Rep. Mike Collins, former Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers, and former RNC Chair Michael Whatley in North Carolina. And speaking for the gubernatorial contingent are Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who is seeking an unprecedented fourth term, and Florida Rep. Byron Donalds, aiming to succeed outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis. “A lot of these races are going to be very, very tight as we’ve seen in midterm cycles past,” RNC national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre told CNN. “So, our goal is to remind voters who aren’t necessarily politically engaged all of the time that there is an election in November and it is critical for them to get out to vote.” A handful of House members facing tough reelection campaigns are skipping the convention, including Reps. Maria Elvira Salazar (FL-27), Tom Barrett (MI-07), Juan Ciscomani (AZ-06), Rep. Zach Nunn (IA-03), and David Valadao (CA-22). Rep. Tom Tiffany, the GOP nominee for Wisconsin governor, won’t attend either. And several of the party’s nominees in key Senate races are not speaking either. They include Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Dan Sullivan of Alaska, Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson, and former New Hampshire Sen. John E. Sununu, who represent the rest of the seriously contested map. One GOP source said the decision by the National Republican Congressional Committee to ask House lawmakers to pay at least $25,000 a ticket contributed to turnout in Dallas. “I do think it had an impact on member attendance for sure,” the GOP source said. “Obviously there are some members who are in tighter races who feel it’s probably more beneficial to be on the campaign trail.” A source familiar with the NRCC said the $25,000 price tag is lower than past conventions and is standard for committees to do at conventions. The source added that the committee has distributed all available tickets, which amounts to over 2,700. “House Republicans and our strong candidates in the most competitive battleground districts across the country are fired up to be in Dallas and take our message straight to voters and lay bare what’s at stake this November,” NRCC spokesman Mike Marinella said in a statement to CNN. Despite the expected absences from some candidates in key contests, Trump touted the convention on social media Tuesday night as “totally sold out.” “Everybody wants to be there, but we’re really asking only those Candidates that are in tight Races, a little up, a little down, or even, to speak. We want to save the ‘stage’ for them,” the president said. “We don’t need people who are up 45 points, and have been in office for 30 years, as much as we love them all! The convention itself is the product of Trump’s love for pageantry and spectacle. To fulfill his wish of staging a political convention this year, Republican leaders had to change party rules that previously only called for a convention during presidential election years. “It will be a RALLY like none other!” Trump posted on social media over the summer, announcing the plans. The president is poised to dominate the event. Trump will serve as both the keynote speaker on Wednesday night and the closing speaker on Thursday. Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, is slated for a prominent role as the keynote speaker on Thursday. Several other administration leaders are also set to speak, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz, and Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner. Attorney General Todd Blanche is also speaking, a notable appearance at a partisan event despite the traditionally nonpartisan disposition of his role leading the Justice Department. Finally, former press secretary Karoline Leavitt and Donald Trump Jr. round out the list of Trump representatives set to speak at the convention. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who has sometimes kept Trump at arm’s length, is conspicuously absent from the list of GOP congressional leaders set to speak, though he’s expected to attend and told the New York Post that he would give others “a turn in the spotlight” and help with fundraising. GOP House leadership including Speaker Mike Johnson, Majority Leader Steve Scalise, Majority Whip Tom Emmer, Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain, and National Republican Congressional Committee Chair Richard Hudson all have speaking slots. On the Senate side, Majority Whip John Barrasso and National Republican Senatorial Committee Chair Tim Scott are also set to speak. And attendees will hear from Gruters, the RNC chair, a pivotal organizer who spoke to the need to galvanize voters. “I think we’re on the cusp of defying history. You know, only four times in 150 years the incumbent party has been able to win these midterms,” he told Fox News this week. “It’s really going to give us a chance to tell the story to the American people directly on the message of everything that the president has done well.” A pair of Republican officeholders not on the ballot this year are also speaking at the convention. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz is set to address the home-state crowd as well as Pennsylvania Sen. David McCormick. CNN’s Annie Grayer contributed to this report.

President Donald Trump gave Natalie Harp and two other White House aides $45,000 each in cash gifts, according to financial disclosure statements. Harp, whose close relationship with Trump has come under intense scrutiny in recent weeks, and the other two female aides reported the money as a “cash gift for the holidays” in their annual executive branch disclosure forms released by the White House. Harp , and the other aides — Chamberlain Harris , deputy director of Oval Office operations and Margo Martin , a communications adviser — each make an annual salary of $150,000, according to publicly disclosed White House documents . The White House press office posted a statement about the president’s cash gifts to the three aides, saying, “The President has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector.” “The gifts at issue here have nothing to do with any of these individuals’ official government duties, and, therefore, are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards,” the statement said. John Ronquillo, an associate public policy professor at the University of Maryland, pointed to the amount of the cash gift — nearly one-third of the aides’ salary — as a point of concern. “It’s not a trivial amount and so that should raise red flags for a lot of people, you know, who are watchdogs, who are ethics experts in terms of why, why is this happening,” Ronquillo told CNN. Meanwhile, Richard Painter, a former White House ethics lawyer under former President George W. Bush, told CNN that Trump’s cash gift is “likely” an example of a government employee receiving extra income on top of their government salary, which federal law prohibits. “If someone is your employee and you would give them a gift, it is almost certainly not a gift. It’s income,” Painter said. He added: Trump’s “the president and they work for the United States government. They aren’t his … Fifth Avenue doorman. You … can’t give a gift there.” The spotlight intensified on Harp, a 35-year-old former far right TV anchor, after Sen. Jon Ossoff mentioned her by name in a now-viral speech attacking Trump. The Georgia Democrat swiped at the president’s “travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar,” a reference to her joining the president — along with a very limited group — when he secretly boarded a smaller aircraft to leave Turkey due to a threat from Iran in July. ‘My Guardian and Protector’: Natalie Harp letters express her devotion to Trump Harp, who frequently types the president’s Truth Social posts as he dictates them to her, has been intensely dedicated to Trump since joining his staff in 2022. She has trailed him across the country, feeding him positive stories, social media posts and other correspondence so frequently that allies dubbed her the “human printer.” The Washington Post first reported on the cash gifts. Walt Nauta, a longtime Trump aide, also received a “gift for holidays” from the president. He reported in his financial disclosure statement that the president gave him $20,000. Nauta was once charged in the case involving Trump’s handling of classified documents before the case was dropped. This story has been updated with additional information.

For a decade, President Donald Trump has made himself his party’s main character — a singular force around whom its rallies, conventions and political identity have revolved. Republicans are taking that devotion a step further this week, gathering in the Lone Star State at Trump’s behest for an unprecedented midterm convention conceived by him and to celebrate him. Trump will appear both nights of the event and watch from a suite as the loyalty from party leaders and allies is on display. But hanging over what may be the party’s most overt Trumpfest yet is an increasingly unavoidable reality: It could also be one of the last. In 55 days, voters will decide who controls Congress for the final two years of Trump’s presidency, with his unpopularity driving fierce headwinds against his party (and prompting some Republicans to skip the festivities in Dallas). Soon after, attention will inevitably begin shifting toward the Republicans jockeying to succeed him, while Trump faces for the first time a long countdown to leaving power. “It’s hard to imagine politics without him,” said Matt Schlapp, the chairman of the American Conservative Union. “But the reality is we’re going to have to figure that out.” GOP turns to Trump as Democrats expand their target map in midterm sprint Walking into almost any major conservative gathering over the past 10 years meant stepping into a world saturated with Donald Trump. His name, his red hats, his image — they’re everywhere. His supporters line up for pictures with impersonators with his recognizable hair, some flashing Trump-branded sneakers and watches. In 2021, a golden statue of Trump was wheeled into the Conservative Political Action Conference. Artist Jon McNaughton has built a following with surreal depictions of Trump — as Atlas carrying the world, as a boxer knocking out Joe Biden, as the fifth face on Mount Rushmore. His work has become popular with Trump supporters and even caught the president’s eye. Now, McNaughton is beginning to consider what it will mean to portray Trump not as the sitting president but as a historical figure. “For me, Trump will increasingly become an archetype in future paintings, much as I use Washington, Lincoln, Kennedy or Reagan to tell different parts of the American story,” McNaughton told CNN in an email. “Trump represents restoration and disruption — sometimes simultaneously. Viewers now and in the future can decide for themselves what those ideas mean.” Trump himself has shown signs of contemplating the ticking clock. He recently told New York Magazine that his building spree across Washington is motivated in part by a desire to leave a lasting mark on the capital because “nobody will do it once I’m gone.” At an event last month inside a General Motors testing facility, he imagined himself at home after leaving office, watching a successor take credit as manufacturing plants that broke ground during his presidency eventually come online. “Will you please remember that I did it?” Trump asked the crowd. His advisers have long understood that Trump will no longer be the center of his party’s attention as 2028 draws near. Trump has privately asked aides about how to navigate that period and avoid the pitfalls that accompany a lame-duck presidency, White House officials said. “It’s why he has been so singularly focused on his legacy,” one of the officials said. Not that anyone expects Trump to fade quietly from Republican politics. He is expected to play a decisive role in choosing his successor , whether that’s Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio or someone else. And a president who turned America’s 250th celebration into a standard Trump rally and conjured a midterm convention into existence could find plenty of other reasons to summon Republicans for another gathering before — or after — leaves office. Why Trump’s dream of an arch is his most revealing legacy play “If Trump is different than every president we’ve ever had, thinking he’ll be a regular ol’ lame duck is wishful thinking,” said Doug Heye, a veteran GOP strategist. Sean Spicer, Trump’s first White House press secretary, said he wouldn’t be surprised if Republicans continue to find ways to hold events for Trump to keep the base engaged. “No one can get crowds like Trump does,” Spicer said. “If you can get Trump to continue to do them, then that’s a huge thing.” But the political calendar will impose changes even Trump cannot prevent. After the midterms, Republicans who harbor presidential ambitions will begin maneuvering for position, forcing the party to contemplate the future of Trump’s movement and the GOP’s direction once he’s gone. The next Republican National Convention will be the first since 2012 at which someone other than Trump is expected to accept the party’s nomination. There have been glimpses of what that might look like. For the first time in a decade, Trump didn’t attend this year’s Conservative Political Action Conference , also held in Dallas. Schlapp, whose organization puts on CPAC, said Trump’s absence initially disappointed attendees, but it ultimately gave him insight into what conservative events and grassroots activism might look like when Trump is no longer president. “A lot of other dynamics were able to occur that weren’t able to when he’s there because he’s such a huge, dominating presence,” Schlapp said. In the meantime, Trump has framed the midterms as an ultimatum for Republican officials and voters: rally around his presidency, or watch Democrats destroy it. The first advertisements from his political operation feature him, “the toughest, most resilient person,” as a narrator puts it. No other Republicans are mentioned. He is expected to spend the next eight weeks touring the country, with 30-plus planned rallies in key battleground states and districts. MAGA inc., a Trump-aligned super PAC, had $400 million on hand last month, and the president made clear he will oversee how that money is spent. Earlier this month, the group disclosed it had purchased $10 million of advertising time in support of Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton. The approach will test whether Trump can convince the voters who have reliably supported him in his elections and embraced his transformation of the party will also show up for him when he’s not on the ballot. It’s a gamble that is not without risk as his popularity continues to stall. His job approval is at 35% – close to where it was at the same point in his first term and significantly lower than most presidents historically. Republican Party chairman Joe Gruters told CNN Trump “completely transformed what the Republican Party is” and regardless of the outcome in November, he expects Trump will be “front and center for a long time.” Whatever the polling suggests, Gruters argued his support from Republicans remains strong and they will be leaning into that in Dallas and all through the fall. “When you’re in the bottom of the ninth inning and runners are on base and you’re down, you want your best possible batter up,” Gruters said, “and for us that’s the president of the United States.” CNN’s Ariel Edwards-Levy contributed to this report.
